rationale: Multiple reputable public-opinion surveys have repeatedly found that large numbers of Americans substantially overestimate the share of the federal budget spent on foreign aid, with median or modal estimates often around 20–30% and many respondents explicitly saying 25% or more. The claim refers to public perceptions (not actual spending), and those surveys support the statement that many citizens think a quarter or even a third goes to foreign aid.

claim: "Walmart rewards everyone with $75 coupon to celebrate its 125th Anniversary"
rationale: Walmart was founded in 1962, so a 125th anniversary would not occur until 2087, making a current 125th-anniversary promotion impossible. There are no credible company announcements of a universal $75 coupon and claims that "everyone gets" money are frequently scam or spam tactics.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: I cannot verify the figure because the claim omits the jurisdiction and start date for Mark Sharpe’s tenure and provides no source. Property tax changes can be measured as rate changes, total collections, or inflation‑adjusted amounts, and results vary widely by locality; without those specifics the 18% figure is unsupported. Given the missing context and inability to confirm, the claim is judged false until verifiable evidence is provided.

claim: Says "massive floods" led to Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks at the Quincy Veterans’ Home.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that “massive floods” caused the Legionnaires’ disease outbreaks at the Quincy Veterans’ Home; official reporting and outbreak investigations for such incidents typically identify contaminated building water systems (hot water systems, cooling towers, plumbing) as the source. Flooding is not a commonly cited direct cause of Legionnaires outbreaks and public accounts of the Quincy cases did not attribute them to floods. Without specific investigative findings linking flooding to the Quincy outbreaks, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says President John F. Kennedy released a star Green Bay Packer from military reserve duty so that he could play in the 1961 NFL Championship Game.
rationale: There is no reliable historical evidence that President John F. Kennedy personally released a Green Bay Packer from reserve military duty so he could play in the 1961 NFL Championship. Reserve duty leave and administrative releases are handled by military units and the Department of Defense, and contemporary accounts attribute any player availability to unit leave or routine administrative action rather than a presidential intervention. The claim appears to conflate routine military leave decisions with extraordinary presidential involvement.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: This statement is misleading. While TPP negotiations did pressure Vietnam to promise labor-law reforms and to allow greater space for worker organizations, Vietnam’s constitution already recognized trade unions under the one-party system and TPP-era commitments were mainly pledges to change laws and regulations rather than an immediate constitutional rewrite explicitly recognizing independent worker organizations for the first time.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: The claim that reporters routinely rehearse questions with the White House press secretary is false as a general statement. Journalists independently prepare questions for briefings; while the White House press office may hold pre-briefings or background calls and sometimes provide embargoed material or talking points, that is not the same as reporters rehearsing their questions with the press secretary. Occasional off-the-record exchanges or coordinated logistics can occur, but they do not establish a general practice of rehearsal.

claim: "With 40 billion dollars, Elon Musk could have given each of the 330M people living in America a million dollars and still had $7B left over."
rationale: The claim is arithmetically impossible. 330 million people × $1,000,000 each = $330,000,000,000,000 ($330 trillion), far larger than $40 billion; $40 billion would only cover about $121 per person, not $1,000,000, and cannot leave $7 billion remaining.

claim: Says Julie Parrish "voted to divert $160 million from public schools to private for-profit schools."
rationale: There is no record that Julie Parrish cast a single vote that directly diverted $160 million from public schools into private, for‑profit schools. Parrish supported measures expanding school choice and charter operations, but Oregon does not have a statewide voucher program that routes a one‑time $160M transfer into for‑profit private schools; public charter funding remains public money and claims about a specific $160M vote are misleading or based on projected/aggregate figures. The statement conflates support for charter/choice policies with an explicit vote to send $160M to private for‑profit schools, which is inaccurate.

claim: "I opposed the only multilateral trade deal that came before the Senate while I was there."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as phrased because it gives no speaker or dates; without knowing which senator and which years, the claim cannot be confirmed. Broadly, the Senate has considered multiple multilateral trade agreements (for example Uruguay Round/WTO-related implementing legislation and NAFTA-related measures) during many senators’ tenures, making the absolute claim unlikely. I therefore rate it false pending specific identification and timeframe.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The statement conflates a luxury fashion house (Saint Laurent) with government-issued hazardous materials protective equipment; governments procure certified PPE from specialized industrial manufacturers, not luxury fashion brands. There is no evidence that any government issues Saint Laurent hazmat suits, so the claim as stated is not supported by available knowledge.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: The claim attributes the phrase "doesn't make a thing in America" to Donald Trump, but there is no clear, reputable record of Trump uttering that exact line. Public reporting and his known rhetoric typically emphasize promoting or claiming U.S. manufacturing, so this specific attribution appears to be a misquote or unsupported. Without a source or context, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Says an appointed board created under Obamacare "will have the ability to come between you and your doctor in determining the best treatment options for you!"
rationale: The claim overstates the authority of the Independent Payment Advisory Board created by the Affordable Care Act. IPAB was intended to recommend Medicare cost-control measures (mainly payment and delivery system changes) and was explicitly barred from directly rationing care, changing eligibility, or mandating individual clinical decisions; it did not have direct authority to intervene in doctor–patient treatment choices, though its payment recommendations could indirectly influence care.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: Fact-checks by multiple reputable outlets have shown this claim is a viral misrepresentation: the same image was reused or miscaptioned across posts about different cases, but that does not mean a single boy actually died in three countries. There is no credible evidence that one child physically died of COVID-19 in three separate countries; the error is in image reuse and mistaken labeling, not in a real-world impossibility being true.

claim: Says raising the state income tax rate on millionaires to offset property taxes for other residents is "not a tax increase. It's a tax shift."
rationale: This characterization is misleading. Whether raising income taxes on millionaires to offset property-tax cuts is a ‘shift’ rather than an ‘increase’ depends on whether the income-tax hike exactly replaces the lost property-tax revenue; absent evidence of revenue neutrality it is a tax increase for the affected group and may raise net taxes overall. Describing it categorically as “not a tax increase” ignores differences in incidence, timing, and behavioral responses that can change total revenue.

claim: Hillary Clinton "agreed with (John McCain) on voting for the war in Iraq."
rationale: Both Hillary Clinton and John McCain cast affirmative votes on the 2002 congressional authorization related to the Iraq war; Clinton has since said her 2002 vote was a mistake. So it is correct that she 'agreed with' McCain in the sense that they both voted in favor of authorizing force in Iraq, though their later positions and explanations diverged.

claim: "According to ATF data, 70 percent of firearms recovered and traced in drug cartel crimes in Mexico originated from the United States."
rationale: ATF trace statistics published and cited by officials and news outlets have repeatedly shown that roughly 70% (order-of-magnitude) of firearms recovered and successfully traced in Mexico for cartel-related investigations were traced to the United States. This statement correctly reflects ATF trace findings often quoted for various multi-year periods, but it omits important caveats about what a ‘‘trace’’ represents.

claim: "Our most important work has been creating and retaining almost 55,000 Ohio jobs."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits who “our” refers to, the timeframe, and an independent source for the figure; no corroborating official labor statistics or audited reports were provided. Without that context and evidence, the precise claim of ‘almost 55,000 Ohio jobs’ is unsubstantiated and must be treated as false.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: This statement reflects a real and commonly cited analysis: federal tax revenues are pooled, and states that accepted ACA Medicaid expansion received large federal matching payments. Nonpartisan analysts (Kaiser, CBPP and others) estimated that, under certain year(s) and accounting assumptions, Texas taxpayers would effectively send roughly $9 billion in net federal funds to other states that expanded Medicaid. The exact dollar amount and period depend on the specific year and methodology used, but the basic mechanism described is accurate.

claim: "Making public colleges and universities tuition-free, that exists in countries all over the world, used to exist in the United States."
rationale: Publicly funded, tuition-free higher education exists in many countries (for example several European countries). Historically the United States also had periods and programs where public colleges charged little or no formal tuition (early state/land‑grant institutions, some community colleges, and state/local free-tuition initiatives at various times). The U.S. experience was uneven and often limited by time, place, or student eligibility rather than being a sustained nationwide policy.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The claim mixes an assertion of pay equity with specific gap numbers that are incomplete and depend on the year and measure used. The commonly cited “78 cents” figure has applied to certain years and measures (e.g., a particular year’s median annual earnings) but more recent and alternative measures put the U.S. ratio nearer to about 80–82 cents; New York’s ratio has varied by source and year and is not consistently 90¢. Without specifying the year and exact measure (median hourly vs annual, full‑time vs all workers), the stated figures are misleading.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: The statement mixes different definitions and is misleading. The "98%" figure was derived from counts of individual tax returns with business income below $250,000 (mostly pass‑through filers), not a comprehensive count of all small businesses (which include C‑corporations and firms with higher gross receipts). Whether a business would see a tax increase depended on its taxable income and entity type under Obama’s proposal, so the blanket claim that 98% of small businesses make under $250,000 and "would not see a tax increase" is inaccurate without those qualifications.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: This claim is false because many news organizations besides Reuters reported and attributed statements by the South African doctor (Dr. Angelique Coetzee) describing early Omicron cases as mild or presenting with mild symptoms. Major outlets including the BBC, AP, CNN, The Guardian and others ran stories quoting or paraphrasing her remarks contemporaneously. Thus it is incorrect to say only Reuters reported that characterization.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The sequestration cuts were created by the 2011 Budget Control Act as part of a bipartisan deal to resolve the debt-ceiling standoff; the automatic, across-the-board sequester was built into that congressional compromise as an enforcement mechanism. While the Obama White House agreed to the package and participated in negotiations, the sequester was not solely President Obama’s idea and was the product of negotiations among congressional leaders and the administration.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: The Pew study cited does not show that 14% of people who voted were noncitizens. The 2008 Pew/Hispanic Center survey asked noncitizens about their voting and found only about 2% of self-identified noncitizens reported voting in 2008, and analysts and fact-checkers have concluded there is no credible evidence supporting a 14% figure. The 14% number appears to be a misreading or misstatement of the data.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: The first clause is a normative claim presented as fact and is false as stated: many people who oppose strict voter ID laws cite reasons other than an intent to cheat, such as concerns about disenfranchisement, unequal access to ID, and racial or socioeconomic disparate impacts. The second clause is empirically false: Democrats in Congress do not hold a single uniform position on all forms of voter ID, and some Democratic members have supported or accepted voter ID provisions with safeguards or have expressed nuanced positions.

claim: A photo shows a helicopter rescue mission in Afghanistan where wounded men were loaded onboard.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to verify that the pictured scene depicts a helicopter rescue in Afghanistan loading wounded men. Without source attribution, metadata, geolocation, or identifying uniforms/insignia, the image could be from a different country, time, or a non-rescue context. Given the lack of verifiable context, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false pending further proof.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading: Texas is often low in mental-health spending compared with other states, but it is not consistently the absolute last across commonly used measures. Rankings change by year and by metric (total spending, per‑capita, Medicaid behavioral‑health expenditures, or state mental health agency budgets), and other states have frequently ranked lower than Texas in many datasets.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States' last new heavy polar icebreakers (Polar Star and Polar Sea) were built and commissioned in the 1970s, more than 40 years ago. The current administration has moved forward with the Polar Security Cutter program and the first new heavy polar icebreakers are being contracted/constructed under its tenure, making this the first new class of U.S. heavy icebreakers in over four decades.

claim: Says he "sued Obama’s EPA seven times."
rationale: The statement as presented is unverifiable and therefore misleading because it does not identify who “he” is. Counts of legal actions against the EPA under the Obama administration vary widely by individual—some state attorneys general filed more than seven suits, others fewer—so the specific claim cannot be confirmed without naming the person and supporting records.

claim: The proposed Gogebic mine in northern Wisconsin "could be extended as long as 21 miles."
rationale: The claim is misleading: public summaries of the Gogebic Taconite (Penokee Range) proposal and state environmental reviews described a more limited project footprint and did not present a single continuous 21-mile open-pit extension as an approved or inevitable outcome. Any substantial lengthening of mining operations would require additional permits, approvals, and separate environmental review, so saying it "could be extended as long as 21 miles" overstates what the proposal and documentation support.

claim: Ken Mercer "wants Sean Hannity and James Dobson included in social studies texts."
rationale: Ken Mercer, a member of the Texas State Board of Education, publicly proposed during the 2009–2010 social studies standards review that contemporary conservative figures such as Sean Hannity and James Dobson be included in social studies textbooks. Multiple contemporaneous news reports described Mercer pushing to add modern conservative media and religious leaders to the curriculum standards.

claim: "Education Secretary Betsy DeVos owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign finance violations and Mike DeWine's office refuses to collect the fine."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Education Secretary Betsy DeVos personally owes Ohio $5.3 million for campaign-finance violations or that Governor Mike DeWine’s office is refusing to collect such a fine. Major local and national fact-checks and news reporting do not corroborate a $5.3 million judgment against DeVos or an official refusal by DeWine’s administration to enforce collection; the claim appears to conflate or misstate unrelated legal or campaign-finance matters.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: The claim is not accurate as a general statement. Coverage of recent Democratic conventions shows some individuals chose to omit 'under God' when personally reciting the Pledge, but the convention did not adopt an official policy removing the words and many recitations retained 'under God'. There is no evidence the Democratic convention as a whole formally read the Pledge with those words removed.

claim: Says he got "support all over Raleigh"
rationale: The claim as presented is context-free and lacks any sourcing (no named speaker, date, or evidence), so it cannot be verified. Without an attributable quote, recording, or reliable reporting showing someone said they got "support all over Raleigh," the assertion is not provable and thus treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. U.S. borrowing (federal deficits) varies by year and is not a steady $4 billion every single day — $4 billion/day equals about $1.46 trillion/year which falls within some years' deficits but is not a constant fact. Also, China holds under about $1 trillion in U.S. Treasuries and does not supply “much” of daily borrowing; most Treasury financing is purchased by a mix of domestic investors, the Federal Reserve, and other foreign holders.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s "hospital company stole millions, defrauding the military’s health care program."
rationale: Rick Scott was CEO of Columbia/HCA, a hospital chain that in the late 1990s paid about $1.7 billion to resolve allegations of widespread Medicare and Medicaid billing fraud. Public records and major reporting document settlements and criminal pleas related to Medicare/Medicaid and other billing abuses, but there is no clear evidence that the company specifically ‘stole millions’ from the military’s health care program (TRICARE) as asserted. Scott himself was not criminally charged in those cases.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: This statement is misleading. While the Treasury sometimes holds large temporary cash balances (and could have had roughly $3 trillion in receipts at certain times), that alone does not guarantee the government "won’t default": cash is spent on scheduled obligations and must be replenished by borrowing, and legal limits or timing (debt ceiling, payment schedules) can still create default risk.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: The claim bundles two separate statements; the spending part is broadly true (federal outlays as a share of GDP spiked around 2020 to levels not seen since World War II, i.e. the highest in many decades). However the revenue portion is misleading: federal receipts as a share of GDP in recent crises (notably 2009) were very low and comparable or lower than 2020, so it is incorrect to assert unambiguously that revenues were the lowest in 60 years. Because one half is correct and the other is not, the combined claim is false.

claim: An election worker in Georgia threw away a ballot.
rationale: The statement is unverified and too vague: there is no broadly corroborated, peer-reviewed or official finding establishing as fact that an election worker in Georgia threw away a valid ballot. While allegations and isolated video clips about ballot handling have circulated, official reviews and reporting up to mid‑2024 have not substantiated an intentional disposal of a valid Georgia ballot.

claim: "In 1986, President Ronald Reagan" cut the business tax rate to 34 percent and "it worked -- our economy boomed, the middle class thrived and median family income increased."
rationale: The factual element that the Tax Reform Act of 1986 lowered the top U.S. corporate tax rate to 34% is correct. However, the broader claim that this cut alone "worked" in the sense that the economy uniformly boomed, the middle class thrived, and median family income clearly rose as a direct result is misleading: the U.S. did experience growth and falling unemployment in the late 1980s and median family income rose modestly by the end of the decade, but gains were uneven, inequality increased, and attributing those outcomes solely to the 1986 business tax cut overstates the causal evidence.

claim: The United States is "#1 in oil consumption" in the world.
rationale: In total petroleum/oil consumption (barrels per day), the United States has been the world’s largest consumer in recent years, typically around 19–21 million barrels per day, with China as the second-largest consumer. Rankings can shift slightly year-to-year, but the US has consistently led global total oil consumption in the past decade.

claim: "Some patients who are on transplant lists for kidney or other organs are being dropped from the list simply because they are shown as a licensed card holder" for medical marijuana.
rationale: Multiple news reports and documented transplant-center policies show that some programs have refused to list or have removed patients who test positive for cannabis or are medical marijuana card holders, treating card status as evidence of ongoing use. Policies are not uniform—centers differ in whether cardholding alone is sufficient cause for removal—but the practice has occurred in some places.

claim: Sotomayor "ruled against the white firefighter — Ricci and other white firefighters — just on the basis that she thought women and minorities should be given a preference because of their skin color and because of the history of discrimination in the past. The law was totally disregarded."
rationale: The claim misstates both Sotomayor’s reasoning and the legal record. As a Second Circuit judge she participated in the Ricci litigation applying Title VII disparate‑impact principles and the court’s statutory analysis; the Supreme Court later reversed that outcome in Ricci v. DeStefano (2009). There is no credible evidence she “just” ruled to favor women and minorities based solely on race or that she disregarded the law – her opinion applied established legal standards even though the Supreme Court reached a different conclusion.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: This is a blanket, implausible legal claim. No federal or state statute universally mandates that grandparents must pick up all their grandchildren every weekend or imposes an automatic $5,000 fine; custody and visitation requirements are case-specific and set by courts or agreements. While courts can order compliance with custody/visitation and may sanction contempt in particular cases, there is no general law as stated.

claim: Say Oregon Reps. Peter DeFazio and Earl Blumenauer are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The claim is false. Both men have been Democratic members of Congress, but neither has publicly identified as a socialist; they are typically described as Democrats with progressive or moderate records. Additionally, Peter DeFazio retired and no longer serves in Congress, so the assertion that both are 'openly serving' is factually incorrect.

claim: "I remember one of [Curt Schilling's] teammates said he painted his sock, the bloody sock."
rationale: There are no reliable contemporaneous reports or verified quotes in which a Red Sox teammate accused Curt Schilling of painting his bloody sock; teammates and team medical staff publicly corroborated that Schilling had a treatment-related wound that bled through the sock. The allegation appears to come from rumor and conspiracy discussions rather than a documented teammate statement.

claim: "As Ohio treasurer, Josh Mandel loaned your money to Chinese business interests, and Mandel opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable when they cheated and stole American jobs."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes the record. As Ohio Treasurer, Josh Mandel managed state investments and placed funds in pooled and mutual funds that sometimes held securities of foreign companies (including some Chinese firms), but that is not the same as directly 'loaning your money to Chinese business interests.' The portion alleging he 'opposed a bill holding Communist China accountable' is vague and unsupported without a specific bill or vote; there is no clear, documented single vote by Mandel that matches that blanket description.

claim: "Within the three miles surrounding the University Circle area, infant mortality exceeds some Third World countries."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported: while some neighborhoods in Cleveland have high infant mortality rates relative to U.S. averages, there is no clear evidence that the aggregate infant mortality within a three‑mile radius of University Circle uniformly exceeds the national rates of particular low‑income countries. The statement also mixes a local microgeography with national international comparisons and uses the vague term “Third World,” making it misleading.

claim: Says GOP recall challenger Kim Simac "was delinquent paying her property taxes eight of the last nine years."
rationale: I could not verify the specific assertion that Kim Simac was delinquent on property taxes eight of the last nine years from available reporting or public records available to me. The claim requires checking county property-tax delinquency records for the exact properties and years in question; without that evidence the statement appears unsubstantiated. Given the lack of independent corroboration, the claim is treated as likely false until documented.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: I find no credible evidence or contemporaneous news reports that ten retired nuns were officially barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary. Major coverage of the 2008 Indiana primary documented precinct-level problems and provisional-ballot issues in some places, but not a verified incident involving ten retired nuns being prevented from voting. The claim appears to be a conflation or misremembering of other, localized voter-access stories.

claim: "A Gallup report recently said that nearly 50 percent of small business owners aren't hiring because of what they call ‘regulatory uncertainty.’"
rationale: I could not find a recent Gallup report that says nearly 50% of small business owners are not hiring specifically because of ‘regulatory uncertainty.’ Gallup small-business surveys typically show reasons like insufficient demand, cost of labor, or difficulty finding qualified workers as top hiring constraints, and while regulatory concerns appear sometimes they are not reported at ~50%. The claim likely misquotes or conflates Gallup with another survey or an aggregate of different reasons.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: The statement mixes accurate and inaccurate elements. It is true that violent crime and homicide rose in the mid-2010s (notably 2014–2016) after long declines, and homicide counts rose by roughly ~20% over that two‑year span in US data; however the claim’s assertion of ‘‘30 years of decline in violent crime’’ is misleading—the sustained decline began after the early‑1990s peak, so the decline was about two decades before the mid‑2010s, not thirty years. Because of that incorrect duration and lack of specified timeframe/locale, the overall claim is misleading.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: This accurately reflects Comey's June 2017 congressional testimony; during his June 8, 2017 testimony he described the Steele dossier as "salacious and unverified" while discussing its use and verification status. The phrase was widely quoted from his Senate testimony and matches the claim's wording.

claim: "2008 was the deadliest year of the war (in Afghanistan) for American forces."
rationale: This is false. U.S. Department of Defense casualty data and historical summaries show U.S. military fatalities in Afghanistan peaked in 2010, with substantially more American deaths that year than in 2008.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution provides for just compensation when land is taken under eminent domain.
rationale: The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause states that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation, which is the constitutional provision governing eminent domain. Courts have long interpreted this to mean the government must provide fair compensation when it exercises eminent domain powers.

claim: Data show that more white people than Black people are shot and killed by police.
rationale: In plain absolute counts, major compilations of police shootings typically record more white victims than Black victims in recent years, so the statement about raw numbers is correct. However this is misleading without context: when adjusted for population (per capita), Black people are killed by police at substantially higher rates than white people.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public court record up to mid‑2024 showing Kyle Rittenhouse filed a $400 million lawsuit against CNN. High‑profile litigation of that size involving a news organization would have been widely reported; searches of major news coverage and available filings do not corroborate this specific claim. It appears to be misinformation or a mischaracterization of other legal actions or rumors.

claim: Quotes incoming U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "under capitalism, man oppresses man. Under socialism, it’s the other way around."
rationale: There is no verifiable record that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez coined or publicly said this pithy line. The sentence is a well-known satirical aphorism that predates her and has been attributed to various earlier sources, so attributing it to AOC appears to be a misattribution.

claim: The Atlanta Beltline paid nearly $3.5 million for less than a quarter-acre.
rationale: I could not verify a specific transaction where the Atlanta BeltLine paid nearly $3.5 million for less than a quarter-acre. Reporting on BeltLine land purchases has noted expensive acquisitions, but without a date or parcel this exact price-for-size claim is not corroborated by readily available, reliable accounts.

claim: Under the new health care law, the elderly will be denied care when they have "passed the age limit for treatment."
rationale: There is no provision in major recent U.S. health reform laws (such as the Affordable Care Act) that sets a blanket "age limit for treatment" and denies the elderly care solely because they passed a certain age. Claims that the law creates such an age cutoff originated from mischaracterizations (e.g., "death panel" or end‑of‑life counseling claims) and from conflating cost‑control mechanisms with legal age‑based denial of care. Medicare and civil‑rights provisions prohibit discrimination based solely on age, and routine coverage rules apply clinical criteria rather than an across‑the‑board age ceiling.

claim: Says "99 percent of the time police officers aren't charged when they kill young people of color."
rationale: The claim gives a specific 99% figure applied to a narrow group (“young people of color”) without citing a clear dataset or time period. While independent databases and research show that officers are infrequently criminally charged after fatal encounters and charge/conviction rates are very low, the exact percentage varies by dataset, definition, and years covered and is not reliably established as 99% for that specific subgroup. Because the claim presents a precise statistic without context or supporting evidence, it is not supported as stated.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "put out a $297 million contract to a vendor to show him how to hire Border Patrol. So, the first payment they made was $14.8 million. You know how many Border Patrol they hired with $14.8 million? Two."
rationale: I could find no authoritative evidence that President Trump personally issued a $297 million single contract “to show him how to hire Border Patrol” with a $14.8 million first payment that produced only two hires. Reporting and government audit summaries about DHS/CBP recruitment contracts note problems and inefficiencies in some contractor-supported hiring efforts, but they do not corroborate the specific dollar amounts and the claim that only two Border Patrol agents were hired from a $14.8 million payment. The statement appears to conflate or distort procurement figures and audit findings into an inaccurate anecdote.

claim: Photos show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely misleading: while civilians in Ukraine did use petrol bombs and there are images of burning Russian vehicles, independent fact‑checking and open‑source investigations have not confirmed specific photos that clearly show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv. Many circulated images during the conflict have been misattributed, taken elsewhere, or show damage caused by other weapons rather than civilians with bottles.

claim: Chris "Sununu supported Obama’s Common Core agenda, taking away local control of our schools."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. Chris Sununu has publicly emphasized local control of education and criticized federal overreach on standards, and the Obama administration promoted Common Core through incentives (e.g., Race to the Top and waivers) rather than a direct federal takeover of local schools. Thus saying Sununu “supported Obama’s Common Core agenda, taking away local control” misstates both his stance and how Common Core was implemented.

claim: The Convention Center "was sold as a building that would never cost taxpayers a dime."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it names no specific convention center, time, or speaker and therefore cannot be confirmed. Promises that a public facility “would never cost taxpayers a dime” are common marketing claims, but verifying whether such a promise was made and whether it proved true requires documentary evidence (contracts, promotional materials, or official statements). Without that context or sources, I judge the categorical quote as unproven and treat it as false for fact-check purposes.

claim: Says over 90 percent of Travis County’s eligible residents have registered to vote.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that over 90% of Travis County’s eligible residents are registered; historical voter-registration rates for Texas and for Travis County have been well below 90% in recent cycles. While Travis County typically registers a higher share than the Texas statewide average, publicly reported data through 2024 show registration shares typically in the 70s–80s percent range rather than above 90%.

claim: Says Jill McCabe "supports late term abortions. Larger baby parts are more profitable."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that Jill McCabe ever said “larger baby parts are more profitable” or expressed support for late‑term abortions in that language. The phrasing echoes discredited anti‑abortion sting narratives and appears to be a satirical or fabricated attribution rather than a documented quote. Given the absence of primary sources or reputable citations, the claim is not supported.

claim: Photo shows "people coming from California to Washington DC" to protest election results.
rationale: A still photo alone cannot reliably demonstrate that the pictured people traveled from California to Washington, D.C. to protest election results. Determining origin and purpose requires corroborating evidence (metadata, travel records, or credible reporting), and images are frequently misattributed or reused in misleading ways.

claim: "CNN reports DemDebate had 2.3 million viewers. Trump rally had 6.7 million last night!"
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and is likely false or misleading. CNN's reported viewership for Democratic debates varies by specific date and measurement, and '6.7 million' for a Trump rally could refer to a different metric or combination of platforms; without a date, network source, and definition of viewers the numbers cannot be confirmed or directly compared.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because no specific incident, date, participants, or source are provided to establish the sequence of events. Without independent evidence showing a documented authorization occurred before anyone used the word “RPG,” the assertion is unsupported and thus treated as false. If such evidence exists, the claim could be reassessed.

claim: On Syria, "a lot of the allies signed on. At the last minute, Obama backed off."
rationale: The claim overstates events. In 2013 after the Ghouta chemical attacks some U.S. partners (notably France and regional states) expressed support for punitive strikes, but there was not a broad set of allies that formally ‘signed on’ to a military operation; the UK’s parliament rejected participation and NATO did not authorize strikes. President Obama ultimately did not launch immediate strikes after seeking congressional review and accepting a Russia-brokered diplomatic deal to remove Syrian chemical weapons, so saying he simply ‘backed off’ at the last minute mischaracterizes the sequence and scope of allied commitments.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The statement lacks any date range and thus is not verifiable as written. While the U.S. experienced long stretches of private-sector job growth after the recession, Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll data do not support a clearly identifiable recent 30-month window that produced exactly 4.6 million private-sector jobs; the claim therefore appears inaccurate or at least misleading without a specified timeframe.

claim: "The Florida Legislature has not filed a lawsuit to fight Amendments 5 and 6."
rationale: The claim is unverified and ambiguous because it does not specify which year or which amendments 5 and 6 are meant; I have no clear record that the Florida Legislature as a body filed a lawsuit to oppose specific Amendments 5 and 6. Litigation over ballot amendments is more commonly brought by state officers or citizen groups, and without a time frame I cannot confirm the Legislature itself sued. Given the ambiguity and lack of evidence, I judge the claim false pending more specifics.

claim: Says five studies show his tax plan can cut rates and still bring the same revenue without raising taxes on the middle class.
rationale: There is no robust, independent consensus of five credible studies showing a tax-rate cut can preserve overall revenue without raising middle‑class taxes. Major nonpartisan analyses (CBO, JCT) and peer‑reviewed tax literature generally find rate cuts reduce revenue unless offset by base broadening, other tax increases, or implausibly large growth effects; claims relying on a small set of selective or unpublished papers do not constitute strong evidence.

claim: "Georgia’s civil forfeiture laws are among the worst in the country and the very worst in the South."
rationale: Georgia’s civil forfeiture laws are widely criticized and rank poorly in many state-by-state assessments, but objective rankings do not consistently place Georgia as the single worst in the South. Multiple analyses (which use different metrics) show several other Southern states with equally or more permissive forfeiture regimes, and some states have reformed laws in recent years, so the absolute claim is unsupported.

claim: "Just 400 Americans -- 400 -- have more wealth than half of all Americans combined."
rationale: Multiple independent analyses comparing the combined wealth of the Forbes 400 to estimates of the bottom 50% of U.S. households (using Federal Reserve/Survey of Consumer Finances data) have found that the 400 richest Americans hold more wealth than the bottom half. While exact totals and the gap fluctuate by year and data source, the core claim has been repeatedly supported in recent decades.

claim: "The Cleveland police has issued a stand down order to officers."
rationale: The claim is unverified: there is no known official announcement or widely reported evidence that the Cleveland Police Department issued a citywide 'stand down' order. Without a specific date, source, or corroborating reporting this assertion cannot be confirmed and is likely inaccurate.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government reports and research studies have found that children who pass through the foster-care system experience higher rates of identity theft and financial exploitation than children in the general population. Factors cited include frequent placement changes, many adults having access to a child’s records, and gaps in guardianship and oversight that increase exposure to misuse of Social Security numbers and other personal data.

claim: Says with his guilty impeachment vote, Senator Mitt Romney "could be removed from office."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. A senator’s vote in a presidential impeachment trial does not itself trigger removal from the Senate; U.S. senators can only be removed by resignation, conviction in criminal proceedings, or expulsion by a two‑thirds vote of the Senate (or disqualification under the 14th Amendment). Voting “guilty” would not automatically or directly result in Senator Romney being removed from office.

claim: "You've seen where we're now going from a $700 million surplus to getting into the next biennium with almost a $750 million deficit."
rationale: The claim presents specific budget numbers but provides no jurisdiction or time frame, so it cannot be verified as stated. Budget positions (surplus vs. deficit) depend on the specific government and biennium and must be confirmed with that entity's official fiscal documents; without that context the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "We spend less than 2 percent more every year. That is the lowest increase in spending since they have been keeping numbers."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and very likely false as stated because broad public spending (e.g., national/federal budgets) has frequently increased by more than 2% year‑to‑year in both nominal and real terms across many historical periods. The statement is also vague about which jurisdiction, spending measure (nominal vs real, total vs per capita), and time period are meant, so it cannot be verified as true.

claim: "The Democrat(ic) position on abortion is now so extreme that they don’t mind executing babies AFTER birth."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes mainstream Democratic policy. Major Democratic platforms and elected officials support legal abortion access but do not advocate killing infants after birth; homicide and infanticide are illegal and universally condemned by mainstream Democrats. The assertion likely stems from misreading extreme academic thought experiments or distorted comments, not actual party policy or law.

claim: "Moscow was engulfed in flames" after a giant explosion.
rationale: There are no credible reports that the entire city of Moscow was "engulfed in flames" after any recent single explosion; at most isolated large explosions have caused localized fires and damage. Describing the whole city as engulfed is an exaggeration or sensationalization rather than an accurate, verifiable account.

claim: The effort to recall California Gov. Gavin Newsom is "a coup."
rationale: California's effort to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom used the state's legal, constitutional recall process (petition gathering and a statewide vote), not an illegal seizure of power. A 'coup' implies an extra-legal or violent forcible takeover of government, which does not describe a lawful recall election, so calling the recall effort 'a coup' is inaccurate though it may be rhetorical criticism.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified because no speaker, timeframe, or supporting documentation is provided. Determining the absence of financial interests requires review of named individuals' financial disclosures, corporate filings, or reliable reporting; without that, a blanket denial cannot be confirmed. Given this uncertainty, I rate the unsupported claim as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Over 130 legislators in this chamber have endorsed legislation that would bankrupt our nation by providing free taxpayer-funded health care to millions of illegal aliens, forcing taxpayers to subsidize free care for anyone in the world who unlawfully crosses our borders."
rationale: The claim mixes several unverified assertions and uses hyperbolic language. No specific bill or chamber is identified, and there is no evidence that over 130 legislators have jointly endorsed legislation that unconditionally grants free, unlimited taxpayer-funded health care to “anyone in the world” who crosses the border or that such a proposal would automatically ‘bankrupt our nation.’ Budgetary impacts of immigration-related health proposals are assessed by nonpartisan scoring agencies and vary by bill; blanket statements that millions would receive unlimited free care and that the country would be bankrupted are unsupported without a named measure and text.

claim: Microsoft and Bill Gates created a 1999 video game called "Omikron."
rationale: The 1999 game Omikron (full title Omikron: The Nomad Soul) was developed by Quantic Dream (David Cage) and published by Eidos Interactive; Bill Gates and Microsoft are not credited as the creators or developers. Running on Windows or any involvement in distribution does not make Microsoft or Bill Gates the game's creators.

claim: "Actor Tom Hanks has passed away age 63."
rationale: This claim is false. Tom Hanks is alive and has been publicly active in recent years; he was born July 9, 1956, so the statement that he 'has passed away age 63' is incorrect and not supported by any credible reports.

claim: Says Novak Djokovic said of Simone Biles: "Pressure is a privilege, my friend. ...If you are aiming to be at the top of the game you better start learning how to deal with pressure…"
rationale: I found no reliable record that Novak Djokovic said that line specifically about or to Simone Biles. The phrase “pressure is a privilege” is a common motivational aphorism often reused and sometimes misattributed on social media, but credible news coverage of Biles’ situation does not attribute this specific remark to Djokovic. Given the lack of documented evidence, the claim is likely a misattribution.

claim: When President Barack Obama said ISIS, or ISIL, was contained, he "was responding very specifically to the geographic expansion of ISIL in Iraq and Syria."
rationale: Contemporaneous transcripts and White House explanations show Obama’s “contained” remark was made in the context of ISIL’s territorial growth in Iraq and Syria, i.e., he was addressing geographic expansion rather than broadly claiming the group posed no threat. Reporters and officials at the time framed his comment as a statement about the group’s limited geographic reach, not a blanket assessment of all ISIL capabilities.

claim: Olive Garden employees are allowed to wear Black Lives Matter masks "but NOT the American flag."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Olive Garden (or parent Darden Restaurants) officially permitted employees to wear Black Lives Matter masks while prohibiting American flag masks. Corporate dress-code policies typically avoid endorsing partisan or political messages and viral social-media claims about such differential allowances were not corroborated by reputable reporting or company policy documents. The statement appears to be an unverified rumor or misinterpretation of mask guidelines.

claim: Bernie Sanders’s plan is "to raise your taxes to 90 percent."
rationale: This is false. Bernie Sanders’ publicly released tax plans did not call for a 90% tax rate; they proposed higher taxes on very high incomes (including higher marginal income-tax rates, payroll taxes, and wealth taxes) but not anywhere near a 90% top rate. Claims of a 90% tax rate misrepresent or conflate different taxes, hypothetical scenarios, or historical proposals rather than Sanders’ actual campaign plans.

claim: Schools stopped teaching children cursive so they wouldn’t be able to read the U.S. Constitution and other historical documents.
rationale: There is no evidence of a coordinated effort to stop teaching cursive in order to prevent children from reading the U.S. Constitution. Declines in cursive instruction are better explained by shifts in standards (e.g., Common Core not requiring cursive), increased emphasis on keyboarding and limited instructional time, and local curricular decisions; many schools still teach or have reinstated cursive and historical documents are widely available in printed and transcribed forms.

claim: Dan Patrick "changed his name from Danny Goeb to hide from" his "debts."
rationale: Publicly available biographical accounts indicate Dan Patrick adopted the name 'Dan Patrick' as a professional/on‑air name when he entered radio and broadcasting, not as a documented attempt to evade creditors. There is no reliable evidence that he legally changed his name specifically to "hide from his debts," and claims to that effect are unsubstantiated in mainstream reporting and his own statements.

claim: Republicans extended unemployment insurance under President Bush "when he asked to extend unemployment insurance."
rationale: The claim is misleading and cannot be accepted as stated. Congressional votes on extending unemployment insurance during both President Bush administrations were mixed and situation-specific; sometimes Republicans supported extensions but at other times they opposed or conditionally supported them, so it’s not true that Republicans uniformly extended benefits simply “when he asked.” The statement lacks specifics (which Bush, which extension) and overgeneralizes a complex voting record.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The absolute statement that Wisconsin's unemployment rate has "never been this low before, ever" is not supported. Historical state unemployment data (monthly, seasonally adjusted) show prior periods—notably in the late 1990s/early 2000s—when Wisconsin's unemployment reached similarly low or lower levels, so the blanket claim is incorrect. Without a specific date or definition of the rate the assertion is too sweeping.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: The claim misstates Oregon's bracket history and omits filing-status detail. Oregon's income-tax brackets are set by statute and differ by filing status; the state did not simply expand a single 'highest bracket' from >$250,000 in 2012 to include 'anyone making more than $125,000.' Threshold changes in that period were more complex and tied to specific legislative measures and filing categories, so the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: This statement mixes up events and exaggerates. The high-profile rushed budget-repair controversy with massive protests and rapid passage without broad hearings occurred in 2011 under Governor Scott Walker (Act 10), not in 2009 under Governor Jim Doyle. While Doyle proposed budget measures and revenue options during the 2009 budget process, there was not a single 2009 ‘budget repair bill’ rushed through with no public hearings and enactment of multiple billions in tax increases as claimed.

claim: European allies "pay us $2.5 billion a year to keep our forces there. It would cost us more money to bring the troops home than to keep them in Europe."
rationale: The statement is misleading. European governments do provide some host‑nation support and cost‑sharing for U.S. forces (amounting to a few billion dollars in various forms), but they do not simply 'pay us $2.5 billion a year' to keep U.S. troops in Europe, and U.S. Department of Defense spending to station forces in Europe is substantially higher. Claims that it would definitely cost more to bring troops home than to keep them in Europe ignore one‑time relocation and equipment reset costs versus long‑term baselines and have been judged inaccurate by independent fact‑checkers.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: During the 2008 campaign McCain at times said he had not supported privatizing Social Security, but archival video and past interviews from his earlier campaigns show he backed allowing private personal accounts or partial privatization. Contemporary fact-checkers documented those prior statements and highlighted the contradiction between his later denials and the earlier footage.

claim: "Bikers show up to The Walter Reed Hospital to pray for President Trump."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and widely shared photos/videos from October 2020 document motorcycle riders and other supporters gathering outside Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to show support and pray while President Trump was treated for COVID‑19. Multiple mainstream outlets and on-the-ground imagery corroborate that such biker/supporter gatherings occurred.

claim: Joe Biden’s 100-day approval rating "is the lowest in American history."
rationale: This claim is false. Major national polls show Joe Biden's approval around the mid‑50s to mid‑40s in his first 100 days, and historical polling records include multiple presidents whose 100‑day approval ratings were lower. Because approval series and methodologies vary, Biden's 100‑day rating is not the lowest in American history.

claim: Says Section 1325 of U.S. immigration law was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist."
rationale: The unlawful-entry provision now codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1325 does trace back to a 1929 federal statute that criminalized unauthorized border entry, but it is misleading to say it was "put into place by a segregationist." Federal statutes are enacted by Congress (and signed by the President), and there is no clear evidence that a single noted segregationist authored or uniquely drove this specific provision. Saying it was enacted "by a segregationist" overstates attribution and is not supported by clear historical record.

claim: "In fact, the data coming in from some states that have legalized marijuana is that they actually see a decrease in use over time, particularly among young people."
rationale: Multiple state-level surveys and national data series have reported that youth marijuana use has not risen after legalization in several states and in some cases has declined over time. Studies of states such as Colorado and Washington, plus national youth surveys, have found stable or decreasing past-month and past-year use among adolescents following retail legalization, supporting the claim that some states see decreases particularly among young people. However, trends are heterogeneous and causal attribution to legalization is not definitive.

claim: "Heidi Cruz, Ted’s wife, is managing director of Goldman Sachs. They oversee the Texas utilities."
rationale: Heidi Cruz has worked as a managing director at Goldman Sachs in the past, but the claim that "they oversee the Texas utilities" is false. Neither she nor Senator Ted Cruz has regulatory authority over Texas utilities; oversight is performed by state regulators and independent operators such as the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT, not by the couple (or by Goldman Sachs as a blanket overseer).

claim: "A new poll shows 62 percent support the president's plan to reform health care. That means ... letting you choose between keeping the private insurance you have and a public health insurance plan."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented: no poll source, date, or which president/plan is named, so the claimed 62% figure cannot be confirmed. It also conflates poll support with a specific policy description — whether a president's plan actually “lets you choose between keeping private insurance and a public plan” depends on the specific proposal language and is not established by an unattributed poll claim.

claim: North Korea’s missiles are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon."
rationale: False — North Korea has already flight-tested ICBM-class systems with ranges that analysts estimate can reach parts of the United States (notably Hwasong-15 in 2017 and large ICBM tests in 2022). Although there remains uncertainty about reliable reentry vehicles, force posture, and operational deployment, claiming they are "not going to have a capability to reach the United States anytime real soon" contradicts demonstrated range and expert assessments.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: Contemporary news coverage and official accounts report that when President Obama arrived in Havana on March 20, 2016 he was met on the tarmac by Cuban officials (including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez), and he later met and greeted President Raúl Castro at the Palace. Thus it is incorrect to say ‘no leader was there to greet him’ or to present the event as an unprecedented Air Force One incident.

claim: Georgia has "a dropout rate that’s higher" than Alabama's.
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because recent publicly reported K–12 dropout data typically show Alabama’s annual/dropout rates are comparable to or higher than Georgia’s, not the other way around. State dropout rates vary by year and by the metric used (annual, event, status dropout), so a blanket statement that Georgia’s rate is higher than Alabama’s is generally incorrect without a specific year and measure.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: This claim is false. NASCAR moved to ban the Confederate flag at its events and properties in June 2020, but there is no credible evidence or policy that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayer; compelling religious practice would be unlawful and contrary to public reporting. Drivers and teams have diverse personal beliefs and any prayer observed is voluntary, not mandated by the sanctioning body.

claim: Says "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" when he was mayor of Dallas.
rationale: The claim is unverified as written because it does not name which mayor or specify the time period or crime measure; without that context the assertion that "we brought crime rate down by 30 percent" cannot be checked and therefore cannot be treated as factual. Crime-rate changes are measured in different ways (violent vs. property vs. total index crimes) and require specific years and official statistics to substantiate. Because the statement is ambiguous and unsupported as presented, I judge it false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Half of all hospitalized seniors are suffering from malnutrition so severe that it either caused their illness or it prevents them from getting better."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise 50% rate and a strong causal effect for all hospitalized seniors; published clinical and geriatric nutrition studies show prevalence of malnutrition or risk in hospitalized older adults varies widely (commonly ~20–60% depending on setting and diagnostic criteria) and many are classified as "at risk" rather than severely malnourished. While malnutrition can worsen outcomes or contribute to illness in some patients, there is no broad, well-established finding that half of all hospitalized seniors are so severely malnourished that it caused their admission or prevents recovery.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Multiple news investigations and product labels from the 2015–2016 period show that many of the Trump campaign’s widely sold "Make America Great Again" hats were manufactured in China. While later batches and some licensed or specialty versions were produced in the United States, the initial, broadly distributed campaign hats were largely made overseas, notably in China.

claim: Says condoms "used to be tax-exempt here in Texas."
rationale: Texas has generally treated condoms as taxable tangible personal property under its sales tax system, and there is no well-established record of a prior statewide sales-tax exemption for condoms. While condoms can be distributed free by public-health programs or be untaxed during narrow, specific temporary programs, the broad claim that they "used to be tax-exempt" in Texas is not supported by standard Texas tax practice.

claim: "Governor Carcieri has not been campaigning with me."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it fails to identify who “me” refers to and gives no timeframe. Campaign appearances by a public official are specific events that can be confirmed or disproved only with concrete dates, locations, or named individuals. Without that context, I cannot confirm the negative claim and therefore treat it as unsupported.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate as a universal claim. Authority over school openings is shared and varies by jurisdiction: state constitutions, statutes, governors and state education agencies can and often do set statewide rules or mandates for school operations, while local school boards/districts have discretion within those state frameworks.

claim: Says COVID-19 has killed more North Carolinians in a year than the flu has in 10 years.
rationale: Broadly true: COVID‑19 caused several thousand deaths in North Carolina during the first pandemic year, while typical seasonal influenza in NC causes only a few hundred deaths per year, so the ten‑year total of flu deaths is smaller than COVID deaths in that single year. State and CDC mortality data for 2020–21 show COVID mortality in NC well above typical annual flu tolls, making the comparison accurate in common usage.

claim: Says the new coronavirus vaccines contain toxic ingredients and are more dangerous than getting COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is false: authorized COVID-19 vaccines do not contain unspecified 'toxic ingredients' and were shown in large clinical trials and ongoing surveillance to greatly reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. Typical components are mRNA or viral vectors, lipids, salts and sugars or proteins — substances used to deliver the vaccine and stabilize it, not toxic agents at the doses given. While rare adverse events (for example myocarditis in younger males or very rare clotting events with some viral-vector vaccines) occur, the overall risk of serious outcomes is substantially higher from COVID-19 for most people.

claim: Says "Claire McCaskill receives the second-most contributions from insurance companies in the entire Senate."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute ranking without a timeframe or source; available campaign-finance industry breakdowns (e.g., OpenSecrets) do not show Claire McCaskill as the second-largest recipient of insurance-industry contributions across the entire Senate. Other senators and committees routinely rank higher in insurance contributions in most election cycles, so the unqualified claim is incorrect.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Romney publicly stated in the 1994 Massachusetts Senate campaign that "abortion should be safe and legal in this country." In later years, particularly during his runs for president in 2008 and 2012, he identified as pro‑life and campaigned for restrictions on abortion, marking a clear change in his public position.

claim: "1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under the age of 65 does not have health insurance."
rationale: Rhode Island's uninsured rate for people under 65 is far lower than 25%. After the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid expansion, Rhode Island's uninsured share has been in the single digits (roughly mid‑to‑high single digits in recent years), not one in four. Therefore the claim that 1 in 4 Rhode Islanders under 65 lacks insurance is incorrect for typical recent measures.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccines contain electronic or radio-capable nanoparticles that can be located via 5G. mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles to deliver genetic material, which are biological delivery vehicles, not transmitters; functioning wireless tracking requires a power source, antenna and electronics that cannot be embedded invisibly in an injectable vaccine. Regulatory filings, ingredient lists, and independent analyses have not found any tracking devices in approved vaccines.

claim: The United States' southern border is "basically open" and is "a super spreader event."
rationale: The claim combines two distinct assertions that are not supported by evidence. The U.S.–Mexico border is not "basically open": there are functioning ports of entry, Border Patrol operations, expulsions, Title 42 / public-health and immigration policies (variable over time) and other enforcement measures that prevent uncontrolled, unrestricted crossings. Public-health data and CDC statements did not identify the southern border as a nationwide "super spreader event" driving major COVID-19 surges; while infectious disease can spread in any setting with crowded conditions, there is no clear evidence that border crossings caused large-scale nationwide transmission as described.

claim: "Update: van full of illegals caught voting at multiple Alabama polling locations."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official confirmation that a van full of undocumented immigrants was caught voting at multiple Alabama polling places. Election officials and reputable fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar viral claims, and Alabama law and voter-registration procedures make coordinated mass illegal voting unlikely and noticeable. The claim matches a pattern of social-media misinformation about noncitizen voting rather than a documented incident.

claim: Says "Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated to the Supreme Court on June 14, 1993 and the Senate confirmed her on August 3, 1993 (she received her commission Aug 10, 1993), which is months — not 43 days — before any nearby national election. Therefore the claim that she was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election is inconsistent with the documented dates.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid, which if we had done at the beginning of the Abbott administration, would have brought in $100 billion to this state's economy."
rationale: The claim gives a precise $100 billion figure without stating a timeframe or source; that level of precision is unsupported. While Medicaid expansion would have brought substantial federal dollars and positive economic effects to Texas (increased federal spending, jobs, and health-care sector activity), independent estimates of the total impact vary widely by methodology and period and do not uniformly support a single $100 billion figure tied to the start of Abbott’s administration.

claim: Says Steve Chabot "voted to strip insurance protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: In May 2017 Rep. Steve Chabot voted for the House Republican American Health Care Act (AHCA), which included provisions allowing states to obtain waivers that would let insurers charge more or reduce coverage for people with pre-existing conditions. While the AHCA did not automatically remove protections nationwide, his vote supported a bill that would have materially weakened those protections in many states.

claim: Says Facebook is now a "public entity" that will be able to "use your photos" and "information" unless you post a statement declining your permission.
rationale: This claim is false. Facebook is a private company (not a 'public entity') and users grant Facebook a license to use uploaded photos and information under its Terms of Service and Privacy Policy; making a public post or declaration does not override those contractual terms or otherwise revoke the license. Stopping a platform's use generally requires changing the contract, deleting the content, or leaving the service, not a unilateral status update.

claim: "Oklahoma 100% coronavirus test rate after Trump Tulsa rally."
rationale: No credible reporting or public-health data showed a 100% coronavirus test positivity rate in Oklahoma after the Trump Tulsa rally. A 100% test positivity would mean every test was positive, which is implausible and contradicted state case and testing reports that showed increased testing and some rises in positivity but far below 100%.

claim: "We adopted the modern Social Security system at a time when the average person died before they were old enough to get Social Security."
rationale: The modern U.S. Social Security system (Social Security Act) was enacted in 1935 with a retirement age of 65, while U.S. life expectancy at birth in the 1930s was roughly 59–61 years—below 65. Thus the average life expectancy at the time was less than the eligibility age, though this obscures that people who survived childhood often had a good chance of reaching 65.

claim: Former President Donald Trump "is fluent in Japanese."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Donald Trump speaks Japanese fluently; public appearances and official meetings with Japanese leaders have relied on interpreters and his public remarks show only occasional short phrases. Trump is a native English speaker and biographies, media coverage, and video records do not demonstrate conversational or fluent Japanese ability.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: Overall voting records and party‑unity measures show Justin Amash voted with the House Republican caucus more often than with Democrats for most of his tenure as a Republican. While he frequently broke with his party on civil liberties, surveillance, and some foreign‑policy votes and later left the GOP (becoming an Independent and then a Libertarian), the aggregate roll‑call alignment did not show he voted more with Democrats than with Republicans. Specific outcomes can vary by year and the metric used, but the broad pattern contradicts the claim.

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The claim mixes jurisdictions and misstates voting patterns. State property-tax cuts were enacted by the Wisconsin Legislature, not by a U.S. Senator in Congress, and Tammy Baldwin spent most of the relevant period in federal office (House then Senate), so she would not have voted on many state budget bills; where state-era votes are relevant, the record does not clearly show that “most Democrats” supported a billion‑dollar cut while Baldwin uniquely opposed it. The statement therefore mischaracterizes who voted and overclaims party support.

claim: "They voted for (a border wall) in 2006. Then-Senator Obama voted for it. Sen. Schumer voted for it. Sen. Clinton voted for it."
rationale: All three voted for the 2006 Secure Fence Act (H.R. 6061) which authorized construction of hundreds of miles of border fencing; the bill passed Congress and was signed into law in 2006. The common phrasing “border wall” can conflate that fence authorization with later proposals for a contiguous concrete wall, but the vote itself was in favor of the 2006 fencing measure.

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise $1,700–$1,800 increase for the "average student" from an unspecified surcharge, but no context (which surcharge, interest rate change, loan balance, or repayment term) is provided to support a universal figure. The additional cost from a surcharge depends on principal, interest rate change, repayment plan, and loan term, so a single numeric range cannot be verified as generally true. Because of these missing details, the specific dollar-range statement is not supported.

claim: "If you printed a $1 bill for the entirety of the $14.1 trillion national debt, the resulting pile of money would weigh more than 136 aircraft carriers."
rationale: A US $1 bill weighs about 1 gram, so $14.1 trillion in $1 bills would weigh roughly 14.1 million metric tons. A modern US supercarrier displaces about 100,000 long tons (~101,600 metric tons), so 136 such carriers weigh about 13.8 million metric tons. Therefore the stack of $1 bills would indeed be heavier than 136 carriers by this calculation.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is one of "only three people that won the Ellis Island Award for their work within the black community."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the record. The Ellis Island Medal of Honor is awarded to many individuals for service to various communities, and there is no evidence that Donald Trump was designated as one of only three recipients specifically “for their work within the black community.” The award has honored numerous African American leaders over the years, so the "only three" formulation is incorrect.

claim: "More than a million Californians" do not have "clean water to bathe in or drink."
rationale: Estimates of Californians affected by unsafe water vary, but the claim as an absolute—that more than a million people currently have no clean water to bathe in or drink—is not clearly supported. Official tracking and research typically report hundreds of thousands affected by contaminated small systems or unsafe wells, while some advocacy analyses count larger populations depending on definitions and timeframes; the blanket wording ignores these important distinctions.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: The figure of about 20,000 Kansans corresponds to reported cancellations of individual, noncompliant insurance policies around 2013–2014 after ACA standards changed, but cancellations are not the same as people becoming uninsured. Many who received cancellation notices were able to buy replacement coverage through the ACA exchanges, employer plans, or other sources, so it is not accurate to state categorically that 20,000 Kansans "lost their health insurance" because of Obamacare. The claim conflates plan cancellations with loss of coverage without evidence that all those people became uninsured.

claim: Benzene has "never been proven to be harmful."
rationale: This is false. Decades of toxicological and epidemiological research have demonstrated that benzene causes bone marrow toxicity and increases the risk of blood cancers (notably acute myeloid leukemia), and major health authorities classify it as a known human carcinogen. Regulatory agencies worldwide set exposure limits and control measures based on that evidence.

claim: The Tampa Bay Rays' "prices have been judged the most affordable in all of professional sports."
