claim: "You may not have stayed in a hotel in the past year, but illegals arriving since Biden’s inauguration, they get to stay free of charge."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While some migrants have been temporarily housed in hotels paid for by federal, state, or local governments or contractors in specific places and periods since 2021, it is not true that all or even most undocumented arrivals since Biden’s inauguration universally “get to stay free of charge.” Many are processed, released with alternatives, detained when eligible, or assisted through other shelter programs; hotel use has been limited, local, and time‑bound.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: A 59% unemployment rate for African-American youths is not supported by standard labor statistics. BLS youth unemployment series (commonly 16–19 or 16–24 age groups) have shown much lower peaks in recent decades (typically in the 20–40% range for teenagers, and lower for broader youth groups), and no nationwide, recent official series reports a 59% rate. The claim appears to conflate different measures or lacks timeframe/age-group context.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "himself has granted waivers allowing into the United States refugees who provided material support to terrorists."
rationale: False. While U.S. immigration law permits narrow, case-by-case waivers for certain inadmissibility grounds (including some limited or coerced instances of 'material support'), there is no evidence President Obama personally granted waivers to admit refugees who provided material support to terrorists. Fact-checkers and public records show waivers were rare, handled through agencies, and not used to admit known terrorists.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: The Keystone XL was designed to transport Canadian crude oil to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries and terminals and would have supplied oil to American refineries and markets. Although some of the crude arriving at Gulf terminals could be exported, it is incorrect to assert the pipeline would deliver no oil 'for America.'

claim: "Health care premiums up 90 percent in New Hampshire."
rationale: The claim is presented without a timeframe or plan type and is therefore unsupported as a general statement about New Hampshire health care premiums. Available historical data and reporting on both ACA marketplace and employer-sponsored premiums show increases over years but not a uniform 90% statewide jump; isolated plans or a single insurer could see very large year-to-year rate changes, but that is not the same as overall premiums rising 90%. Without a specified period, population, or data source the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "$1.8 billion Of Soros’ money just intercepted – he could officially go to prison for years"
rationale: There are no credible reports or public records showing that $1.8 billion of George Soros's funds were seized or that he faces imprisonment; such an event would be major international news. The claim appears to be a viral misinformation item with no supporting evidence from reputable news outlets or official legal filings.

claim: "Two-thirds of our economy is a consumer economy."
rationale: In the United States, personal consumption expenditures typically account for roughly two-thirds of GDP (commonly in the mid-60s percent range), so describing the economy as a "consumer economy" at two-thirds is a reasonable approximation. Exact percentage varies by year and the specific GDP measure used, but the general claim is accurate for recent U.S. data.

claim: Says Tennessee has some of the lowest beer excise tax rates in the country.
rationale: This is likely false — Tennessee is not typically ranked among the very lowest beer excise tax states. Several states have historically had substantially lower per‑gallon beer excise taxes, and Tennessee's rate more often appears in the middle or higher end of state rankings. I could not verify a current official ranking at the moment, so I am cautious.

claim: Says there are thousands of registered voters over 110 years old in North Carolina, including one who is 219 years old.
rationale: This claim is not supported by credible evidence. Voter files occasionally show implausible ages because of data-entry mistakes or default/placeholder birth years, but audits and longevity records do not support thousands of genuine registered voters over 110 in North Carolina, and a claimed age of 219 is biologically impossible and far beyond the validated human lifespan (~122 years).

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: The claim is misleading. New York City’s mayor does have substantial authority over the NYC Department of Education and school operations, but that authority is constrained by state education law, the governor’s emergency powers, public‑health orders, and collective‑bargaining and safety requirements; those other legal constraints can prevent or condition reopening, but it is inaccurate to say the mayor categorically “can’t open” schools under the law. Whether the mayor can reopen on a given date depends on specific state or public‑health orders and the legal landscape at that time.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The claim provides no specific date, location details, or identifying information about the alleged 'raid' or 'seizure,' so it cannot be verified as stated. Without named agencies, timestamps, or corroborating reports, there is no basis to assert both that a raid occurred 'just five days ago' and that there was 'no news coverage.' Local and national outlets typically report border seizures, so the blanket claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted for regime change with respect to Libya."
rationale: This claim is misleading. In 2011 the U.S. took part in a NATO/UN-authorized operation in Libya framed as civilian protection under UN Resolution 1973; Sanders supported limited measures tied to that mission but there was no explicit congressional authorization vote to enact "regime change," and Sanders has said he opposed a policy of regime change. Saying he "voted for regime change" overstates what his votes and public statements authorized or endorsed.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: It is true that some buyers of Trump‑branded condominium projects (including in Florida) lost sizeable deposits when developers collapsed or projects were canceled, but there is no credible evidence that Donald Trump personally “pocketed” those funds and walked away. Most Trump‑branded projects were developed by third parties under licensing or joint‑venture arrangements, and reporting and legal records attribute lost deposits to developers, bankruptcies, or escrow/contractual arrangements rather than to Trump taking the money for himself.

claim: "Corrupt political bosses. Money laundering. Fraud. It’s just another day at the office for Vin Gopal."
rationale: The claim accuses Vin Gopal of routine corruption, money laundering, and fraud, but there are no public indictments, convictions, or credible reports as of June 2024 that substantiate those specific criminal allegations. Making blanket criminal accusations without documented legal findings is unsupported. Unless reliable evidence (charges or convictions) is produced, the assertion is false.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
rationale: Beto O'Rourke did publicly call for President Trump’s impeachment, but he was not uniquely the only candidate for the U.S. Senate to do so. Multiple other Senate candidates and sitting members of Congress publicly advocated for or supported impeachment during the same period, so the exclusivity claim is incorrect.

claim: Says the Obama administration plans to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration planned to ban all weapons for U.S. citizens through international treaties. The administration participated in negotiating the UN Arms Trade Treaty, which regulates international transfers of conventional arms and does not prohibit domestic civilian firearm ownership; furthermore treaties require Senate ratification and cannot unilaterally outlaw domestic gun ownership.

claim: "New Jersey has the largest transit system in the entire country."
rationale: The claim is false. The New York Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) operates the largest transit network in the U.S. by ridership and system size; New Jersey Transit is a large statewide agency but does not exceed the MTA and ranks below the largest metropolitan systems on common metrics.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: There is no verifiable record that Patrick Rose cast a floor vote specifically 'to explore a state income tax.' Public legislative records and contemporaneous reporting from his tenure do not show an explicit vote authorizing a state income tax study; accusations of this nature typically conflate votes on budget, tax policy study resolutions, or committee work with an endorsement of creating an income tax. Thus the claim as stated is misleading.

claim: The Obama administration is using as its "legal justification for these airstrikes (on the Islamic State), an authorization for military force that the president himself has called for repeal of."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and administration legal guidance show the Obama administration relied principally on the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) as part of its legal justification for strikes against ISIS. President Obama had previously and publicly called for Congress to repeal or replace the 2001 AUMF and to update the statutory authorizations for force, creating the apparent inconsistency described in the claim.

claim: "Bill Nelson actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times."
rationale: There is no authoritative, time-bounded roll-call record that corroborates the specific claim that Bill Nelson “actually voted in favor of higher taxes 272 times.” Partisan tallies that produce such large totals use varying and expansive counting rules (counting procedural motions, amendments, or votes that merely affected revenue estimates) and do not match independent roll-call databases when clearly specified. Without a named source, timeframe, and methodology the precise figure is unsupported and likely misleading.

claim: Protest vandalism in Richmond "all started two weeks ago when Mayor Stoney’s police gassed - tear gassed - a peaceful crowd of protesters, moms and children, at 7:30 p.m. sharp."
rationale: The claim mixes a kernel of truth with inaccurate and unproven specifics. While local reporting from Richmond around the George Floyd protests did document law enforcement using chemical agents on crowds, multiple agencies were involved and reports do not substantiate the precise claim that ‘Mayor Stoney’s police’ alone tear-gassed a crowd of ‘moms and children’ exactly at 7:30 p.m. or that all subsequent vandalism ‘started’ from that single event. The causal and time-specific assertions are not supported by authoritative sources.

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: There is no evidence that any city named Richmond built a $14 million stadium for an NFL franchise, and it is implausible: NFL teams’ stadium projects cost hundreds of millions and are rarely described as a $14M build by a city. Also Richmond (e.g., Richmond, VA) is not home to an NFL team, and publicly funded NFL stadium subsidies historically far exceed $14M. Given those facts, the claim is false or at least misleading without further context.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: The claim lacks any verifiable context (who “I” is, what location “here” refers to, and the time period covered), so it cannot be confirmed. Without supporting evidence such as attendance records, timestamps, or corroborating witnesses, the statement is unverified and thus judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: The claim is false: Joe Biden has not resigned and Nancy Pelosi has not been detained. Both would be major, widely reported developments and there are no credible official or mainstream news reports confirming either event. Therefore the statement is incorrect.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks a specific vote; there is no reliable record that Rep. Kurt Schrader voted for a measure that cut Medicare by $500 billion. Schrader is a Democratic member of Congress and has not been documented as supporting major GOP budget plans that would enact a $500B Medicare cut, so the statement appears to misattribute or exaggerate a vote. Without a named bill or roll-call, the charge cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Joe Biden canceled the Keystone pipeline because Warren Buffett "donated $58 million" to his campaign.
rationale: This claim is false. President Biden revoked the Keystone XL permit citing climate and environmental review considerations, and there is no credible evidence that Warren Buffett donated $58 million to Biden’s campaign or that any such donation motivated the decision. Public campaign finance records and reporting do not show a $58 million donation from Buffett to Biden, and no documentary evidence links Buffett payments to the pipeline cancellation.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. Sanctioning a central bank can severely damage a country’s external payments, access to reserves, and trade (hurting growth, causing inflation and shortages), but historically Iranian central-bank and banking sanctions have imposed heavy costs without literally “shutting down” the entire economy. Iran has continued domestic economic activity and found alternative channels (barter, non‑SWIFT routes, third‑country intermediaries, trading partners) and humanitarian trade is often exempted, so a central-bank sanction alone does not guarantee a total economic shutdown.

claim: "We cut taxes for 95 percent of working families."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it lacks any reference to which law, time period, or country it describes. Effects of tax changes vary by the specific legislation, income levels, family size, and whether cuts are temporary or permanent; prior U.S. tax bills have produced widely different estimates and never universally benefitted 95% of all working families on a sustained basis. Without those specifics the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Delaware has the "eighth-largest black population in the country"
rationale: The claim is false as stated for absolute numbers: Delaware is a relatively small state by total population, so its Black population in absolute terms is far smaller than in many larger states (e.g., Texas, Florida, Georgia, New York, California, North Carolina, Illinois, Maryland). That list shows Delaware is not eighth-largest by Black population.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: The statement that there are “600-plus” police and fire pension funds Downstate is consistent with reported counts of Illinois municipal police and firefighter pension funds outside Chicago, and state audits and news reporting show many of those small local funds are underfunded and face revenue shortfalls. Saying they are “on the cusp of insolvency” is a bit interpretive, but many of these funds lack stable revenue sources (relying on limited local property taxes and employer contributions) and have raised warnings about insolvency risk.

claim: "The State of Texas is funding … women’s health services at historically high levels; they just increased their level another $50 million for the next two years."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not corroborated by clear, specific budget language—Texas appropriations must be tied to named programs or line items, and there is no widely reported, single statewide announcement that Texas increased all “women’s health services” funding by $50 million for the next two years. Without identification of the exact program(s), timeframe, or legislative appropriation, the statement is unsubstantiated. Given the lack of clear supporting evidence, the claim is rated false.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: I cannot find a verifiable attribution for this exact quote to a known political figure or a reliable transcript. While politicians have expressed similar sentiments about religion and candidate selection, the precise wording as presented is not documented in major speech records or reputable quote databases. Because the speaker and sourcing are missing, the claim as stated is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "This idea that it's the pandemic of the unvaccinated, it's just a total lie."
rationale: The claim is false because extensive public-health data and peer-reviewed studies show that unvaccinated people have had substantially higher per-capita risks of infection-related severe illness, hospitalization, and death compared with vaccinated people. Breakthrough infections and shifts in case proportions (especially with immune-evasive variants or high vaccination coverage) do occur, but they do not negate the consistent finding that vaccination markedly reduced severe COVID-19 outcomes for most of the pandemic period.

claim: Says his budget provides "the highest state funding level in history" for education.
rationale: The statement as presented is too vague to verify and is therefore judged false under the instruction to prefer false when uncertain. Whether a budget is “the highest state funding level in history” depends on which state, which fiscal year, whether totals are nominal or inflation-adjusted, and whether one‑time federal transfers are included; absent those specifics the claim cannot be confirmed. Historical comparisons often flip when adjusted for inflation or excluding temporary federal funds.

claim: "The total (state) payroll has gone down. The total amount of the number of workers in the state has gone down. I like the fact that the bulk of that is just by retirements."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not specify which state or the time period, and I cannot confirm aggregate payroll or headcount declines or that retirements were the primary cause without official payroll/HR data. State payroll and worker counts vary widely by jurisdiction and year, and attributing most of any decline to retirements requires evidence (e.g., retirement filings, separation reasons) that is not provided. Without those specifics, the claim is unsupported.

claim: A letter from BP to the Minerals Management Service "actually recommends improvements and specific recommendations around safety regulations should they choose to change them."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim as stated — there is no readily available, corroborated public record or reliable reporting that a BP letter to the Minerals Management Service contained the quoted wording or explicitly 'recommends improvements and specific recommendations around safety regulations should they choose to change them.' Corporations sometimes submit comments or proposals to regulators, but this particular assertion lacks a cited source and therefore cannot be confirmed as fact.

claim: Says of El Paso that some years, "in a city of almost 700,000, we had five murders the entire year. Our average over the last 10 years is 18 (murders per year). We exceeded that average just on one day" after a gunman opened fire at a Walmart in the city.
rationale: This statement reflects widely reported facts after the August 2019 El Paso Walmart shooting: El Paso is a city of roughly 680–700k and historically has had very low annual homicide counts (some years had as few as five homicides). The mass shooter killed 22 people, which exceeded the city’s roughly decade-long annual average in the mid-teens to high-teens (about 18) in a single day. The quote is a reasonable summary of those facts by local officials.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation is a charity where President and Secretary Clinton and their daughter, they take no salary, they get no money from it, they take no personal benefit from it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. Public nonprofit tax filings and contemporary reporting show Chelsea Clinton was paid by the Clinton Foundation in a leadership role, and the Foundation frequently paid for Bill Clinton’s travel, security and related expenses; those are forms of compensation or personal benefit. While Hillary Clinton did not draw a Foundation salary during her time as Secretary of State and Bill’s paid speeches were separate from the Foundation, the blanket statement that the family received no money or personal benefit is false.

claim: "Border agents discover body of 6-year-old girl: 'She was raped By 30 men'."
rationale: No credible news outlets or official law‑enforcement agencies reported a case in which border agents found the body of a 6‑year‑old who had been raped by 30 men. The claim mirrors recurring sensational social‑media fabrications that include implausible numeric details and lack verifiable sources or corroborating official statements.

claim: Says images show migrants on trains and buses heading toward the United States, not walking.
rationale: The claim is unverified and context‑dependent: photographs of people on trains or buses do not by themselves prove they are migrants ‘heading toward the United States’ rather than traveling within another country or for another purpose. Without image metadata, corroborating reporting, or geolocation, the direction and intent of travel cannot be established. Many viral images are miscaptioned or lack provenance, so the assertion as stated is not supported.

claim: "There's nothing in the voting instructions that we've been getting in the last several elections that lets you know" about the limitations of the master lever.
rationale: The claim is overly absolute and not supported by general practice: jurisdictions that use a master (straight‑ticket) lever commonly include information or sample‑ballot instructions describing how it works and its limitations, and election boards have issued guidance in recent elections. While wording and prominence vary by place and year, it is incorrect to assert there was "nothing" in the voting instructions over the last several elections.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot verify the precise claim that 87% of participants in a 2,000-household, year-long Portland composting pilot reported being satisfied. While Portland has run multi-thousand-household curbside/composting pilots and city summaries have reported generally high satisfaction, I could not confirm the exact 87% figure from authoritative program reports. Because the specific percentage is unverified, I flag the claim as false until a primary source is provided.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is, which state, or when he served as governor. Without a named individual and timeframe, I cannot check records or public statements to confirm that he took credit for reining in state spending. Because the necessary identifying details are missing, the claim cannot be substantiated and is treated as false.

claim: "Under Gov. Kasich, Ohio wages have increased by $10.3 billion."
rationale: The $10.3 billion figure corresponds to the measured rise in Ohio’s aggregate payroll wages reported by federal/state labor data during Kasich’s time in office (the figure cited in multiple public fact-checks). The statement is accurate as an aggregate, nominal increase in total wages, but it omits context about timing, inflation adjustment and per-worker or median wage changes.

claim: "Jim Renacci cheated on his income taxes" and is a "deadbeat citizen."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record that Jim Renacci was convicted of tax fraud or legally proven to have "cheated" on his income taxes; allegations or reporting of unpaid or disputed tax liabilities are not the same as proven tax evasion. Calling him a "deadbeat citizen" is a pejorative judgment that depends on context and evidence (e.g., court judgments or tax liens) which are not established as proving criminal wrongdoing in this claim.

claim: "I have spent virtually every weekend since Memorial Day in the Panhandle."
rationale: This is a first‑person claim about private travel that cannot be independently verified from the statement alone. The claim gives no dates, no corroborating evidence, and 'Panhandle' and 'since Memorial Day' are ambiguous, so it is unsubstantiated rather than confirmed. Because of the lack of verifiable evidence, I judge the claim false for fact‑checking purposes.

claim: Blue Cross headquarters has "a $30,000 granite table."
rationale: I found no authoritative, corroborated evidence that any Blue Cross corporate headquarters contains specifically “a $30,000 granite table.” While media reports sometimes note expensive furnishings in insurers’ offices, the specific dollar-value table claim appears anecdotal and unverified. Without a clear source or identification of which Blue Cross entity and when, the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim is presented without jurisdiction, source, or supporting fiscal estimates, so it cannot be verified as stated. Whether a specific measure is expensive depends on official fiscal impact statements and implementation details; there is no general rule that a measure numbered 3-386 would 'cost a fortune' while 3-388 'will cost less.' Without the specific ballot context and authoritative cost analyses, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: A photo shows "the Lincoln Memorial. His head damaged and defaced."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements that the marble statue of Abraham Lincoln in the Lincoln Memorial has been physically decapitated or defaced as described; such major damage would have been widely reported and documented. Viral images purporting to show the statue damaged have circulated before and have been shown to be digitally altered or miscaptioned. Without provenance for the specific photo, the claim that the photo shows genuine damage is not supported.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: There is no evidence that House Republicans issued any mandate forcing use of 'Styrofoam' cups in House cafeterias, nor that House cafeterias are 'part of Koch Industries.' House dining services are run by congressional/Architect of the Capitol operations, not by Koch. Additionally, 'Styrofoam' is a trademark associated with Dow, not Koch, so the claim conflates ownership and control without supporting facts.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The claim is an unsubstantiated, opinionated assertion that cannot be verified as a factual statement without specific evidence. Whether the Powell Butte reservoir costs could have been avoided depends on engineering, regulatory, and policy analyses (demand forecasts, seismic and redundancy requirements, alternatives studied) that are not provided here. Absent concrete studies or authoritative reports demonstrating a viable, less-costly alternative, the blanket claim is not supportable as fact.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: State-level estimates from Social Security and public policy analyses show that Social Security benefits lift well over one million Floridians above the federal poverty line in recent years. Florida’s large population of beneficiaries (older adults and their dependents) makes a >1 million figure plausible and consistent with SSA state-by-state impact tables, though the exact count varies by year and methodology.

claim: Says Travis County, home to Austin, is the most liberal county in the United States.
rationale: Travis County is a strongly Democratic county and a liberal urban center, but it is not uniquely or consistently the "most liberal" county in the U.S. Other counties (for example San Francisco County, Bronx County, and several small, heavily Democratic counties) typically show equal or higher measures of Democratic vote share and liberal indicators. Whether a county is "most liberal" depends on the metric and year, so the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: "Common welfare programs give income of $43,330 or $20.83 an hour."
rationale: This is false. Typical means-tested welfare benefits are far lower than $43,330/year: SNAP averages only a few hundred dollars per month per person, TANF cash assistance is often under several hundred dollars per month, and SSI or most cash benefits are well below $20k/year for most recipients. The $43,330 figure equals $20.83/hr only if one assumes 2,080 work hours, which is not how welfare benefits are usually measured and does not match observed benefit levels.

claim: "Science says that being single will kill you faster than obesity."
rationale: This statement misrepresents the evidence. Meta-analyses have found that weak social relationships and social isolation are associated with increased mortality risk that in some analyses is comparable to or larger than that attributed to obesity, but being "single" (unmarried) is not the same as being socially isolated and studies show association, not direct proof that being single "will kill you faster." The claim overgeneralizes, implies causation and a speed-of-death comparison that the science does not support without much more nuance (age, health, obesity severity, and social support all matter).

claim: Video shows Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez pouring shots for a group of people "days before testing positive" for COVID-19.
rationale: Fact-checks showed the circulating clip was not recorded days before Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tested positive for COVID-19; the footage dates from well before her positive test and was miscontextualized to imply recent exposure. Therefore the claim that the video shows her pouring shots days before testing positive is false.

claim: "Probably one out of every two households in Oklahoma has a gun."
rationale: Multiple state-level surveys have found that roughly half (or slightly more) of Oklahoma households report having a firearm, so the statement that about one out of every two households has a gun is consistent with available polling. Different surveys and years produce somewhat different estimates, but they generally place Oklahoma near the ~50% mark.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: The claim is misleading: peer‑reviewed trial papers report relative risk reduction (e.g., Pfizer ~95% RRR) while the much smaller numbers cited are the absolute risk reductions (ARR) computed from raw event rates in the trials. Some publications (Lancet/NEJM) report the event counts from which ARRs of roughly those magnitudes can be calculated, but that does not “disprove” the commonly reported ~95% efficacy metric because that 95% is a relative reduction in risk. The Lancet did not re‑label overall vaccine efficacy as ~1% — the difference is a metrics/interpretation issue, not contradicting trial efficacy findings.

claim: Says the Wisconsin Republican Party tweeted "Happy International Women's Day! You ladies should get paid less and not be able to make health care decisions."
rationale: There is no credible record or widely reported evidence that the official Wisconsin Republican Party account tweeted that message; it reads like a fabricated or parody post. Such an inflammatory, explicitly discriminatory statement from an official party account would have been documented and debunked by fact-checkers and major outlets. Given the lack of verification and the plausibility of doctored screenshots, the claim is false.

claim: "It's just outrageous that under President Bush, the National Institutes of Health have been basically decreased in funding."
rationale: As phrased, the claim is misleading: NIH appropriations did not fall in nominal dollars during President George W. Bush's time in office — funding rose through the early 2000s and then largely plateaued. However, when adjusted for inflation (real purchasing power), NIH funding declined for several years in his presidency, so the statement depends on which measure is meant.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that public school in the United States "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law."
rationale: There is no Supreme Court decision that literally rules public schools "will not teach the tenets of Islam or Sharia Law." The Court has long held public schools cannot endorse or proselytize religious doctrine (e.g., Engel v. Vitale, Abington v. Schempp, Lemon v. Kurtzman), but it has not issued a decision singling out Islam or Sharia with the quoted wording. Such statements are misattributions or paraphrases of general Establishment Clause principles or of state-level measures unrelated to a Supreme Court ruling.

claim: Obamacare has led to fewer health insurance options for millions of Americans.
rationale: The Affordable Care Act prompted some insurers to leave individual marketplaces and required many noncompliant plans to be discontinued, which reduced the number of insurer choices in numerous counties and affected millions of people seeking individual market coverage. While the law also expanded coverage (Medicaid expansion, new marketplace plans) and increased options for some, the net effect in many regions and years was fewer competing insurers on the individual exchanges for millions of Americans.

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: The claim is incorrect for the commonly meant person, Queen Elizabeth II. Official announcements and major news outlets reported that Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8, 2022 at age 96, not 95. If the claim refers to a different person titled 'Queen Elizabeth' it should be specified.

claim: "Parents and teachers are already worrying about what they call the ‘Trump Effect.’ They report that bullying and harassment are on the rise in our schools, especially targeting students of color, Muslims and immigrants."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and surveys after the 2016 campaign and early presidency documented that many parents and teachers expressed concern about a so-called 'Trump Effect' and reported increases in bullying and harassment in schools, particularly aimed at students of color, Muslims, and immigrants. Although official crime statistics vary and causation is debated, the volume of anecdotal reports and targeted-survey results supports the claim that such worries and reports were widespread.

claim: "Nearly 60% of all student loan debt is held by the rich and upper-middle class," so forgiveness would give the wealthy a "financial windfall" but not really help low-income people.
rationale: This statement overstates and mischaracterizes the distribution. Empirical analyses (Fed, Urban Institute, Brookings and census-based studies) show a large share of outstanding student debt is held by households above the median income or by older, higher-earning cohorts, but whether that equals “nearly 60%” held by the “rich and upper‑middle class” depends on imprecise definitions and is not consistently supported. Moreover, forgiveness effects vary by program design — many lower-income and distressed borrowers receive substantial benefit even if some higher‑earning borrowers also gain.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: This statement is generally true: Texas public high school graduation rates (the four‑year adjusted cohort graduation rate) have risen and been reported by the Texas Education Agency as reaching record highs for several recent graduating classes. Exact figures depend on the cohort year and the metric used, but state reports show a multi‑year upward trend culminating in record rates in recent years.

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because a Supreme Court nominee was both nominated and confirmed during the 2020 presidential election year: Amy Coney Barrett was nominated in late September 2020 and confirmed in October 2020. While it was true for many decades prior (the previous election-year confirmation dated to the early 1930s), the 2020 confirmation ended that long gap.

claim: "Of those 850,000 (new Texas) jobs, most were public-sector jobs and minimum-wage jobs."
rationale: This is incorrect: employment data for Texas show that the majority of job gains are in private-sector industries (e.g., trade/transportation, professional/business services, leisure/hospitality), not public-sector payrolls, and while a substantial share of new jobs are lower-paying, they do not constitute a majority that are minimum-wage jobs. Public-sector employment typically represents a minority of total payroll jobs, and Texas does not have a state minimum above the federal level, so most of 850,000 new jobs would not be classified as public-sector or minimum-wage.

claim: "Our last budget committed the highest level of need-based financial aid in state history."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits the state and which budget year is meant; without that context one cannot confirm it was the highest level in state history. Determining the truth requires comparing specific historical appropriations for need-based financial aid, accounting for inflation and program inclusions, none of which are provided. Because of the missing critical details, I treat the assertion as false until evidence is produced.

claim: "Women still earn about 77 cents for every dollar a man earns for working the same job."
rationale: The frequently cited “77 cents” figure is an unadjusted median comparison of all women's to all men's earnings and does not compare men and women doing the same job. When analyses control for occupation, hours worked, experience, education and other factors (i.e., comparing the same job or similar workers), the pay gap is much smaller, with only a single-digit percent unexplained difference in most studies.

claim: Says Military Times reported that a study found "60% of sailors who had been fully vaccinated with 2-shot series vaccines are now at risk for heart disease."
rationale: There is no credible Military Times report nor peer-reviewed study showing that 60% of fully vaccinated sailors are now at risk for heart disease. Reporting and public-health data on COVID-19 mRNA vaccines have identified rare cases of myocarditis, primarily in younger males, but rates are far below 60% and cases are usually mild and transient. The 60% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or misrepresentation of other statistics rather than a documented finding.

claim: Photo shows R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021.
rationale: No photo or source was provided to verify that the image depicts R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021. Many images of public figures are miscaptioned or repurposed online; without provenance, caption, or corroboration from reputable news outlets, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false. Verification would require the original image, metadata, or independent reporting matching the event and date.

claim: "The video doesn't show the broader picture of the firing that was going on at American troops."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because no specific video, date, location, or incident is identified; without those details one cannot determine whether the footage omitted broader context of firing at American troops. Because the claim could be true for some videos and false for others, it is not established here.

claim: Says photos show the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower with Chuck Schumer, Elizabeth Warren, Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checks and reporting found that the widely shared photos were misattributed and do not reliably identify the Trump-Ukraine whistleblower. The whistleblower's identity was not publicly confirmed and was legally protected at the time, and images circulated online were of other individuals or taken out of context, not showing the whistleblower meeting Schumer, Warren, Pelosi, and Clinton.

claim: "In West Virginia alone, overdoses have increased by 50% during the #COVID-19 pandemic."
rationale: Available statewide and federal data from the pandemic period do not show a clear, uniform 50% increase in overdoses in West Virginia; nationwide overdose deaths rose substantially but the percent change varied by state and county, and West Virginia’s statewide increases reported were smaller than 50% in most official sources. Media stories documented sharp local spikes in some jurisdictions, but that is not the same as a 50% statewide rise attributed solely to COVID-19.

claim: "MSNBC actually said on air ‘I hope enough people die from coronavirus that it harms Trump’s re-election.’"
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or verified on‑air video showing MSNBC saying the quoted line. The statement circulated on social media was a misattribution and has been debunked by fact‑checking efforts that found no broadcast evidence of an MSNBC host saying those words.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is false because prosecutions of former leaders are not limited to what the speaker calls the 'Third World' and have occurred in many developed democracies. Recent examples include convictions or indictments of former leaders in South Korea (Park Geun-hye, Lee Myung-bak), France (Jacques Chirac was convicted in 2011), Italy (Silvio Berlusconi faced multiple trials), and high-profile criminal cases or investigations involving former U.S. and Israeli leaders. While the frequency and political context vary by country, prosecutions of ex-leaders are a global phenomenon, not exclusive to less-developed states.

claim: "American coronavirus vaccine killed five Ukrainians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an “American coronavirus vaccine” directly killed five Ukrainians. Ukrainian health authorities and independent fact‑checkers investigated reported post‑vaccination deaths and found no causal link, with deaths attributed to underlying health conditions or coincidental timing rather than the vaccine.

claim: Due to U.S. Senate rules, Democrats need "more than a majority ... to codify Roe vs. Wade."
rationale: Under current Senate practice the filibuster means most major legislation requires 60 votes to invoke cloture and end debate, so a bare simple majority (50+1) is normally insufficient to pass a bill codifying Roe v. Wade. The vice president’s tie-breaking vote produces a bare majority but does not overcome a filibuster. There are narrow procedural exceptions (e.g., reconciliation) or a Senate rule change that could allow passage by a simple majority, but those are unusual or politically difficult.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits which state and which time period or data source are referenced; rankings of the percentage of deaths in nursing homes have varied by state and over time during the COVID-19 pandemic. Without a specific state, date, and dataset, the assertion that “we’re No. 46 out of 50” cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false. If a precise state and dataset were provided the claim could be checked and might be true or false depending on that context.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a 1776 flag was flown over the White House in January 2021; official White House flag protocol and contemporary news coverage would have documented such an unusual action and did not. Images and social-media posts claiming a “1776” or ‘revolution’ flag over the White House were misidentified or taken out of context (showing a flag on a nearby building, vehicle, or a different location).

claim: The U.S. Justice Department "conservatively estimated that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives."
rationale: This is a misattribution. The U.S. Department of Justice has not issued an official ‘‘conservative’’ estimate that guns are used 1.5 million times per year to save lives. The 1.5 million figure is tied to academic survey-based estimates of defensive gun use (notably work by criminologists such as Gary Kleck) and has been repeatedly misquoted as a DOJ estimate; government surveys (NCVS/BJS) produce much lower counts and DOJ has not endorsed a 1.5 million figure.

claim: Say Apple’s Tim Cook "will not do business with Indiana."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Apple CEO Tim Cook declared he “will not do business with Indiana.” In 2015 Cook and Apple publicly criticized Indiana’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act and expressed disappointment, but they did not announce an absolute refusal to conduct business in the state and Apple continued normal operations. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or misattribution of critical statements about the law rather than a factual quote about refusing business.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Congressional records and summaries (e.g., Congressional Research Service tallies) report that more than 11,000 proposed constitutional amendments have been introduced in the U.S. Congress since 1789. If “attempts” is understood as proposals introduced in Congress, the claim is accurate; only a tiny fraction of those were ever sent to the states or ratified.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While Iowa doesn’t mechanically determine the Republican nominee, it has historically shaped races by providing early momentum, media attention, and winnowing the field (e.g., Trump won Iowa in 2016 and secured the nomination, while other winners like Huckabee in 2008 or Santorum in 2012 did not). Recent changes and controversies have reduced Iowa’s predictiveness in some cycles, but it still can matter for nomination dynamics.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no evidence that any authorized, nationwide military tribunals were scheduled to begin on January 20, 2021. The U.S. presidential inauguration occurred that day and no executive order or statute established the start of military tribunals then, and no such tribunals began on that date. Assertions claiming otherwise stem from rumor and political speculation rather than verifiable official action.

claim: "The deficit was on track to top $1 trillion the year I took office."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because the pronoun “I” and the year are unspecified; whether the deficit was projected to top $1 trillion depends entirely on which incoming president and which fiscal year are meant. Historical data show some incoming years (e.g., FY2009) did see deficits above $1 trillion, while others (e.g., FY2017) did not, so the blanket claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false in this form.

claim: U.S. Rep. Scott Rigell "wants gun owners in a federal registration system."
rationale: There is no reliable public record showing Rep. Scott Rigell advocated creating a federal registry of gun owners; his known public positions were broadly pro-Second Amendment and did not include proposals to register lawful gun owners. Claims like this often arise from conflating support for certain background-check processes or database recordkeeping with advocating an ownership registry. Given the absence of direct evidence of Rigell calling for a federal gun-owner registry, the statement is false.

claim: Said President Barack Obama "said he was going to stop (signature strikes)."
rationale: There is no clear public record of President Obama explicitly saying he would categorically “stop” signature strikes. The Obama administration did announce tighter rules, greater oversight, and sought to limit particular drone practices, but reports and statements described restrictions rather than an unequivocal promise to end signature strikes altogether. Because reporting on administration policy changed over time and varied by theater, a blanket quotation attributing a categorical stop is not supported.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The claim that "Japan drops vax rollout" is false as a broad statement: Japan did not discontinue its COVID-19 vaccination program. Japan launched and continued national vaccination and booster campaigns (using Pfizer and later Moderna, with limited AstraZeneca use) rather than abandoning rollout, though there were occasional pauses or investigations of specific batches.

claim: Says Sen. Tim Kaine "approves of and even applauds his son's participation in a known terrorist organization, #Antifa."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or record that Sen. Tim Kaine publicly 'approves of and even applauds' his son's participation in Antifa. Major news outlets and Kaine’s public statements do not support this attribution, and the claim appears to be a mischaracterization or social-media falsehood. Additionally, the statement misframes 'Antifa' as a single 'known terrorist organization' when it is a loosely affiliated movement rather than a designated terrorist group.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the U.S. did not experience multiyear economic decay immediately before Trump—rather, the economy had been expanding for years with falling unemployment and rising GDP since the post-2009 recovery. While the Trump administration implemented tax cuts and deregulation that supporters credit with boosting growth, economic performance under Trump was mixed, deficits increased, and the COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp recession in 2020, so it is incorrect to state categorically that years of decay were ended solely by reversing prior policies.

claim: Says Romney and Ryan "both backed proposals that would outlaw abortions even in cases of rape or incest."
rationale: The claim overstates the record. Mitt Romney has repeatedly said he supports some exceptions (rape, incest, life of the mother) at various times and did not consistently back a federal proposal that categorically outlawed abortion with no rape/incest exceptions. Paul Ryan has backed very restrictive anti‑abortion measures, but the evidence that he explicitly backed a proposal that universally outlawed abortion even in rape/incest is mixed and depends on which specific bill and year are cited. Because both records vary by bill and time, the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "CNN-NPR photojournalist Jade Sacker was embedded with antifa leader" during the U.S. Capitol attack.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jade Sacker was an employee photojournalist for CNN or NPR or that she was “embedded with an antifa leader” during the U.S. Capitol attack. Public reporting and her own social-media posts identify her as a freelance photographer who provided images to various outlets, and the allegation of being embedded with an “antifa leader” appears to be a social-media mischaracterization without documentary support.

claim: Says that under President Donald Trump, "not only have we not gone after al-Qaida ... our president is supporting al-Qaida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Trump directly supported al-Qaida; during his term the U.S. continued counterterrorism operations, airstrikes, and special-operations missions against al-Qaida and its regional affiliates. Critics sometimes point to policy choices (e.g., troop withdrawals or support for Syrian rebel groups) as indirectly benefiting extremist actors, but those are not the same as actively supporting al-Qaida.

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The claim is false because many well-documented factors besides forest management cause California's massive, deadly, and costly fires. Climate change (higher temperatures, prolonged droughts and extreme fire weather), expanded development in the wildland–urban interface, utility equipment failures and other human ignitions, insect outbreaks and historical suppression policies all contribute; poor forest management can matter in some places but is not the sole cause.

claim: "Joe Biden wants to end school choice."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes Biden's position. While Biden has opposed federal voucher programs that divert public funds to private schools, he has not advocated abolishing all forms of school choice — his platform has supported strengthening public schools and allowing expansion/accountability for high-quality charter options and other parental supports.

claim: "Hillary Clinton leaves the country as Mueller indictment is announced."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream news reporting that Hillary Clinton left the country in direct response to any Mueller indictment announcement. Major Mueller indictment announcements were widely covered and did not report Clinton departing the U.S. due to those announcements; she was not a target of the special counsel. The claim appears to be a baseless timing/causation rumor without supporting documentation.

claim: This is the 911 call placed by the migrants trapped in the truck found in San Antonio, Texas.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a 911 call recording exists that was placed by the migrants inside the San Antonio truck; official reports and contemporaneous news coverage of the truck deaths do not cite a 911 call from inside the trailer. Viral audio clips have been circulated and debunked or remain unverified and unrelated to the incident. Given the lack of authoritative sourcing, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Congresswoman Frederica Wilson successfully postpones closure of the North Perry airport tower."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Rep. Frederica Wilson caused a successful postponement of the North Perry Airport control tower closure. While she and local officials publicly urged the FAA/DOT to keep the tower open, FAA contract-tower closure decisions were made by federal authorities and coverage shows no documented, lasting postponement attributable to her actions. The claim overstates her impact without corroborating evidence.

claim: "Nearly 20% of our residents" are born abroad.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify which 'residents' (what place or population) or what time period is meant. Foreign-born shares vary widely — some countries or cities are near 20% while others are far below — so without a specified jurisdiction and data year the statement cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: When it comes to income taxes, Wisconsin is "one of the best places in the country to be poor" but "top 4 or 5 worst" for middle-income earners.
rationale: The assertion presents a specific, extreme ranking for Wisconsin without citing a metric or year and is therefore misleading. Wisconsin does have a progressive income tax and refundable credits that reduce burdens on low‑income filers, but independent analyses of state and local tax burdens (which include sales and property taxes) do not consistently place Wisconsin as universally “one of the best” for the poor and simultaneously a top 4–5 worst for middle‑income households. Rankings vary by methodology, income cutoff, and year, so the blanket claim is unsupported as stated.

claim: Says The Washington Times ran a front-page headline that said, "President Gore."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that The Washington Times ran a front-page headline reading simply “President Gore.” Major newspapers that made premature calls in the 2000 election are documented, but The Washington Times is not recorded as having run such a front‑page headline. The claim likely confuses another outlet, an online headline, or an internal/dated edition rather than a standard front page.

claim: "Wisconsin lost more jobs over the past 12 months than any other state."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or data source and is unlikely: absolute job losses are typically largest in the most populous states (e.g., California, Texas, New York). Historical Bureau of Labor Statistics state employment data show Wisconsin is a mid‑sized state and rarely tops all others in absolute 12‑month job losses. Without a specific 12‑month period and corroborating BLS or state employment data, the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: Wisconsin's $3 billion incentive offer to Foxconn is "the largest gift ever by a state to a foreign company."
rationale: The $3 billion Wisconsin package for Foxconn was one of the largest state incentive offers to a foreign firm, but it is not clearly the single largest ever. Fact‑checking and reporting at the time noted that comparable or larger incentive packages exist depending on how incentives are counted (state vs. local/federal, tax credits vs. direct grants) and that prior deals to foreign automakers and other firms rivaled it.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people in the state of New Jersey want marriage equality."
rationale: The claim gives a precise percentage without a date or source; public support for “marriage equality” (same‑sex marriage) has risen and has been near or above 70% in some national and state polls at particular times, but results vary by survey, wording, and timing. Because the statement is absolute and unsourced, it cannot be confirmed as universally true for New Jersey at all times.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: False. There is no evidence that President Joe Biden uses a license plate reading “THEBIGGUY.” Images circulated showing that plate have been misattributed; presidential vehicles are government-owned, protected, and do not display personal vanity plates. Fact-checks found the plate/vehicle pictured is not Biden’s official car.

claim: "Gas prices have never been higher, and Exxon Mobil's profits have never been higher."
rationale: The statement is an unqualified absolute and lacks timeframe or geography. U.S. retail gasoline prices did reach nominal all-time highs in mid‑2022, but not when adjusted for inflation (2008 was comparable or higher on an inflation‑adjusted basis); Exxon Mobil did report record annual profits in 2022, so the combined blanket claim is misleading without context.

claim: It was President Obama's "inaction that caused over three weeks to go by before he even approved the governor's plan to protect our marsh."
rationale: The statement blames President Obama personally for a specific three-week approval delay, but without context or evidence this is unlikely: most approvals to ‘protect marsh’ would be handled by federal agencies (e.g., EPA, Army Corps) after a governor’s request, not by an immediate presidential sign‑off. Public records and reporting typically show administrative processes and interagency reviews, so attributing the delay solely to presidential inaction is unsupported. Because the claim lacks specifics and documentation, it cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Emails show that Fauci knew "hydroxychloroquine worked [and] emailed friends about it being effective."
rationale: This is false because the FOIA‑released emails do not show Fauci stating he knew hydroxychloroquine definitively worked and emailing friends that it was effective. The released correspondence shows he reviewed and forwarded early, often preliminary or conflicted reports and repeatedly emphasized the need for randomized trials; he did not assert proven efficacy. Subsequent large randomized trials also failed to demonstrate benefit, consistent with his caution.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on an assault weapons ban.
rationale: There is no clear, well-documented instance where Mitt Romney explicitly endorsed a federal assault-weapons ban and later reversed that position. Romney has sometimes supported specific gun-safety measures (expanded background checks, red-flag laws, and mental-health interventions) while generally opposing broad new bans on firearms; claims of a "flip-flop" typically conflate those distinctions.

claim: Getting the COVID-19 vaccine jeopardizes life insurance policies.
rationale: This claim is false. Major insurers and regulators have stated that receiving a COVID-19 vaccine does not, by itself, void or jeopardize existing life insurance policies; claims are evaluated on cause of death and policy terms, and routine vaccination is not a standard exclusion. An insurer could deny a claim only for contractually valid reasons such as material misrepresentation on the application or a specific, disclosed exclusion, not merely because the person was vaccinated.

claim: "Daniel Webster said he's out. Now he says he's in."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated—no time, source, or which Daniel Webster is identified. There are multiple public figures named Daniel Webster (a 19th‑century statesman and at least one modern politician), and without specifics there is no reliable evidence to confirm a retraction or reversal. Because the statement lacks context and supporting facts, it cannot be treated as true.

claim: Says Target installed urinals in a women’s bathroom to "accommodate the ones who have giblets."
rationale: There are no credible reports or evidence that Target installed urinals in women’s bathrooms or that Target staff made the quoted remark. Reporting around Target has focused on adding single-occupancy or gender-neutral restrooms, not converting multi-stall women’s rooms with urinals, and the quoted phrase appears to originate from social media satire or misattribution. Claims about specific installations and that exact quote are unsubstantiated.

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: This claim is unsupported. There is no authoritative count that the New York bike-path attack was specifically the "ninth" vehicle assault by ISIS; multiple vehicle attacks before and after have been described as ISIS-inspired or -claimed and counts vary by how one defines "used by ISIS" (directly ordered, claimed, or merely inspired). Naming it the ninth is therefore inaccurate without a clear, cited counting method.

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: The claim is unverified and too vague: it gives no date, specific hearing, or citation for an analysis showing Fox News allotted Republican senators exactly twice the airtime of Democrats for a hearing on the Islamic State. Establishing such a ratio requires a time-coded content analysis of Fox News’ coverage and a clear definition of which phrases or clips count as ‘air time.’ Without specific evidence, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as unsupported.

claim: "If I mail in my ballot on Sunday and show up to the polling station on Tuesday, they won’t know if I’ve already voted or not. That, my friends, is a serious concern for all of us."
rationale: This claim is not generally true. In most U.S. jurisdictions election officials update voter records/poll books when a mailed/absentee ballot is received and accepted, so poll workers can tell if a voter’s mail ballot has been returned; if a mailed ballot has not yet been received or processed by Election Day, voters are typically offered a provisional or affidavit ballot that will be reconciled later. Procedures and timing vary by state, but the blanket statement that poll workers won’t know is incorrect.

claim: "Last year, we were in the range of 850,000 and that was the most in five years. … We are letting more people become citizens than has happened in years."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not clearly supported by official immigration statistics. Annual naturalization and citizenship counts reported by DHS/USCIS vary by fiscal vs calendar year, and available data for recent years do not unambiguously show “about 850,000” that was definitively “the most in five years” without specifying which year or whether it refers to naturalizations vs lawful permanent resident admissions. Because the claim lacks a clear timeframe and the numeric assertion does not match readily verifiable yearly totals, it is misleading.

claim: The United States has "the highest corporate tax rate in the free world."
rationale: This is inaccurate as stated. The U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut from 35% to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and even when state-level taxes are added the combined rate is generally lower than the single highest statutory corporate rates in some other countries. The claim may have reflected the pre-2018 situation or a selective definition of "free world," but it is not true under typical present comparisons.

claim: Says a photo shows a "lithium mine for hybrid cars."
rationale: There is no way to verify the claim without the original image, geolocation, or independent provenance; many landscapes (salt flats, evaporation ponds, tailings, or non-lithium quarries) can look similar and are frequently misidentified. The assertion also conflates extraction site with specific end-use—lithium can be mined for many uses and not all batteries in hybrid cars use lithium chemistry. Because the claim lacks verifiable evidence and is plausibly misattributed, I judge it false until corroborating information is provided.

claim: Says there are fewer than 2,000 confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations in the U.S.
rationale: The claim lacks a timeframe or definition (current vs cumulative), but taken as a general statement it is false: U.S. COVID-19 hospitalizations have repeatedly exceeded 2,000 at any given time during major waves and cumulative hospitalizations are in the hundreds of thousands to millions. Public health reporting (CDC and state dashboards) documents peaks of tens of thousands of current hospitalizations and far larger cumulative totals.

claim: "I've created over 40,000 jobs."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “I” refers to, nor provide time period or evidence linking that person to creation of 40,000 jobs. Job‑creation numbers require documentation (payroll/tax records, independent audits) and clarification of whether jobs are direct, indirect, or temporary; absent that, the statement cannot be substantiated and is treated as false. If verifiable records were supplied, the assessment could change.

claim: An episode of "The Simpsons" showed Donald Trump in a coffin.
rationale: There is no known canonical episode of The Simpsons that depicts Donald Trump in a coffin. The series has parodied and referenced Trump (notably the 2000 episode 'Bart to the Future' and later satirical mentions), but reports or images claiming a coffin scene are from doctored images, fan edits, or non‑canonical viral material rather than an actual episode.

claim: Cher "is moving to Canada because of President Trump."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Cher has actually moved to Canada because of President Trump. While she and other celebrities publicly joked or threatened to leave the U.S. after Trump’s 2016 election, reporting and her public appearances indicate she has remained U.S.-based rather than emigrating. The claim conflates rhetorical statements with an actual move.

claim: "Wind powers nearly 13 million homes across the country."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and likely inaccurate without a date or country: the common “homes powered” metric varies by how you convert annual wind generation to household electricity use, and U.S. wind generation figures change year to year. Recent U.S. wind output divided by the typical household consumption yields different results (and industry press claims have varied), so the blanket statement that wind currently powers nearly 13 million homes is unsupported as presented.

claim: More than 1.5 million people moved into Georgia between the past two Census counts, and a majority consider themselves, African-American, Latino or Asian-American.
rationale: Georgia’s population increased by about 1.02 million between the 2010 and 2020 censuses (roughly 9.69M to 10.71M), not more than 1.5 million, and the claim conflates total population change with people who ‘moved into’ the state. While Black, Latino and Asian populations grew substantially, available census data do not show that a majority of the net increase were people identifying as African‑American, Latino or Asian‑American once natural increase and internal demographic factors are considered.

claim: Zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago.
rationale: Multiple reputable sources and statements from Chicago-area zoos (e.g., Lincoln Park Zoo and Brookfield Zoo) during recent protests reported that animals were secured and not released; viral social-media posts claiming otherwise were miscaptioned or from unrelated events. There is no credible evidence that zoo animals were set free during protests in Chicago.

claim: Says "about 100,000 kids in this country leave their home state and go to another state to be educated. Out of that 100,000 young people, 30,000 of them are from New Jersey, by far the largest amount."
rationale: The numbers conflict with known enrollment patterns: nationally, far more than 100,000 students attend school outside their home state when counting college-age students (estimates of out-of-state undergraduates are on the order of hundreds of thousands to over a million). It is implausible that New Jersey would supply 30,000 of only 100,000 out-migrating students and be “by far the largest” share given state population shares and typical interstate student flows.

claim: "If we use (Tax Increment Financing) funding, that's going to take funds from the general fund for Pinellas County, as it will take funds from the general fund for the city of St. Pete."
rationale: Tax increment financing (TIF) diverts the incremental growth in property tax revenue for a defined area into TIF/CRA accounts to repay project costs rather than allowing that increment to flow into the regular budgets of taxing authorities. That means county and city governments will not receive the extra tax revenue growth that would otherwise have bolstered their general funds while the TIF is in effect. The exact immediate impact varies by local law and how the TIF is structured (base revenue is typically preserved).

claim: "I’ve been against that war in Afghanistan from the very beginning."
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because no speaker, time frame, or which Afghanistan war is specified. Determining whether someone opposed the U.S. invasion of Afghanistan from its outset requires checking that person's contemporaneous public statements, voting record, or written positions; absent that evidence the claim is unverified and therefore treated as false.

claim: "Since I was elected, crime rates have been at their lowest in over a decade."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits which office/jurisdiction, the election date, and which crime measures are meant. Crime trends differ by location and category (violent vs. property) and many jurisdictions have not seen uniformly decade-low rates since a particular official took office. Without specific, time-stamped official statistics this broad claim cannot be substantiated, so I mark it FALSE.

claim: "Bad math (is) driving Wisconsin’s exploding positive test rate."
rationale: Available public-health reporting and contemporaneous news coverage indicate Wisconsin’s rising percent-positive reflected a genuine increase in detected infections and limited testing capacity, not simply a sustained calculation error. While there were some reporting quirks and short-term data anomalies that briefly distorted percentages, those issues do not account for the overall upward trend in test positivity. Therefore the claim that “bad math” is driving the exploding positive rate overstates the role of reporting errors.

claim: "State Rep. Kathleen Peters has a 100 percent pro-abortion voting record – even voting against a ban on sex-selection abortions."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that State Rep. Kathleen Peters held a flawless “100% pro‑abortion” voting record; public roll‑call records and interest‑group scorecards do not support a claim of every vote being pro‑abortion. The specific assertion that she “even voted against a ban on sex‑selection abortions” is not corroborated by a clear, documented single roll call attributed to her as described in the claim.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden "flashed the 'white power' sign" last week; similar claims have circulated online but were unverified and frequently stem from misinterpretation of common gestures or manipulated images. Furthermore, Biden has a documented history of publicly condemning white supremacists, so the suggestion that he has not condemned them is misleading without a specific date or citation. The claim appears to conflate an unverified gesture with a broader accusation about his statements.

claim: Say North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County.
rationale: This claim is false — there are no credible news reports, official statements, or public arrest records indicating that North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County. An arrest of a sitting governor would be widely reported by major media and state authorities, which did not occur through mid-2024.

claim: "Fauci admits Covid vax doesn't work"
rationale: This claim is false. Dr. Anthony Fauci has not admitted that COVID vaccines "don't work"; he has repeatedly acknowledged that vaccines are not 100% effective at preventing infection (especially with new variants and over time) while emphasizing they substantially reduce risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death. Statements about breakthrough infections or waning protection have been taken out of context to create the misleading claim that vaccines do not work at all.

claim: "More Americans have died from guns in the United States since 1968 than on battlefields of all the wars in American history."
rationale: Public-health data show roughly 1.4–1.6 million firearm deaths in the U.S. from 1968 through recent years, while commonly cited historical totals for U.S. deaths in all wars combined (Revolutionary War through present) are on the order of about 1.3–1.4 million. Even with conservative counting, cumulative gun deaths since 1968 exceed typical estimates of U.S. war fatalities, so the claim is supported.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: The statement is overly absolute. Bernie Sanders has publicly refused corporate PAC money in his recent presidential campaigns and frequently touts that stance, but historical campaign finance records show he accepted some contributions tied to PACs or lobbyists earlier in his long political career, so the claim that he 'never' took corporate lobbyist money is incorrect.

claim: Says that when adjusted for inflation and population growth, state general revenue spending has decreased 10.7 percent on his watch.
rationale: The claim lacks any identifying details (which state, which official, and what exact time period), so it cannot be verified as stated. Determining a 10.7% decline requires specific data on state general revenue, a chosen inflation index, and population during the claimed period; absent those inputs the numeric assertion is unsupported.

claim: Joe Biden and Kamala Harris "continuously questioned the vaccine during the campaign" but now "they support vaccine cards and forced vaccinations."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. During the 2020–2021 campaign Biden and Harris generally promoted COVID-19 vaccination rather than “continuously question[ing]” it, and while the Biden administration has backed vaccine mandates for certain settings (federal employees, contractors, some health-care workers) and allowed/encouraged proof of vaccination in many contexts, it did not create a single federal “vaccine passport” nor impose universal forced vaccination for all Americans. The statement conflates different policies and misrepresents their campaign rhetoric.

claim: "Tonight in Ohio, more people came out to vote for Barack Obama in an unopposed race than voted for (Mitt) Romney and (Rick) Santorum combined."
rationale: The statement is almost certainly false. In the relevant Ohio contest (the 2012 primaries) the combined Republican totals for Romney and Santorum exceeded the votes cast for Barack Obama in the uncontested Democratic primary, and more generally incumbents unopposed in primaries rarely outpoll competitive opposition contests in a large state like Ohio. The claim also lacks a specific date or election to verify, which makes it unreliable as stated.

claim: A map shows "all the cargo ships backed up by the Suez Canal. Get ready for shortages and prices to skyrocket."
rationale: The claim is misleading.
