claim: "Cory Gardner is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions right now."
rationale: Cory Gardner is a former U.S. senator (left office in 2021) and there is no evidence he is currently sponsoring federal legislation to ban all abortions. While Gardner has supported abortion restrictions in the past as a senator, that is different from actively sponsoring an across-the-board abortion ban right now. The claim conflates past positions with current legislative activity and overstates the scope of measures he has backed.

claim: "Wife of Pfizer’s CEO dies after complications from the vaccine."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the spouse of Pfizer’s CEO died from COVID-19 vaccination. Major fact-checkers and public records show no reports of such a death, and Pfizer and public sources have not confirmed any such incident; the claim appears to be misinformation or a conflation with unrelated events.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: Poliquin did vote for House Republican health bills (notably the 2017 AHCA) that independent analyses projected would increase the number of uninsured, including in Maine. However, there is no definitive, authoritative finding that his vote directly and immediately "stripped 117,000 Mainers of their insurance" — state-level projections of coverage losses vary by model and the claim presents a precise causal outcome that the record does not unambiguously support.

claim: The new health care law "will cut $500 billion from Medicare. That will hurt the quality of our care."
rationale: The law did include provisions that federal analysts (CBO) estimated would reduce Medicare spending by roughly $500 billion over a decade, but those are primarily slower spending growth and reduced payments (not direct benefit eliminations for traditional Medicare). The assertion that those savings "will hurt the quality of our care" is speculative and not established — many savings targeted overpayments and private-plan payments, and experts disagree about any net effect on care quality.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: Scott Walker took office in January 2011. State and FBI crime-data series show that Wisconsin’s violent-crime rate declined through much of the 2010s (covering most of Walker’s tenure) and only saw notable upticks around 2020–2021. Because the claim gives no timeframe and treats the trend as uniformly worse than 2011, it is misleading — the data do not unambiguously show Wisconsin is overall less safe than at Walker’s inauguration.

claim: ABC News recently banned reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official ABC News statement showing a recent, network-wide ban on American-flag lapel pins for reporters. While broadcast outlets sometimes issue guidance about on-air neutrality or attire for specific events, that is not the same as an outright ban, and the claim appears to conflate or misstate such practices. Without verifiable evidence of a formal ABC ban, the claim is false.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: Reporting on Rep. Sean Casten shows he held a mix of public/virtual town halls and smaller constituent briefings that required RSVP, but there is no clear evidence that he repeatedly held numerous exclusive "invite-only" town halls. Characterizing his meetings as broadly "invite-only" overstates the available evidence and conflates RSVP/registration or small-group constituent meetings with closed, invitation-only events.

claim: "We have that program where immigrants come here and they have to bring a million dollars in order to get a green card if they’re going to create jobs."
rationale: This statement is misleading. There is an EB‑5 immigrant investor program that can lead to a conditional green card for foreign investors who create 10 jobs, but the required investment is not universally $1,000,000 — historically it has been $1,000,000 or $500,000 in targeted employment areas and the dollar thresholds have changed over time and by rule. Also approval is not automatic and yields conditional residence subject to requirements.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The statement is an exclusive claim about “the only candidate” and lacks any identifying context (which candidate, what years). Without specifics it cannot be verified and is implausible because multiple Providence officials and candidates have presided over balanced budgets or supported job-creation efforts at different times. Attributing both unique budget-balancing and job-creation accomplishments to a single candidate is therefore unsupported.

claim: "The pension fund in the city of Providence is only 30 percent funded, about the same level as when he [Taveras] took office."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate. Public reports and actuarial valuations show Providence’s funded ratio changed over time — it was substantially higher (roughly in the 40s percent range) around when Mayor Taveras took office in 2011 and later declined toward the low‑30s, so it was not “about the same level” at both points. The exact funded percentage depends on the valuation date and assumptions, so the claim’s framing as unchanged and “only 30 percent” is misleading.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: The statement is a speculative counterfactual rather than a verifiable fact. While modern GOP litmus tests (e.g., demands for loyalty to a particular leader or stricter stances on specific contemporary issues) differ from 1980s politics, there is no evidence that the party would have formally expelled Ronald Reagan; Reagan's positions on taxes, defense, and anti-communism were central to the GOP and he remains an honored party icon. Because the claim asserts a definitive historical outcome about a hypothetical scenario, it cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Make no mistake: They’re not after me. They are after you; your guns, your Christian values, your freedom. I’m just in their way."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of Donald Trump saying this exact sentence; it appears to be a paraphrase that compresses themes he often uses (portraying prosecutions as attacks on supporters and invoking guns/Christian values). Without primary-source audio or a reliable transcript matching these words, the quoted sentence should be treated as fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "Special education categorical aid" from the state "hasn’t been raised in over a decade."
rationale: The claim is unverifyable as stated because it names no state and presents a blanket assertion; state education funding varies and many states have changed or increased special education categorical aid within the last ten years. Without a specific state and a clear definition of 'raised' (nominal increase, per‑pupil, or inflation‑adjusted), the broad claim is not supported.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: The claim is a hyperbolic mischaracterization. Republican Party platforms call for stronger border security, enforcement measures and removal of unauthorized immigrants in many cases, but they do not literally state or endorse a blanket slogan like “deport everybody and to hell with it.” The platform language is formal policy proposals rather than that crude phrasing.

claim: Says that Biden’s ban on new federal leases will kill 120,000 Texas jobs.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Biden’s pause on new federal oil and gas leases by itself will 'kill 120,000 Texas jobs.' The pause applies only to federal lands and waters and much Texas oil and gas activity occurs on private and state leases; the 120,000 figure originates from industry or advocacy estimates that assume broad, cumulative effects and include indirect jobs over uncertain time frames. Independent government analyses do not corroborate a direct, immediate loss of that magnitude attributable solely to the leasing pause.

claim: "The median income in America has dropped by 10 percent in the last four years."
rationale: This is false as stated. Official U.S. data (Census Bureau household median income series) show that median household income did not fall by 10% over the past four years in nominal terms, and reported year-to-year changes have been much smaller; even when accounting for inflation the change is not a uniform 10% drop nationwide. The claim also omits whether it means nominal vs. real income or individual vs. household median, which changes interpretation.

claim: Says the 2008 book "End of Days" predicted the current coronavirus outbreak.
rationale: The 2008 book End of Days (by Sylvia Browne) contains a vague passage about a 2020 ‘severe pneumonia‑like illness,’ but it does not identify SARS‑CoV‑2, name coronavirus, or provide verifiable specific details that match the COVID‑19 outbreak. Claiming the book predicted the current coronavirus outbreak overstates and misattributes a nonspecific prophecy to a specific modern virus and pandemic timeline.

claim: In the past decade in New York State "more than 30 current and former state officeholders have been convicted, sanctioned or accused of wrongdoing — more than any other state."
rationale: I could not corroborate a reliable, authoritative tally showing that New York had more than 30 current or former state officeholders convicted, sanctioned, or accused in the past decade and that this total exceeded every other state. Counts of convictions, sanctions and accusations vary by definition and source, and major reporting and public records do not support the definitive comparative claim as stated. Because the claim mixes convictions, sanctions and mere accusations and asserts a national ranking, it is unsubstantiated without a clear, consistent dataset.

claim: "This year, Eric Cantor has received more money from oil companies than any other member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and ambiguous because it does not specify which year is meant. Public campaign-finance databases (FEC/OpenSecrets) provide year-by-year totals and do not show Eric Cantor as the single largest recipient of oil-industry contributions across Congress in any widely reported cycle; he has been a significant recipient but not conclusively the top recipient. Without a precise year and citation, the assertion is false as stated.

claim: The Washington D.C.-area "never has a recession."
rationale: The D.C. metro is more economically resilient due to large federal employment and contracting, but it has nonetheless experienced recessions and clear downturns (notably around 2001, the 2008–2009 Great Recession, and the 2020 COVID shock) with job and output losses. Saying it "never has a recession" is inaccurate because regional GDP and employment data show contractions during national recessions.

claim: Wagon arriving at Detroit counting center after deadline "may have been a ballot box."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the wagon shown arriving at the Detroit counting center contained an illicit "ballot box" or improperly counted ballots. Video clips are ambiguous about contents and context, and Detroit and Michigan election officials, as well as post-election audits and recounts, found no proof of late or fraudulent ballots being introduced via a wagon. The claim is speculative and contradicted by official chain-of-custody and audit findings.

claim: "McDonald’s (makes) you all sign noncompete contracts that you cannot go across town to try to get a job at Burger King."
rationale: The claim that McDonald’s makes all employees sign noncompete agreements barring them from working across town at Burger King is inaccurate. While some franchisees have asked certain managers or higher-level employees to sign noncompete or restrictive agreements, entry-level crew typically are not subject to broad noncompetes and enforceability varies by state and role.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: I am not aware of credible reporting or campaign finance disclosures showing that Rep. John Culberson was caught spending campaign funds on collectibles such as Civil War memorabilia and fossils. Major news outlets and public FEC filings do not document such purchases tied to Culberson; the claim appears to be a misattribution or unsubstantiated allegation. Without a specific, verifiable source, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Official US Department of Defense and independent trackers report varying "confirmed" and "suspected" reengagement rates for released Guantanamo detainees (typically reported in the mid-teens to low-20s percent range when combined) depending on definitions and cut-off dates, not a clear, nearly 29% figure universally. Moreover, the reported rates have fluctuated as more transfers, new information, and changing classification criteria have occurred rather than showing a consistent, steady climb from the first releases.

claim: Says Charlie "Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money."
rationale: I cannot verify that Charlie Crist uttered the exact statement 'Crist made it easier for Duke to take your money.' There is no clear, attributable record of Crist saying that phrase; it reads like an attack-line or misquotation rather than a documented quote. Without a primary source (ad, speech transcript, or reliable reporting) the claim is unsupported.

claim: "We are currently using only around 20% of our testing capacity."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits any jurisdiction, time period, or definition of "testing capacity." Percent utilization of testing capacity is a measurable statistic that varies widely by location, lab network, and date; a blanket statement of "only around 20%" is unlikely to be accurate without supporting data. Given the ambiguity and lack of cited evidence, the claim cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says Stacey Evans "voted for (school) vouchers...in the beginning."
rationale: There is no clear legislative record showing Stacey Evans cast a vote in favor of a statewide private-school voucher program; during her gubernatorial campaign she publicly opposed voucher-style privatization and framed herself as a supporter of public schools. Claims that she "voted for vouchers in the beginning" appear to conflate different bills or rely on ambiguous phrasing rather than a specific documented floor vote in favor of vouchers. Without a specific bill and date the assertion is not supported by known public records and her campaign statements.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: While it is correct that the state provided an $80 million contribution toward the Bucks’ new arena, the claim that new income-tax revenue from basketball events alone is “probably over $600 million over the life of the lease” is unsupported and inconsistent with independent analyses. Public and nonpartisan reviews of the arena deal found that optimistic economic-impact or gross-revenue figures were often conflated with actual net tax receipts, and credible estimates of tax revenue tied solely to basketball events are much lower. The $600 million figure appears to be an exaggerated aggregate or mischaracterized projection rather than a defensible estimate of income-tax revenue from games alone.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The claim mixes a near-accurate election fact with ambiguous assertions. Trump did win West Virginia by roughly 42 percentage points in 2016 (so “almost 43” is reasonable) and WV was among his strongest states by vote share, but saying he “has the strongest support … than any other state” and that he’s been “carrying close to 60 percent approval” is ambiguous and not universally true across time or poll measures. Without a specific timeframe or poll source the broader claim is misleading.

claim: Says he banned texting while driving in Austin.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unverified as written: it uses the pronoun “he” without identifying who, and bans on texting while driving in Austin would be established by a city ordinance or state law rather than a single individual acting alone. Without a named actor, date, or official record, the assertion that “he banned texting while driving in Austin” cannot be substantiated.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: The statement lacks a timeframe and is inconsistent with available evidence: U.S. government data and independent analyses show large numbers of migrant encounters at the southern border in recent years and an unauthorized immigrant population that has been stable or increasing rather than showing a sustained net outflow to Mexico. While expulsions/returns (e.g., Title 42, removals, and some returns to Mexico) have occurred, they have not produced a sustained net outflow greater than arrivals and overall unauthorized presence in the U.S.

claim: "Sixteen [federal] programs exist to fight homelessness" and some of them are duplicative.
rationale: Multiple oversight and policy reports have identified roughly sixteen distinct federal programs across several agencies that fund homelessness prevention and services, and these analyses have flagged overlap and fragmented responsibilities among programs. While exact counts can vary by how programs are defined, the core claim that about sixteen programs exist and some are duplicative is supported by GAO/CRS and homelessness-policy reviews.

claim: "Without a shred of clinical data to support its decision, the Biden Administration has revoked the emergency use authorization for lifesaving monoclonal antibody treatments."
rationale: The EUA revocations targeted specific monoclonal antibodies after laboratory neutralization studies and SARS‑CoV‑2 variant surveillance showed those products no longer neutralized the then‑circulating variants. That means the decision was based on scientific evidence of loss of activity (largely in vitro and epidemiologic), not “without a shred of clinical data.” Also the action was taken by the FDA (an independent regulator) regarding particular mAbs, not a blanket political decision.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating evidence that Gov. Rick Scott skipped his own education summit and attended a Tea Party convention the same week. High‑profile schedule choices like that would have been reported by contemporary news outlets and official schedules; without a clear date or sources the claim appears unverified and likely misleading.

claim: The only budget Ted Cruz "ever voted for in his time in the Senate is a budget that cut defense spending by more than Barack Obama proposes we cut it."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: Cruz has participated in multiple budget-related votes during his Senate tenure and the statement’s absolute wording (“the only budget…”) is unlikely to be correct. Moreover, comparing cuts requires naming specific budget resolutions and the particular Obama proposal being referenced; without that specificity the numerical comparison cannot be verified.

claim: Trade deals are negotiated in "secret" and, unlike corporate interests, politicians never invite "the leaders of the AFL-CIO or steelworkers or the mine workers to come in and sit down in these meetings."
rationale: The claim's absolute wording (“never”) is incorrect. While specific negotiating sessions are often confidential, governments commonly run formal consultation processes and advisory bodies that include labor representatives, and unions such as the AFL‑CIO and national steel and mine workers’ organizations have been invited to meetings and consultations on trade policy. Access and influence may be uneven compared with corporate actors, but labor participation is not categorically excluded.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: There is no clear, documented statement or policy from Trump explicitly calling for abolishing the federal minimum wage. He has often said during campaigns that he favors letting states set wages or tailoring rules locally, which opponents sometimes portray as effectively eliminating a federal floor, but that is not the same as an explicit stated goal to 'get rid of' the federal minimum wage.

claim: "There's going to be a slowdown and delays in flights" as a result of the sequester.
rationale: Across-the-board sequester cuts reduce funding for FAA operations and can force furloughs, reduced staffing, or curtailed contract tower hours, which in turn slow air traffic handling and increase delays—this occurred during the 2013 U.S. sequester when FAA warned of and implemented measures that caused delays at busy airports. The claim is a general prediction that is consistent with how sequester-driven cuts impact flight operations.

claim: Says Josh Mandel bet against Ohio families
rationale: The statement is vague and there is no credible evidence that Josh Mandel literally "bet against Ohio families." While Mandel has faced political attacks over his investment decisions, public records and reporting do not support a charge that he took financial positions specifically designed to harm or profit from Ohio families. Without a specific, documented transaction or reliable source tying him to such a action, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "Speaker Rubio supported gun restrictions that included background checks and waiting periods."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. Marco Rubio was not commonly known as “Speaker Rubio,” and his record does not show consistent support for broad gun restrictions that included universal background checks and mandatory waiting periods; he has generally opposed sweeping gun-control measures while supporting limited, targeted steps (e.g., some mental-health reporting and age restrictions after Parkland).

claim: "Zach Nunn took money from Adventureland’s CEO, then sponsored legislation to loosen amusement park safety rules. A child died. Zach Nunn put his big donor first, ahead of the safety of Iowa families."
rationale: There is no reliable public evidence tying Zach Nunn to sponsorship of legislation that loosened amusement-park safety rules, nor proof that Adventureland’s CEO gave him money for that purpose, or that such actions directly led to a child’s death. The claim asserts a specific causal chain (donation → bill sponsorship → loosened rules → death) that is unsupported by available legislative records and reporting through mid-2024.

claim: "In campaigns in the past with Sen. McCain and President George W. Bush and others, they have tended to release tax records in April."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. While many candidates time releases near the April tax-filing season, there is no consistent pattern showing that Sen. John McCain, President George W. Bush and others “tended” to release returns specifically in April across their campaigns; release timing has varied by year and campaign. Without specific years or citations the claim is not supported.

claim: "Now, 50% of all of America, more than any other country, is fully vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about timeframe and about whether 'America' means the United States or the continents, but as stated it is incorrect: while the U.S. did reach roughly 50% of its population fully vaccinated in mid-2021, many other countries (for example several in Western Europe, the Gulf, and Latin America) have had higher fully-vaccinated shares. Therefore the statement that '50% ... is fully vaccinated' and that this is 'more than any other country' is not supported.

claim: "At my first ‘Let’s Get to Work Day’ … we sold out;" more than 240 dozen doughnuts by 8:30 a.m.
rationale: The claim that more than 240 dozen (2,880) doughnuts were sold out by 8:30 a.m. at a single ‘Let’s Get to Work Day’ event cannot be corroborated with available public evidence and is implausible without receipts or independent reporting. The number is unusually large for a single early-morning community event and would typically require documentation (vendor invoices, media coverage, or witness counts) which is not provided. Because the claim lacks verifiable support, it is rated false pending substantiation.

claim: "Reagan took the deficit from $70 billion to $175 billion. Bush 41 took it to $300 billion. Clinton got it to zero. Bush 43 took it from zero to $1.2 trillion. Obama halved it to $600 billion. Trump’s got it back to a trillion."
rationale: The claim mixes roughly correct trends with several incorrect attributions and numbers. While deficits rose in the Reagan and Bush 41 eras and Clinton oversaw a shift to budget surpluses in the late 1990s, Clinton did not merely “get it to zero” (there were multi-year surpluses). The largest single-year deficit often cited (~$1.4T) occurred in FY2009 during the financial crisis as Obama took office, not solely under Bush 43, and Trump-era deficits were near $1T pre-pandemic but surged far beyond $1T in 2020 due to COVID relief. Overall the statement is misleading and factually inaccurate in multiple specifics.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: After the Aug 2020 Kenosha unrest following the police shooting of Jacob Blake, Gov. Tony Evers publicly complained that assistance did not arrive until after people were killed and explicitly said it took loss of life before help came. Multiple contemporaneous news reports quoted Evers making that point while criticizing the delayed deployment of assistance (state Guard/federal help).

claim: A government analysis shows under a proposed transportation tax, "metro Atlanta will create or support an additional 200,000 new jobs, including jobs that are maintained year over year."
rationale: Available government and regional transportation analyses that cite roughly 200,000 jobs for Atlanta typically refer to cumulative "job-years" or the total number of direct, indirect, and induced jobs supported over the project delivery period (many of them temporary construction jobs), not 200,000 net new permanent jobs maintained year after year. The claim as phrased misstates the usual meaning of those reports by implying sustained annually maintained positions rather than short-term or cumulative employment impacts.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: Contemporary press and fact-checking of Walker’s tenure as Milwaukee County Executive reported that he returned salary increases, bonuses and other compensation items to the county, totaling more than $370,000 over his time in office beginning in 2002. The figure has been repeatedly cited in local news and fact-checks about his record as county executive.

claim: Says Rob Portman "said the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio."
rationale: There is no reliable record attributing the exact phrase "the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio" to Rob Portman. While Portman and other Ohio Republicans criticized aspects of federal auto-industry interventions, I could not find evidence he used that specific language, so the claim appears to be a misquote or paraphrase. If a precise source or date is provided, the determination could change.

claim: "700 jobs (were) lost because Allen Boyd" voted for the health care bill.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a single vote by Rep. Allen Boyd directly caused exactly 700 jobs to be lost. Job losses are typically due to many economic factors, and claims tying a specific number of layoffs to one lawmaker's vote were used rhetorically in political messaging without documented causal proof.

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: The claim that North Carolina hospital beds are "typically 85% full across the state" is not supported as a general, time-independent fact. Pre-pandemic and typical non-surge occupancy rates for U.S. hospitals—including North Carolina—have generally been lower (around mid-60s to low-70s percent) and statewide bed use fluctuates widely by region and during pandemic surges; occasional peaks may approach or exceed 85% but that is not the usual steady-state level. Therefore presenting 85% as a typical, across-the-state occupancy is misleading.

claim: "Congressman Duffy has long record of voting against VA backlog fixes."
rationale: The claim asserts a consistent, long-standing pattern of voting against VA backlog fixes, but available evidence does not show a clear, uniform record of opposing veterans’ backlog reform across time. Members of Congress (including Representative Sean Duffy, the likely subject) have supported some VA reform measures and opposed others depending on specific provisions; there is no clear record that he repeatedly voted against efforts to address the backlog. Without naming specific bills or a specific Duffy, the broad claim overstates the case.

claim: When Sara Gideon "knew the truth about" sexual allegations against a state lawmaker, "she could have called for an immediate investigation, but didn’t…Gideon knew for months, using her power to cover up."
rationale: There is no clear, publicly documented evidence that Sara Gideon "knew the truth" about sexual allegations and then used her power to cover them up for months. Reporting on any allegations tied to the Maine legislature has not substantiated the specific claim that she intentionally suppressed or obstructed an investigation; the accusation appears unproven and politically charged without named incidents or corroborating documentation.

claim: Says former NBA player Rick Fox was also on board with Kobe Bryant
rationale: If the claim means Rick Fox "was also on board" Kobe Bryant's helicopter when it crashed, that is false: the official passenger list and reporting do not include Rick Fox. The known victims were Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna, the pilot Ara Zobayan, and six others (John and Keri Altobelli, Alyssa Altobelli, Christina Mauser, Sarah and Payton Chester). There are no credible reports placing Rick Fox among those aboard or as a casualty.

claim: Says Jason Carter has "gotten David Axelrod to come down and be his campaign advisor."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that David Axelrod formally became Jason Carter’s campaign advisor. Axelrod did make at least one public appearance in Georgia to support Democratic causes around the 2014 race, but that is different from being hired as a campaign adviser. The claim overstates Axelrod’s role.

claim: Says Keene, N.H., requested a "military-grade armored personnel truck," citing their annual Pumpkin Festival as "a possible target" for terrorists.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and the police property-request paperwork show Keene, NH sought a surplus armored vehicle (an MRAP-style personnel carrier) through the federal transfer program and listed its large annual Pumpkin Festival among events that could be potential targets. Multiple news outlets summarized the request as seeking a “military‑grade” armored truck and noted the festival was cited in the application as a security concern.

claim: "I'm pro-life. He's not."
rationale: The statement asserts two people’s positions but provides no identities, timeframe, or supporting evidence. Political labels like 'pro-life' are verifiable only via public statements, policy positions, or voting records, none of which are provided here. As presented the claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: "U.S. teenagers have now fallen behind their counterparts in Ireland, Poland and even Vietnam in math and science."
rationale: International assessments of 15-year-olds (notably the OECD PISA tests in recent cycles) show U.S. students scoring below their peers in countries such as Poland and Ireland, and below Vietnam in the PISA cycles where Vietnam participated. Thus the broad claim that U.S. teenagers lag behind those countries in math and science is supported by those test results, although wording like “fallen behind” can imply a recent decline rather than a relative ranking.

claim: Says Roy Moore "has advocated getting the federal government out of health care altogether, which means doing away with Medicaid, which means doing away with Medicare."
rationale: The claim overstates what Roy Moore has publicly advocated. Moore has called for repealing the Affordable Care Act and reducing federal involvement in health care, and has supported shifting Medicaid to states or market-based alternatives, but there is no clear record of him explicitly calling for abolishing Medicare nationwide. Saying he 'advocated getting the federal government out of health care altogether' and thus ending both Medicaid and Medicare is not supported by his documented public statements.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The statement is too vague and not supported as a general fact: it fails to specify which insurers, which profit metric (net income, after‑tax profit, returns), or what end year. Aggregate industry profit figures have fluctuated with economic cycles and while some companies or segments have seen large gains, broad insurance industry profits do not uniformly show a >400% increase since 2001. Without a clear metric and timeframe the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While visible, high-quality cameras and monitoring can deter many opportunistic robberies by increasing the perceived risk of identification and arrest, empirical evidence is mixed and effectiveness varies greatly; determined offenders, use of masks, poor camera placement or low image quality often negate deterrent and identification effects.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify because it does not specify which "region" or which measure of drought (precipitation, soil moisture, agricultural impact, streamflow) is meant. While 2011 was the worst drought year on record in some places (for example parts of the United States such as Texas experienced historic 2011 drought), many other regions have had worse or different worst years. Without a specific region and metric the blanket statement is not supportable.

claim: The omnibus bill "does not designate a single dollar for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute but lacks context (which omnibus bill/year). Federal omnibus appropriations normally fund programs (Medicaid, Title X, community health centers) rather than naming private providers; Planned Parenthood has historically received federal reimbursements and program grants even when not singled out. Because funds can flow indirectly and some bills have explicitly barred or allowed such funding, the categorical statement that no dollar is designated for Planned Parenthood is false or unsubstantiated without more context.

claim: President Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid support Rick Perry’s "decision to give in-state tuition to illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid have supported federal measures (like versions of the DREAM Act) to allow some undocumented students access to in-state or reduced tuition, there is no clear evidence they explicitly endorsed or praised a specific decision by Texas Governor Rick Perry to grant in-state tuition. Supporting broader federal relief for certain undocumented youth is not the same as publicly supporting a particular state official’s action or policy.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no record in public court documents or reputable news reporting of any court ordering former President Barack Obama to pay $400 million in restitution. The claim appears to be misinformation, likely conflating unrelated events (for example, controversy over a 2016 US payment to Iran) with a nonexistent personal court judgment against Obama.

claim: Texas and Florida have a "balanced budget" while California is "in debt $54 billion and New York is "in debt $6.1 billion."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Most U.S. states (including Texas and Florida) are generally required by law to pass balanced budgets, but that does not mean every fund or liability is without shortfalls; conversely, California and New York were not broadly reported as being 'in debt' by the specific amounts cited (California has had multi‑billion dollar budget surpluses/reserves in recent budget cycles and New York’s fiscal gap figures differ by accounting method). The statement therefore misstates or cherry‑picks numbers and lacks context about which fiscal measure or year is being used.

claim: Cannabis reform "is supported by the majority of the residents of our state, including a majority of Republicans."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it refers to "our state" without naming which state or when. While U.S. national polls typically show a majority favoring cannabis legalization, Republican support varies by state and is not uniformly a majority everywhere, so the blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: "I remember landing under sniper fire."
rationale: The statement is a bare first-person memory with no supporting details (who, when, where, corroborating sources). Personal recollections are not verifiable without independent evidence such as contemporaneous reports, eyewitness accounts, or official records, so the claim cannot be confirmed as presented. Because of that absence of corroboration I classify it as false for fact-checking purposes rather than proven fact.

claim: Says Amazon is "paying full-time employees so little that they require gov food assistance."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While reporting and studies have shown that some Amazon full‑time workers do enroll in government food assistance programs, many full‑time employees earn wages (Amazon raised its minimum to $15/hr in 2018 and provides benefits) and do not require SNAP; whether workers need assistance depends on location, household size, and other income, not a universal company-wide condition.

claim: "Currently, 23 percent of our military's infrastructure is graded as 'poor' while 9 percent is 'failing.'"
rationale: There is no verifiable, current Department of Defense–wide statistic that matches exactly “23% poor” and “9% failing.” DoD and oversight reports use different condition metrics and publish varying percentages by asset class and year, so a blanket, current figure like this is unsupported without a specific source. The claim appears to conflate or misstate selective figures from different reports or time periods.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The statement is presented as a precise, current fact but there is no single authoritative count that supports “ISIS is in 32 countries.” Estimates of where ISIS or its affiliates operate vary widely over time and depend on how one defines "in" (direct control, active affiliates, cells, or ideological influence). Because presence fluctuates and different sources report different country counts, the specific claim of 32 countries is not reliably supported.

claim: Milwaukee "incarcerates 1.2% of white men" and has "incarcerated over 50% of black men in their 30s."
rationale: The claim as worded is misleading and not supported for current incarceration: no credible source shows Milwaukee currently incarcerates >50% of Black men in their 30s, and current incarceration prevalences are far lower than 50%. Some studies and news reports have noted that a very large share of Black men in Milwaukee have been jailed or imprisoned at least once (i.e., “ever incarcerated”), and Milwaukee has unusually high Black male incarceration rates relative to other places — but that is a different measure and depends on precise age cohorts and geography. Because the statement mixes measures (current vs. lifetime incarceration) and lacks clear boundaries, it is false as presented.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The claim is a vague, hyperbolic assertion without supporting evidence — saying Kander is “attending fancy dinners all over the country” implies nationwide, repeated events but no documented record substantiates that level of travel or activity. While candidates often attend fundraising dinners and out-of-state events, the specific claim of attending “fancy dinners all over the country” is not verifiable as stated and appears exaggerated.

claim: Virginia voters are being turned away from polling locations because they were told they already requested absentee ballots when they haven’t.
rationale: There is no evidence of a widespread, ongoing practice in Virginia of routinely turning away voters by falsely saying they had requested absentee ballots. Investigations and statements from Virginia election officials and contemporary fact-checking found only isolated administrative errors or confusion in past elections, and affected voters were generally offered provisional ballots or allowed to cure the issue.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: The Department of Homeland Security (through USCIS, which runs the SAVE system) has publicly warned that the SAVE database is intended to verify immigration status for benefits and related purposes and is not a definitive or foolproof means to establish U.S. citizenship for voter-registration or voter-roll verification. Officials and agency guidance have said SAVE should not be used as the sole source to determine citizenship for voting.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: I find no reliable evidence or reporting up to my 2024-06 knowledge cutoff that Amazon removed an educational game specifically about Gettysburg. While Amazon has removed items for policy reasons at times, there are no documented announcements or credible news stories confirming the removal of a Gettysburg educational game without more specific details (title, platform, date).

claim: After hearing "the frustrations parents and teachers have with the FCAT," next year "we begin improving our testing system."
rationale: The claim is presented as a direct quote promising that improvements to the FCAT will begin next year, but no speaker, date, or source is provided to verify that statement was actually made or that such a commitment exists. Without corroborating evidence of the quote or a formal policy action, the assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the lack of verifiable context, it is treated as unverified/false.

claim: "Texas mothers are dying during childbirth at the highest rates in the nation."
rationale: This claim is not supported by national maternal mortality data. While Texas has had elevated maternal mortality in some years and reporting issues that inflated earlier estimates, recent CDC and state surveillance data do not consistently show Texas as having the highest maternal-death rate; other states (e.g., Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama) have often ranked higher depending on year and measure. The result also depends on which metric is used (pregnancy-related vs. all maternal deaths) and the specific year chosen.

claim: Says the Republican "state convention is actually larger than the Republican National Convention."
rationale: The Republican National Convention is a nationwide event that assembles delegates and participants from all 50 states and U.S. territories and therefore typically totals several thousand people. Individual state party conventions are limited to members and delegates from a single state and are generally much smaller, so the blanket claim that a "state convention is actually larger than the Republican National Convention" is incorrect without specifying a particular state and year.

claim: "The State Department asked all secretaries of state to send their emails over." Hillary Clinton's "the only one who’s done it."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The State Department did ask former officials in 2015 to search for and turn over any work-related emails after Clinton’s private-server issue surfaced, but that request did not literally apply to every past secretary in the same way (some served before widespread email use and had no personal work emails), and other former secretaries and officials also provided records or had no emails to provide. Saying the Department asked “all” secretaries and that Clinton was “the only one who’s done it” misstates the scope and facts of the record requests and responses.

claim: Exporters are using a federal loophole to "deceptively sell products made from cat and dog fur" to U.S. consumers.
rationale: The United States has federal prohibitions and labeling requirements (notably the Dog and Cat Fur Trade Prohibition Act and the Fur Products Labeling Act) that generally ban import/sale and require truthful species labeling. While there have been isolated seizures and cases of mislabeling or fraudulent trim claims, there is no clear evidence of a broadly available legal “loophole” that permits exporters to lawfully and widely sell cat or dog fur to U.S. consumers. Claims of systematic deceptive sales overstate the documented incidents and ignore the existing prohibitions and enforcement actions.

claim: "I have 2 and a half million more votes than he (Sanders) does."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which election, contest, date, or whether it refers to popular votes, state totals, or delegates. Vote totals between two candidates (e.g., Biden and Bernie Sanders) vary by year, primary/caucus, and whether you count pledged delegates or popular votes, so the flat assertion cannot be confirmed without that context. Given the ambiguity, I treat the claim as false until precise parameters are provided.

claim: "This is the same (farm) bill we voted on a few weeks ago, with the exception of one or two sentences."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented: without specifying which bill versions are being compared, it cannot be confirmed that only “one or two sentences” changed. In practice legislative amendments and conference changes commonly alter multiple provisions, and factual verification requires side-by-side text comparison or authoritative summaries. Given the vagueness and typical scope of bill edits, the claim is unlikely to be accurate as stated.

claim: Says Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year.
rationale: The claim as stated is not accurate for recent years. Reliable sources that track abortion counts (state reports compiled by the CDC and independent estimates from the Guttmacher Institute) show Texas had substantially fewer than 80,000 abortions annually in the years immediately prior to and following major 2021–2022 restrictions; the 80,000+ figure is higher than contemporary estimates. Therefore the blanket statement that Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year is false without a specific historical timeframe.

claim: "Trump on revamping the military: We’re bringing back the draft."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Donald Trump has officially announced “We’re bringing back the draft.” He has discussed strengthening and reshaping the military and expressed concern about recruitment, but reinstating conscription would require explicit policy action and congressional legislation and was not declared. Media reporting and public statements from Trump show proposals to expand the military or change enlistment incentives rather than a formal promise to reinstate the draft.

claim: "Since 2011, we have documentation of 1,671 dead bodies we have recovered in Texas, many in Brooks County."
rationale: The specific figure of 1,671 documented dead bodies recovered in Texas since 2011 is not corroborated by authoritative public records; official counts of migrant deaths at the U.S.–Mexico border vary by source and year and do not consistently support that precise total tied to Texas alone. While Brooks County is a known hotspot for recovered remains and many deaths have occurred there, the claim provides no verifiable source and appears to conflate or overstate available aggregated counts.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: This sentence is a widely circulated misattribution; no primary source or citation exists in Einstein’s collected writings or reputable quotation references. Quotation researchers trace it to modern internet memes and attributions rather than any documented statement by Einstein, so the claim that he said it is false.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: I am not aware of any reputable, widely reported poll showing that 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid. Major regional surveys (e.g., Pew, Arab Barometer) show varied and often negative views of U.S. policy or influence, but do not support the specific 80% figure on rejecting U.S. aid as stated. The claim likely misstates or misrepresents survey questions, timing, or sampling.

claim: "Trump’s tax reform plan was nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."
rationale: This is false: the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act lowered individual tax rates, nearly doubled the standard deduction, increased the child tax credit, and — according to analyses by the CBO, JCT, and independent groups — resulted in tax cuts for the majority of middle-income households in the early years after enactment. However, some specific households (depending on state, filing status, and itemized deductions) saw little change or small increases, and most individual provisions are temporary and scheduled to expire after 2025.

claim: "Torture is illegal by our laws. It's illegal by international laws."
rationale: The claim mixes a correct general point about international law with an unqualified claim about unspecified domestic law. Torture is broadly prohibited under binding international instruments and customary international law, but whether it is illegal “by our laws” depends on which country is meant; some states have explicit criminal prohibitions while others have ambiguous statutes or practices that circumvent bans. Because the domestic part is unspecified and not universally true, the overall statement is not fully accurate.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum has a "far left socialist platform."
rationale: This is misleading. Andrew Gillum ran in 2018 as a progressive Democrat advocating policies such as a $15 minimum wage, Medicaid expansion, tuition-free community college, criminal justice reform, and stronger environmental regulation—positions left of center but within mainstream progressive Democratic politics. He did not advocate nationwide public ownership of industry or other hallmark policies of a far‑left socialist platform, and he did not run on an explicit socialist program.

claim: Says Mitch McConnell voted "two times against the Violence Against Women Act."
rationale: I cannot find clear evidence that Mitch McConnell cast votes against the Violence Against Women Act on two distinct occasions. He opposed aspects of the 2013 reauthorization (including voting against cloture) and was publicly critical of that version, but claiming he voted 'two times against' VAWA overstates or mischaracterizes the available voting record without specifying which measures or years are meant.

claim: Says two-thirds of groups targeted for IRS scrutiny were not conservative.
rationale: This is false. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) report and contemporaneous investigations found that the groups singled out for extra IRS scrutiny were predominantly identified with conservative labels (notably 'Tea Party'/'patriot'), so it is incorrect to say two-thirds were not conservative. Subsequent reporting and reviews upheld that the pattern disproportionately affected conservative groups.

claim: Photo of vaccine package with 2018 date stamp shows COVID-19 outbreak was planned.
rationale: A photo of a vaccine package stamped 2018 does not demonstrate that the COVID-19 outbreak was planned. COVID-19 was first identified in late 2019 and vaccines for it were developed in 2020–2021; packaging dates can indicate manufacture or expiry and can belong to entirely different products or be miscaptioned or edited. There is no credible evidence linking an older date stamp on a package to foreknowledge or orchestration of the pandemic.

claim: Says that except for foreign policy, Ron Paul’s voting record and his voting record are virtually identical.
rationale: As written, the claim compares Ron Paul’s voting record to itself, so aside from any subset of votes (e.g., on foreign policy) the records are necessarily identical. This is a tautology: a single individual's record cannot differ from itself. The statement is therefore factually accurate but trivial.

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The statement is too vague and not supported as a universal fact. Rates of Millennials moving back with parents vary widely by country, age range, and year (with spikes during economic downturns and the COVID-19 pandemic), and available surveys do not establish a single, generalizable figure of exactly one‑third of all Millennials having moved back in with their parents. Without a specified timeframe and geography the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: The number of pregnant women who have miscarried increased by "366% in just six weeks" as a result of their receiving a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccination caused a 366% rise in miscarriages over six weeks. Large studies and public-health agency reviews have found no increased risk of miscarriage after COVID-19 vaccination, and dramatic percentage claims typically arise from misinterpreting passive-reporting counts rather than verified incidence or causation.

claim: "In France, they have a (surveillance) program a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States.
rationale: The assertion that France runs a surveillance program "a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States is an unsubstantiated quantitative claim. Public reporting shows both countries have significant intelligence and surveillance capabilities (e.g., U.S. NSA/FBI programs and France's DGSI/DGSE and post‑2015 surveillance laws), but there is no credible metric or evidence demonstrating France is 1,000× more invasive. Without a clear definition or data, the claim is misleading and false.

claim: "The poorest in this country are women."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization without a specified country or poverty measure. While women are disproportionately represented among the poor in many countries (the 'feminization of poverty'), poverty patterns vary by country, age group, household composition and whether poverty is measured at the individual or household level, so the categorical claim that the poorest are women is not universally true.

claim: "In Harrisburg, I passed more bills than all the Democrats combined, in terms of legislation affecting the city."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable and implausible as stated because it lacks the identity of “I,” the timeframe, the legislative body, and a clear definition of what counts as “bills affecting the city.” It is highly unlikely one person passed more such bills than an entire party caucus without documentation. In the absence of specific evidence (bill counts, session dates, and a consistent inclusion rule), the assertion cannot be accepted as true.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: I could not find authoritative data showing that 70 of Ohio’s 88 counties have over 25% of residents eligible for emergency food. Statewide measures of food insecurity and SNAP participation in Ohio are substantially lower than a uniform >25% threshold across nearly 80% of counties, and the claim provides no date or source. Without a clear definition of “eligible for emergency food” or a cited study, the statement is not supported by available population-level estimates.

claim: "New Jersey taxpayers … will now face the highest tolls in the country."
rationale: The statement is too sweeping and unsupported: whether New Jersey has the “highest tolls in the country” depends on the metric used (per-trip, per-mile, or particular crossings) and the time frame. Other states and agencies (for example major New York and California bridges and some tolled express lanes) charge equal or higher rates on specific trips or per-mile bases, so New Jersey cannot be definitively labeled the highest without more precise comparison.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The claim conflates benefit receipt with disability and misstates the relationship. While millions receive SSDI or SSI, SSI includes elderly and non-disabled blind beneficiaries and some people receive both programs, so summing program caseloads does not equal the count of disabled Americans. Also many people with disabilities do not receive SSDI/SSI, so program recipiency understates true disability prevalence.

claim: Obama "voted for and even sponsored amendments that were intended to kill the (immigration overhaul) legislation."
rationale: The claim is unsupported by the public record and is ambiguous about timing and which bill it refers to. Barack Obama repeatedly publicly supported comprehensive immigration reform as a U.S. senator and president, and there is no documented evidence that he sponsored amendments designed to “kill” major immigration overhaul bills; procedural or tactical votes by him do not equate to sponsoring poison‑pill amendments. Given the lack of a clear legislative context and supporting evidence, the assertion is false as stated.

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it omits which state and what time period are being referenced; unemployment rankings and the national rate change monthly. Without a specific state and date you cannot confirm that the state was fifth‑highest, exactly one percentage point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states simultaneously. Such a claim could be true at particular times for particular states, but as presented it is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders marched with Fidel Castro and Che Guevara in Cuba.
rationale: The claim is false. Che Guevara was killed in 1967, so Sanders could not have marched with him; while Sanders did visit Cuba in the 1980s and at times participated in mass events (e.g., a public parade) there is no credible evidence he marched alongside Fidel Castro. Contemporary fact-checks and available photos show Sanders among large crowds, not marching next to Castro or with Che.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The federal government has set minimum energy-efficiency standards (notably the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 and subsequent DOE rules) that phased out many inefficient incandescent bulbs, but it does not literally tell individual consumers which specific bulb brand or model to buy—it restricts which types may be sold by setting performance requirements. Saying the government "tells us which light bulbs to buy" overstates the degree of direct prescription.

claim: "New Jersey today has fewer employees in state government than it had when Christie Whitman left office in January of 2001, and I think that’s good. And we did it without any layoffs. We did it through attrition."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented and is likely false. New Jersey’s state employee headcount has fluctuated since 2001 and depends on precise definitions (state-only vs. state+authorities, inclusion of higher-education, part-time, contractors), and public records indicate workforce changes and some instances of layoffs or targeted reductions during budget crises—so the blanket claim that the state 'today' has fewer employees than in January 2001 and that it was done entirely without layoffs is not supported. Without a specific date and a clear accounting definition the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Rep. Paul Gosar asks Capitol Police to arrest illegal immigrants attending State of the Union."
rationale: There is no credible public record or major news reporting that Rep. Paul Gosar formally asked Capitol Police to arrest undocumented immigrants attending the State of the Union. Capitol Police handle security and access but do not perform routine immigration enforcement, and invited guests to the address are vetted, making the specific claim unlikely. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation of rhetoric about immigration or calls to remove protesters rather than a documented request to arrest attendees for immigration status.

claim: "Forty-seven percent of Americans pay no income tax."
rationale: The widely cited “47%” figure refers to a 2011/2012 estimate of households that paid no federal individual income tax in that year, not to all Americans or to all types of taxes. Many people in that group still pay payroll taxes, state and local taxes, or consumed taxes, and the share varies by year and definition. Without specifying year, population (individuals vs households) and tax type, the claim is misleading.

claim: "The Simpsons" predicted Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
rationale: There is no Simpsons episode that explicitly and accurately foretold the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Viral posts conflate generic jokes, background signs, or fictional plotlines about Russia with the real-world event; The Simpsons is a long-running satirical show whose broad satire and occasional coincidental details are often mischaracterized as specific predictions.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: This claim is misleading and factually incorrect in blanket form. Stimulus (Economic Impact) payments were based on tax filing status, Social Security number, income thresholds and whether someone is a dependent or an inmate of a penal institution — not on criminal convictions per se; many people earning around $80,000 still qualified for at least a partial payment depending on the round and filing status, and many incarcerated people were ineligible, though a small number received payments due to filing circumstances or releases. The statement oversimplifies and conflates separate eligibility rules.

claim: "I believe in tax cuts. I believe in being a supply-sider. I cut the income tax I think it was 24 percent. We got 42 percent more revenues."
rationale: The specific claim that cutting the income tax by "24 percent" produced "42 percent more revenues" is not supported by historical evidence. Major US income-tax cuts (for example in the early 1980s) did not generate an immediate 42% rise in revenues, and empirical public‑finance research shows tax cuts rarely fully offset their revenue loss through growth. The statement also mixes unclear metrics (percent vs percentage points, nominal vs real revenues) which undermines its accuracy.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: The statement mixes a subjective charge (“flip‑flopped”) with a specific factual claim (an NRA “F”). The NRA assigns letter grades that vary by year and office, and Mike DeWine’s record has been mixed—he has supported some gun‑safety measures while earlier receiving pro‑gun ratings—so a blanket claim that he “has earned an F from the NRA” without a timeframe is likely inaccurate. The “flip‑flopped” charge is opinion and depends on which votes or statements are cited.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: The claim overstates and generalizes from anecdote. Systematic reviews and law‑enforcement investigations do not find that a majority of school shooters were ‘‘drugged’’ or had been on Ritalin since kindergarten; while a small number of perpetrators had histories of psychiatric medication, most did not, and no reliable evidence shows that being prescribed stimulants like methylphenidate is a common or causal factor in school shootings. Assertions that ‘‘many’’ shooters were medicated come from selective reporting rather than population‑level data.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This is false. Presidents have long used the executive branch (Department of Justice) to bring suits against states to enforce federal law — for example, Eisenhower's intervention in Little Rock and the Johnson administration's numerous civil-rights and Voting Rights Act suits in the 1960s. Presidents do not personally 'file' suits; the federal government has litigated against states under many administrations before Obama.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Paul Manafort served as Donald Trump’s campaign chairman/manager for several months in 2016 (roughly May–August) and exercised significant authority over campaign strategy, staffing and delegate operations; he was not merely a peripheral or “very limited” actor. While he resigned in August 2016 and his formal role ended, his earlier tenure was substantial and influential during a critical period of the campaign.

claim: Says President Barack Obama’s "own economists say the stimulus cost $278K per job ‘created.’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Obama administration economists concluded the stimulus cost $278,000 per job created. The $278k figure comes from critics who divided total ARRA outlays by a snapshot of jobs (or peak month employment), a misleading arithmetic choice; official CEA/CBO analyses reported millions of job-years supported and much lower cost-per-job-year estimates. Administration economists did not endorse the $278k/person claim.

claim: "Suez Canal blocked by huge container ship named Evergreen. Evergreen shipping is most likely a cover for human and sex trafficking" by Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim mixes a true event (the container ship Ever Given, operated by Evergreen Marine, grounded and blocked the Suez Canal in March 2021) with an unfounded conspiracy and a false attribution. There is no credible evidence that Evergreen is a cover for human or sex trafficking, nor is there a record of Hillary Clinton making such an allegation; the trafficking claim appears baseless and the attribution is incorrect.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: There is insufficient specific evidence to verify the blanket claim that 'Bill White is refusing to debate.' Without a time, source, or which Bill White is meant, this reads as an unsubstantiated accusation or partisan framing rather than a documented fact. Public reporting about known political figures named Bill White does not support a general refusal to debate, so absent corroboration the claim is treated as false.

claim: "794 law enforcement officers have fallen in the line of duty since B.H. Obama took office, with no special recognition from the White House."
rationale: The specific number and the claim of "no special recognition" are not correct. Organizations that track line-of-duty deaths (e.g., Officer Down Memorial Page/National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund) show counts that vary by date and definition, and the Obama White House issued statements/proclamations and participated in national memorial events honoring fallen officers during his presidency. Therefore the blanket claim is misleading or inaccurate.

claim: Says 1 in 5 Texans did not have health insurance coverage before the pandemic, and now "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65 don’t have access to health care insurance."
rationale: The first part (about 1 in 5 Texans being uninsured before the pandemic) is roughly consistent with pre‑pandemic ACS/Census estimates (~18–20%). The second part claiming "nearly 1 in 3 Texans under the age of 65" lack insurance is not supported by major data sources: post‑pandemic estimates for Texas uninsured under 65 have remained in the high teens to low twenties percent, well below ~33%.

claim: When McCain was questioned about hiring lobbyists to his campaign staff, "his top lobbyist actually had the nerve to say, 'The American people won't care about this.' "
rationale: I found no verifiable, attributable source showing a McCain campaign 'top lobbyist' saying the exact line 'The American people won't care about this' when questioned about hiring lobbyists. Contemporary press accounts from the 2008 McCain campaign documented controversy over hiring lobbyists and included various defenses, but this specific quoted sentence is not substantiated by reliable reporting. Given the lack of a clear attribution or primary-source evidence, the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Donald Trump "cancelled Bill Gates project known as ID2020."
rationale: There is no evidence that Donald Trump "cancelled" ID2020. ID2020 is a multi-stakeholder nonprofit initiative tied to digital identity work (involving companies and foundations) rather than a single "Bill Gates project," and it was not a federal program that the president could unilaterally terminate. No executive order, announcement, or credible reporting shows Trump canceled or ended ID2020.

claim: "As a state rep, I was considered the fourth-most conservative in the Legislature."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no identifying information (which state, which person, what year, or who conducted the ranking). Legislative ideological rankings exist but vary by methodology and source, so without specifics the assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the ambiguity, the prudent conclusion is that the claim cannot be reliably verified.

claim: Says President Barack Obama wants to raise "the lowest (income) tax rate from 10 to 15 percent."
rationale: This claim is false. During Barack Obama’s presidency there was no credible policy proposal from the administration to raise the statutory lowest federal individual income tax bracket from 10% to 15%; Obama’s major tax proposals targeted higher-income taxpayers (e.g., higher rates on income above specified high thresholds) rather than raising the bottom marginal rate.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that Meg Whitman both donated to and actively campaigned for Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer. While Whitman has made political donations across party lines at times, contemporaneous reporting and campaign records do not show her campaigning on Boxer's behalf. The claim conflates general cross-party giving with active campaigning, which is not supported by the available record.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: This precise claim is not supported by readily available records and is misleading. Jane Norton’s formal roles (Secretary of State and later Lieutenant Governor) did not entail unilateral management of a statewide “bureaucracy” whose budget can be cleanly attributed to her, and I find no reliable source that documents a $43 million increase tied to her management over a specific three‑year span. Without a stated time period, fund type, or official budget citation, the $43 million figure appears unverified or taken out of context.

claim: "Pfizer and Moderna could share their design with dozens of other pharma companies who stand ready to produce their vaccines and end the pandemic."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the sequences/designs for mRNA vaccines can be shared, producing safe, effective doses at scale requires specialized lipid nanoparticles, equipment, validated processes, quality control, regulatory authorization, and supply chains; simply handing over a design would not instantly enable dozens of manufacturers to produce vaccines and ‘end the pandemic.’ Technology transfer and regulatory work can enable more producers over months, but not immediately or automatically.

claim: "There’s a tremendous other number of public officials who have done the same thing" as Hillary Clinton with a private email server.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and official reviews found that while some public officials used personal email accounts for government business, the specific arrangement of hosting all official email on a privately maintained home server (as Hillary Clinton did) was rare or unique among comparable officials. Therefore the claim that a "tremendous other number" of public officials did the same is incorrect.

claim: Says Patrick Henry said, "The Constitution is not a document for the government to restrain the people: it is an instrument for the people to restrain the government."
rationale: The exact sentence is not found in Patrick Henry’s recorded speeches or contemporary documents and appears to be a 20th-century paraphrase or misattribution. While Henry did argue against a powerful central government and warned about governmental overreach, historians and quote researchers have not located this precise wording in his writings or speeches.

claim: "Seventy percent of all Texans are overweight or obese."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and likely an overgeneralization. State surveillance (BRFSS/CDC) shows roughly two-thirds of Texas adults are classified as overweight or obese in many recent years, but figures vary by year and excluding/including children changes the percentage; saying "seventy percent of all Texans" without specifying age or year is not supportable as a fact.

claim: "Donald Trump to issue an executive order to ban Facebook across U.S."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Trump has issued or announced an enforceable executive order to ban Facebook nationwide. U.S. presidents have limited constitutional authority to outlaw a private social media platform outright, and past attempts to restrict platforms (e.g., actions aimed at TikTok) faced immediate legal challenges. The claim appears to be a rumor or mischaracterization of political rhetoric rather than a factual action.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The claimed $16,400/second over George Allen’s Senate tenure is inaccurate and misleading. Federal debt rose by roughly $2.5–$3.0 trillion from early 2001 to early 2007 (Allen’s six-year Senate term), which works out to on the order of ~$14,000/second, and attributing the entire increase to his votes ignores that debt changes reflect many policies, economic conditions, and votes by many members.

claim: Taxpayers pay $18,000 a month for House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's district office in downtown San Francisco.
rationale: The claim gives a precise monthly figure but is not supported by public lease records or mainstream fact-checking reporting. Congressional district office rents are paid from public funds and vary by location and lease year, but available disclosures and prior fact-checks do not corroborate an $18,000/month rent specifically for Pelosi's San Francisco district office. Without a cited lease and timeframe the statement appears unverified and likely misleading.

claim: "Eighty percent of the net new jobs created in the state of Texas since 2009 went to the foreign-born."
rationale: Public labor‑market and demographic data (CPS/ACS and state employment series) do not support the assertion that 80% of net new Texas jobs since 2009 went to the foreign‑born. Immigrants contributed a disproportionate share of employment growth in some years and industries, but the share is substantially below 80% when measured against net new jobs statewide; the claim appears to conflate or misinterpret different measures (e.g., population growth, worker share, or a limited timeframe).

claim: "When you pull up to the gas pump to fill up your car, get your cell phone and search for Bluetooth devices. If a sequence of letters and numbers show up don’t pay at the pump. One of the pumps has a credit card skimmer inside of it. All of these skimmers run on bluetooth."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some card skimmers have used Bluetooth to transmit stolen data, many skimmers use other methods (internal storage, cellular/GSM transmitters, or shimming devices) and not every Bluetooth device visible at a pump is a skimmer. Relying solely on a Bluetooth scan and generic device names is unreliable and will produce both false positives and false negatives.

claim: "Crisis actor in Germany forgets he’s filming on TV."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that a known "crisis actor" in Germany was caught forgetting he was on TV; repeated investigations into similar viral clips have found misinterpretation or lack of context rather than proof of staged events. Claims that individuals at German incidents are crisis actors are a common form of misinformation and have not been substantiated by reliable news or fact-checking organizations.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because the speaker is unspecified and no supporting evidence is provided.
