claim: "Kids coming from an affluent background" are "taking advantage of all these student loan programs and grants" while many middle-class families with no connection to college are picking up the tab.
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While wealthier students do capture a disproportionate share of some higher-education benefits (e.g., tax breaks, higher attendance rates and some institutional aid), major federal programs like Pell Grants are specifically targeted to low-income students and many student loan programs are need- or income-sensitive; the distribution of benefits and who ultimately 'picks up the tab' is complex and not accurately summarized as affluent kids universally exploiting programs while middle-class non-college families bear the cost.

claim: Facebook users can avoid "problems with your Facebook going against community standards" by changing your settings.
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Facebook account settings can limit who sees your posts (privacy/audience controls) or enable certain content filters, they do not exempt content from Facebook’s Community Standards or its enforcement (removals, restrictions, or penalties). Changing settings may reduce visibility or interactions but cannot prevent moderation action against content that violates rules.

claim: Says Republican lawmakers delayed COVID-19 testing
rationale: The broad claim that 'Republican lawmakers delayed COVID-19 testing' is inaccurate as a blanket statement. Early testing delays in the U.S. were primarily caused by CDC test kit failures and restrictive FDA rules on laboratory-developed tests, along with supply-chain and administrative issues, rather than being principally caused by Republican legislators as a group. While some Republican officials or state governments made policy choices that affected testing rollout, responsibility was distributed across federal agencies and both parties.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This is incorrect. National and international vital‑statistics show that cancer and heart disease remained leading causes of death during the COVID‑19 pandemic with thousands of deaths from those causes continuing each month. While COVID‑19 affected overall mortality and disrupted care, it did not eliminate deaths from cancer or cardiovascular disease.

claim: Says she introduced a ban on "dirty dancing."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it omits who “she” is and when/where the ban was allegedly introduced. There is no widely reported, specific instance tying a named female politician to formally introducing a ban on “dirty dancing”; while some jurisdictions have regulated lewd dancing, the claim as a standalone fact lacks necessary context and evidence. Because of that missing context I judge the claim false as presented.

claim: Under H.R. 1, the Federal Election Commission "for the first time ever, instead of being an equal number of Republicans and Democrats (would be) three of one side and two of the other."
rationale: The bill did propose converting the FEC from six commissioners to five, which would make a 3–2 party split possible when fully seated. However, the claim’s phrase “for the first time ever” is misleading: the FEC has frequently operated with uneven partisan balances (e.g., 3–2) when there were vacancies, and other federal commissions have had 3–2 splits, so it is not literally the first time the commission would have an uneven partisan makeup. Thus the core factual claim is inaccurate or overstated.

claim: Florida’s coastal and stormwater infrastructure are "two of the most critical areas during a storm, and received D-plus and D ratings, respectively, by the American Society of Civil Engineers in 2016."
rationale: The 2016 American Society of Civil Engineers Florida report card gave coastal infrastructure a D+ and stormwater systems a D, and both sectors are commonly described as among the most critical during storms because they protect against flooding, erosion, and storm impacts. The claim accurately reports those grades and the asserted importance in storm contexts.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "said I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject."
rationale: The claim provides an unattributed, oddly phrased quotation without a source, and there is no widely reported or verifiable record of Ted Cruz saying the exact lines quoted. While Cruz has made public comments about U.S. policy in Libya, I could not confirm he ever stated “I was in favor in Libya. I never discussed that subject.” Without a reliable source for this specific quote, the claim is not supported.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The claim states that no jobs were being created while Chris Christie talked about job creation. That absolute statement is inconsistent with statewide labor data: during much of Christie’s tenure New Jersey experienced net job gains and a falling unemployment rate as part of the post‑recession recovery. The claim overstates the situation and ignores measured employment growth, though judgments about sufficiency or distribution of jobs are separate issues.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Small, bird‑sized and even smaller prototype drones with onboard cameras exist and consumer micro‑drones can operate indoors. Many modern drones can stream video in real time to a controller or cloud via Wi‑Fi or cellular, so recording a person inside a home and transmitting that feed immediately to the internet is technically possible, though it may require proximity, pilot skill, and power/connectivity resources.

claim: Paul Ryan would "outlaw in vitro fertilization."
rationale: There is no public record of Paul Ryan explicitly saying he would "outlaw" in vitro fertilization or sponsoring legislation to ban IVF. While Ryan has a strong anti-abortion record and has said he believes life begins at conception—positions critics say could imply restrictions on embryo-destructive IVF practices—those views do not equal a stated commitment to criminalize IVF. The specific claim that he would outlaw IVF is not supported by his documented statements or legislative record.

claim: "70 percent of the income tax that the state collects happens to come from Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk and New York City"
rationale: The assertion overstates what is supported by available revenue breakdowns. While New York City plus Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk do contribute a large share of the state's personal income tax receipts, most recent multi-year data and analyses put their combined share closer to the low‑60% range and it varies by year; the claim of a fixed 70% is not supported without a specific timeframe or source.

claim: "Politicians and their corporate lobbyists are trying to take away my right to spend my paycheck how I want."
rationale: The claim is an overly broad generalization without supporting evidence. While lawmakers and corporate lobbyists sometimes promote taxes, bans, regulations, or private-sector policies that limit or shape particular kinds of spending, that is not the same as a coordinated effort to remove individuals' general right to spend their earnings however they like. Most restrictions are targeted (e.g., illegal goods, age limits, sanctions) or aimed at fiscal policy rather than a wholesale denial of spending freedom.

claim: "Overdoses in Virginia (are) up 35%."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify: it gives no timeframe or metric (fatal overdoses, suspected overdoses, EMS runs, ED visits, or percent change from which baseline year). Virginia has seen increases in overdoses in some periods during the COVID era, but reported percentage changes vary by source and metric and are not universally 35%. Without a specified period and data source, the blanket statement cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: Available data on U.S. federal effective tax rates show million-dollar earners typically pay roughly two times (not four times) the effective rate paid by households around $100,000. For recent years the average federal income-tax rate for $100k earners is roughly 10–15% while for $1M+ it is often in the low-to-mid 20s percent, implying about a twofold difference rather than fourfold.

claim: U.S. Rep. Phil Gingrey wants public schools to teach women to "stay in their place."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reliable reporting that Rep. Phil Gingrey advocated that public schools should teach women to “stay in their place.” While Gingrey has a record of conservative positions on social and reproductive issues, the specific claim about instructing schools to teach women to stay in their place is not supported by documented statements or policy proposals from him.

claim: On extreme-risk guns laws, "This idea has passed Republican legislatures in other states and has been signed by Republican governors."
rationale: This claim overstates the case. While at least one high-profile example exists (Florida’s 2018 red‑flag/‘risk protection order’ measure was passed by a Republican‑controlled legislature and signed by Republican governor Rick Scott), the vast majority of extreme‑risk (red‑flag/ERPO) laws have been enacted in states with Democratic control; multiple Republican legislatures signing such laws is not the norm. The statement’s plural phrasing (“legislatures… governors”) implies a broader pattern that isn’t supported by the overall record.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: This is misleading. The Affordable Care Act introduced a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that can apply to capital gains, but it only affects taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income above statutory thresholds and only on net investment income after exclusions. Most primary-home sales that qualify for the $250k/$500k exclusion and taxpayers below the income thresholds are not subject to a blanket 3.8% tax.

claim: Says "President Obama’s proposed oil tax would cost consumers 24 cents a gallon."
rationale: This specific numeric claim is unsupported and misleading. There was no widely accepted official estimate tying any Barack Obama ‘‘proposed oil tax’’ to an unavoidable 24¢/gallon consumer increase; independent fact‑checks and economists noted that incidence of such a levy would vary with market conditions and would not translate to a fixed per‑gallon charge of 24 cents. Studies cited by proponents used debatable assumptions and other analyses produced smaller or uncertain pass‑through amounts.

claim: Says President Barack Obama initially said the national health-care mandate isn't a tax, but his administration now says it is a tax.
rationale: President Obama and other Democrats publicly described the individual mandate as a penalty and said it was not a tax when promoting the law. Later, the Obama administration’s legal briefs defending the Affordable Care Act asked the Supreme Court to uphold the mandate under Congress’s taxing power, effectively treating the payment as a tax for constitutional purposes. This reflects a change in public versus litigation framing rather than a simple contradiction in all contexts.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated and likely misleading because it omits jurisdiction and specifics; Attorney General guidelines differ by state/country and do not universally bar release of internal affairs records. In many places public‑records laws or courts require disclosure or only permit limited redactions, while AG guidance is often advisory or narrow rather than creating a blanket protection. Without the specific AG guideline and legal context, the assertion that he "can’t" release the record solely because of AG guidelines is not supportable.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy said, "If a Supreme Court Justice died one day before the election, it would be more Constitutional to indefinitely postpone the election than postpone the confirmation a single day."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that John F. Kennedy ever made this statement; the wording does not appear in his speeches, writings, or presidential archives and is not found in reputable quote collections. The line reads like a fabricated or misattributed remark inconsistent with Kennedy's documented public positions and normal constitutional practice regarding elections.

claim: People carrying guns can’t wear face masks to protect against the coronavirus because it’s a "class 4 felony."
rationale: This is false as a blanket claim. U.S. laws about masks and firearms vary by jurisdiction, and there is no general rule that wearing a face covering while carrying a gun is automatically a "class 4 felony." Some states have anti-mask or disguise statutes or specific rules about wearing coverings while committing or intending to commit crimes, but many jurisdictions explicitly allow medical face coverings or have no such prohibition.

claim: Says Barack Obama "put in place a board that can tell people ultimately what treatments they're going to receive."
rationale: This is false. The Obama administration did not create any federal board with authority to tell individual patients what treatments they must receive. Claims conflated entities created or referenced in the Affordable Care Act (like PCORI for research or the Independent Payment Advisory Board for system-level Medicare cost recommendations) with a hypothetical 'death panel,' but none of those bodies had legal power to dictate clinical care for specific patients.

claim: Says Nevada Gov. Steve Sisolak "has banned the use of an anti-malaria drug that might help cure coronavirus."
rationale: Gov. Steve Sisolak did not put a statewide ban on the anti‑malarial drug hydroxychloroquine as a cure for COVID-19. Nevada issued guidance and some limits intended to preserve supply and regulate off‑label prescribing in certain settings, but that was not an outright prohibition of the drug’s use.

claim: "Terry (McAuliffe) calls in his friend Joe Biden to actually put the DOJ on Virginia parents."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Terry McAuliffe personally called President Biden to order the DOJ to go after Virginia parents. The Biden administration did direct DOJ attention to threats and intimidation of school board members in 2021 after complaints and letters from school boards and attorneys general, and McAuliffe made public remarks critical of parent protests, but that is not the same as a verified direct call instructing the DOJ to target parents.

claim: Says CNN reported Ben Carson was "taking a break from campaigning" and the Cruz campaign "forwarded that news to our volunteers."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific two-part claim as stated. While media reported at various times that Ben Carson paused or scaled back campaigning for personal/family reasons, I find no clear evidence that CNN used the exact phrase "taking a break from campaigning" in a standalone report that the Cruz campaign then expressly "forwarded that news to our volunteers." Without a verifiable source or date, the attribution appears unconfirmed and potentially a mischaracterization.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, knowable action by Erika Harold (that she would knowingly favor an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple) but there is no public record of her saying she would make such a choice or of policies she enacted that amount to that outcome. While Harold has opposed same‑sex marriage in the past, opposition to marriage equality is not direct evidence she would explicitly prefer abusive caregivers; adoption placement is governed by statutory and child‑welfare procedures, not individual campaign promises. The claim appears to be rhetorical campaign language rather than a provable factual assertion.

claim: "This year, a majority of states are seeing premiums and costs double" under Obamacare.
rationale: The statement that a majority of states saw premiums and costs double in a single year under the Affordable Care Act is not supported by available marketplace and state insurance filing data. Year‑to‑year changes in benchmark premiums have typically been in the single- or low-double-digit percentages in most states, with only a few states or specific plans/counties seeing very large increases. Thus it is incorrect to say a majority of states experienced a 100% increase in premiums and costs in one year.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The statement implies a specific, recent major incident in Sweden "last night" caused by large numbers of arrivals; no widely reported nationwide event matching that description occurred. While Sweden did accept a relatively high number of refugees per capita in 2015–2016 and faces localized integration and crime challenges, the dramatic claim of unprecedented problems "like they never thought possible" and the reference to a specific nighttime incident is factually unsupported and misleading.

claim: Says "If Oregon’s Legislature simply authorizes $450 million for the CRC, it will … leave Oregon holding the bag for a great deal more cost responsibility."
rationale: Authorizing $450 million by itself would not automatically make Oregon legally responsible for unspecified additional CRC costs. Funding and ongoing liability would depend on subsequent appropriations, bond issuance terms, intergovernmental cost‑sharing agreements, and federal match conditions; critics raised plausible risk scenarios, but authorization alone does not guarantee Oregon would “hold the bag” for much larger overruns. The claim therefore overstates what a simple legislative authorization would cause.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The claim presents a precise number without specifying the election, time period, or who 'you' refers to, so it cannot be verified as stated. Official counts of out-of-state voters in Georgia depend on the specific election cycle, county, and ballot type and must be confirmed against state or county election records; absent that context the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: The claim is a broad causal assertion that under Rick Scott homeowners paid higher premiums for less coverage. While homeowners in Florida generally saw rising insurance premiums during Scott's governorship, those increases were driven by multiple factors (reinsurance costs, hurricane risk, insurers exiting the market) and evidence that coverage was uniformly reduced under Scott is mixed. Scott supported legal and regulatory changes intended to curb litigation/assignment-of-benefits abuse, which proponents say stabilized the market rather than systematically cutting coverage.

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn did vote against a reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act while serving in the House (notably opposing the 2013 reauthorization), and VAWA is federal legislation intended to protect victims of domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault. Her opposition was reported as based on objections to certain expansions in the bill (such as tribal jurisdiction and broader protected categories).

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I know of no reputable, widely cited study that projects Texas would lose up to $8.5 billion in GDP and 185,000 jobs specifically as a result of approving a bathroom-restrictions measure. Prominent economic analyses of similar laws (for example North Carolina’s HB2) estimated much smaller multi-year losses and far fewer jobs affected, so the specific figures here appear misattributed or inflated without a cited source.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. Local reporting and typical school-district practice indicate elections may have replaced one or more seats but not an entire school board at once (board terms are usually staggered), and any change to mask policy would require a board vote and compliance with state/county public-health rules rather than immediate unilateral removal. Without corroborating local news showing a full-board turnover and an immediate, legally effective end to a mask requirement, the blanket assertion is inaccurate.

claim: "The public option is not funded with public money. It's funded with private insurance premiums."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. 'Public option' proposals vary: some are designed to be financed primarily by premiums paid by enrollees, but many proposals include government involvement such as start‑up funding, subsidies for low‑income enrollees, risk‑stabilization payments, or potential taxpayer backstops. Therefore it is incorrect to say categorically that a public option is not funded with public money.

claim: "99 percent of all new income today (is) going to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While research (notably by Piketty and Saez) shows that in some specific years a very large fraction of measured income growth in the U.S. went to the top 1%, it is not true as a blanket statement that 99% of all new income "today" goes to the top 1% across time or consistently. The share of income gains captured by the top 1% varies widely by year, country, and by how "income" is defined (pre/post-tax, capital gains included, etc.).

claim: "Collusion is not illegal."
rationale: The blanket statement is incorrect. Many forms of collusion—such as price‑fixing, bid‑rigging, market allocation, and conspiracies to commit fraud—are illegal and prosecuted under antitrust and criminal statutes, even if the word “collusion” itself is sometimes a non‑technical term. Thus saying “collusion is not illegal” is misleading and false in most legal contexts.

claim: Says Wisconsin’s 2011-13 state budget contains "no fee increases"
rationale: Analyses of Wisconsin’s 2011–13 biennial budget (Act 32) show it included increases in various state fees and charges (for example, regulatory, licensing, and service fees), so the blanket claim that it contained “no fee increases” is incorrect. Public summaries and legislative analyses documented fee changes even where taxes were cut or shifted.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific claim that Bill McCollum spent more than $2.2 million last year on TV ads that featured “you” in almost every frame. The statement is highly specific but there is no publicly available corroboration in campaign finance reports or ad-buy disclosures, and the pronoun “you” and the timeframe are ambiguous. In absence of verifiable evidence, the claim is treated as likely false.

claim: "Half the kids coming out of college this year … can't find a job, or a job that's consistent with a college degree."
rationale: The claim that half of college graduates “can’t find a job, or a job that’s consistent with a college degree” is not supported by labor-market data. Official statistics and surveys show unemployment rates for recent college graduates are far below 50% and most graduates do find employment; estimates of underemployment (working in jobs that don’t require a degree) vary but are generally well under 50%. Without a precise year, cohort definition, or measure of “consistent with a college degree,” the specific 50% figure is not reliable.

claim: The federal government is sending refugees to states with governors who are "Republicans, not to the Democrats."
rationale: Federal refugee resettlement is not allocated based on governors' party affiliation. The federal government and its refugee resettlement partners place refugees primarily according to available sponsors, local resettlement agency capacity, existing community ties, housing and services, so refugees have been settled in both Republican- and Democratic-led states. While there have been political disputes and some short-term transfers of migrants, that is different from the formal refugee resettlement program.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: This is false. Medicaid is a joint federal-state program that continues to cover medically necessary inpatient and surgical care for eligible children, including emergency and congenital cardiac surgeries; there has been no federal policy that universally ended coverage for such life‑saving pediatric surgeries. Individual coverage can vary by state and by eligibility, but there was no blanket stoppage of these services.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely misleading: per‑pupil spending changed after the Great Recession but whether it is exactly $855 lower depends on the baseline year, the comparison year, and whether figures are inflation‑adjusted. North Carolina has often ranked below the national average, but its exact rank fluctuates and it is not consistently among the very lowest states across all common measures. Without a specific year and dollar‑type, the precise $855 figure and the categorical ranking cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: This specific claim is not supported by available official records and major reporting: credible data and news accounts do not document 18 children dying while physically in U.S. Border Patrol custody during the Obama administration (2009–2017). High-profile child deaths in CBP custody occurred in late 2018 under the subsequent administration, and overall counts of deaths in custody during Obama were far lower and involved adults more than children.

claim: "No one visiting Disney can get in" because of protest.
rationale: The claim is absolutist — that nobody visiting Disney can get in — and is not supported by typical protest outcomes. Protests sometimes delay access, close particular entrances, or lead to temporary or partial closures, but they rarely prevent all visitors from entering every Disney property. Without specifying which park, date, or scale of the protest, the universal wording is inaccurate.

claim: "99% of NJ voters do NOT support hunting."
rationale: The claim that 99% of New Jersey voters do not support hunting is implausible and unsupported by known evidence. No reputable poll or official statistic indicates near-unanimous opposition; New Jersey issues hunting licenses and maintains regulated hunting seasons, and public opinion on hunting is mixed rather than nearly unanimous. An extraordinary claim like 99% would require clear, recent, representative polling, which is not available.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely inaccurate as stated because it gives no clear time frame or scope, and known national super PAC fundraising totals for recent two-year election cycles are typically much larger than $180 million. While a small number of wealthy donors often supply a large share of super PAC money and corporations do contribute in some cases, the specific breakdown (half from fewer than 200 people and ~20% from corporations) is not supported by broad, public federal fundraising data without a cited source or defined period.

claim: After Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, "within 24 hours, Americans lost $100 billion from our 401(k)s."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Americans collectively lost exactly $100 billion from 401(k)s within 24 hours of the Brexit vote. News and market analyses at the time reported large global market-cap declines (measured in trillions) and sharp drops in U.S. equity indices, but no authoritative source produced the specific $100 billion 24-hour 401(k) figure; losses would vary by account allocation and are typically reported as broader market-cap or household-wealth changes over longer periods.

claim: "The governor’s cuts would kick over 8,000 people out of their homes."
rationale: The claim as written is unverified because it provides no jurisdiction, governor name, budget line, program, timeframe, or source for the 8,000 figure. I am not aware of any authoritative, general finding that any unspecified governor’s cuts would specifically force 'over 8,000' people from their homes; confirming such a precise impact requires an official impact analysis or independent modelling tied to a named policy. Without those specifics the precise numeric assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This claim is a decades-old urban rumor with no factual basis: Pepsi never admitted that an employee contaminated products with HIV/AIDS. Investigations and company testing in the 1990s found no evidence that beverages were contaminated, and there are no verified reports of HIV transmission via commercial soft drinks. Public health experts also note that HIV is not transmitted by drinking contaminated beverages under ordinary conditions.

claim: "Two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump not wearing a face mask in public."
rationale: The claim lacks a clear time or poll and overstates typical findings. National polls in 2020 about reactions to Trump not wearing a mask generally showed mixed and polarized views, with many results around half of Americans (or modestly above) disapproving — not a consistent two-thirds. No widely reported, consistent national poll established a stable ~66% disapproval figure across the electorate.

claim: Bing Energy said it decided to move to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s "plan to eliminate the corporate tax."
rationale: I found no reliable reporting or public statement showing a company called “Bing Energy” said it moved to Florida because of Gov. Rick Scott’s plan to eliminate the corporate tax. Moreover, Rick Scott is a U.S. senator, not the governor of Florida, so the attribution to “Gov. Rick Scott” is incorrect. The claim appears to be uncorroborated and likely conflates or misstates facts.

claim: "South Florida ranks No. 1 in the gap between wages and housing."
rationale: The claim is too vague and not supported by consistent, authoritative data: major housing-affordability analyses typically list places like San Francisco/Silicon Valley, New York, Los Angeles or Honolulu as having larger wage-to-housing gaps. South Florida (Miami area) has serious affordability issues but is not uniformly ranked No. 1 across standard measures and time periods. Without a cited source, the assertion that “South Florida ranks No. 1” is not verifiable and likely false.

claim: Says David Rivera "allowed House Republican leaders to strip key provisions from the STOCK Act" that would crack down on insider trading by members of Congress.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. David Rivera uniquely "allowed" House Republican leaders to strip key provisions from the STOCK Act. The 2012 STOCK Act was altered through the House amendment and voting process under Republican leadership, and responsibility for changes lies with leadership and the coalition of members who supported the amended measure rather than a single freshman member. Attributing the stripping of provisions solely to Rivera misstates how the legislative process and votes produced the final language.

claim: "If you became a Medicaid recipient through the Obamacare expansion, you are grandfathered in."
rationale: There is no federal "grandfather" protection that permanently preserves Medicaid coverage for people who enrolled under the ACA expansion. Medicaid eligibility is set and administered by states (within federal rules), and a state can change or end its expansion and alter eligibility subject to federal process; enrollees are not guaranteed lifetime coverage simply because they enrolled via expansion. Temporary procedural protections (e.g., until redetermination) may apply, but not a blanket permanent grandfathering.

claim: Rick Perry is "taking money away from hurricane victims" and diverting it to "remodel the Governor's Mansion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Governor Rick Perry directly diverted federally or state-designated hurricane relief funds to pay for a Governor's Mansion remodel. Reporting at the time shows mansion repairs and renovations were funded through state appropriations, private donations, or separate budget items, and federal disaster funds are tightly restricted for disaster-related uses. While Perry faced criticism over budget priorities, the specific claim that hurricane victims' money was taken and used for the mansion is not supported by documented funding records.

claim: "Biden wants to end Shareholder Capitalism.. that's your 401k..your pensions.. your retirement.. are you voting for that???"
rationale: This claim is false. The Biden administration has promoted policies encouraging companies to consider workers, communities, and long-term value (often described as broader stakeholder considerations), but it has not proposed abolishing shareholder capitalism or eliminating 401(k)s, pensions, or retirements. Retirement accounts are private and regulated under laws like ERISA, and ending “shareholder capitalism” would not automatically erase those vehicles and would require explicit legislation. There is no credible evidence of a plan to terminate Americans’ 401(k)s or pensions.

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: The claim is too broad and therefore false as stated. While some large insurers saw substantial gains in certain years after the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded coverage and created new markets, profitability has varied widely by company, market, and year; other insurers lost money or exited ACA markets. Whether insurers “made a fortune” depends on which companies, which years, and what metric (premiums, profits, or market value) are meant, so the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: On financial reform, there is "a million dollars being spent, per congressman, in lobbying expenses on this issue. (The) industry has four lobbyists per member of the House and Senate working on this."
rationale: The statement is an overreach. Public lobbying expenditure reports show the financial sector spent in the low hundreds of millions annually around the financial reform debates—well below $1 million per each of the 535 members of Congress—and while the industry employs many lobbyists, independent counts do not support a consistent ratio of four lobbyists per member specifically working on financial reform. The claim conflates overall industry lobbying and workforce with issue-specific spending and staffing.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific paired claims as stated. Publicly reported traffic fatality and motor-vehicle theft statistics are maintained by Milwaukee Police, state crime reports, and traffic authorities, and the precise figures (65 deaths from “reckless driving” in 2021 and >9,000 cars stolen, exactly double 2020) are not supported by widely cited official summaries; the phrasing conflates categories (reckless driving vs all traffic fatalities) and gives an exact doubling for thefts without a verifiable source. Given the lack of corroboration and ambiguity in definitions, the claim is not reliably true as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: Reporting at the time shows Gov. Tony Evers and his administration declined to name or punish the staffer who secretly recorded a private conversation with Republican legislative leaders. Evers' office publicly resisted demands for identification and said it would not be releasing personnel information or taking public disciplinary action, citing legal/privacy considerations and review processes.

claim: Children born today will carry a $30,000 share of the national debt.
rationale: The statement is misleading and unsupported: it gives a specific per-child dollar figure without defining which portion of federal debt is counted, when “today” is measured, or how a future generation would actually ‘carry’ the debt. Simple division of current U.S. federal debt by the number of births or children produces very different per-child numbers (much higher than $30,000) and ignores that debt burdens depend on future economic growth, taxation, and policy changes. Therefore the claim is an oversimplification and not reliably true as stated.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: While Texas has reported rising on‑time high school graduation rates in recent years and in some recent years reached record highs for the state, national adjusted cohort graduation rate data do not consistently place Texas as the third‑highest state. Multiple states (for example New Jersey, Massachusetts, Vermont, Iowa and others) routinely report higher 4‑year graduation rates, and the claim gives no year or metric to substantiate the specific "third‑highest" ranking.

claim: "One man (New Castle, Del., County Executive, Chris Coons) thought property taxes should be hiked almost 50 percent."
rationale: There is no credible record that New Castle County Executive Chris Coons proposed raising property taxes by almost 50%. Public budgets and contemporary reporting from his tenure do not show a near‑50% tax increase proposal; such large figures appear to be campaign-era exaggerations or misstatements rather than documented county policy proposals.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: There is no authoritative, publicly available nationwide dataset that consistently ranks cities by "staged automobile accidents," and similar tallies have come from insurance-company or local-law-enforcement reports with differing methods and timeframes. Because the claim lacks a cited source, specific year, and definition of "staged accidents," it cannot be reliably verified and is therefore judged false as stated.

claim: The IAEA, or the International Atomic Energy Agency, "last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it uses the ambiguous phrase "last month" without giving a date. While the IAEA has repeatedly reported at various times that Iran was not fully implementing its safeguards obligations (including reports up to mid‑2024), the specific assertion that the IAEA "last month said" this cannot be confirmed without a timestamp. Because of the missing timeframe the statement as presented is judged false.

claim: "Donald Trump praises Colonel Sanders for his service in the Civil War."
rationale: This is false. Harland “Colonel” Sanders, the KFC founder, was born in 1890—25 years after the U.S. Civil War ended in 1865—so he could not have served in that war, and there are no credible reports that Donald Trump praised him for Civil War service. The claim appears to conflate the honorific 'Colonel' with actual Civil War veteran status or confuse individuals with similar names.

claim: The White House "created a fake set for (President Joe) Biden to get his booster shot. The entire Biden presidency is one giant charade."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the White House 'created a fake set' to pretend President Biden received a booster; Biden's booster was administered publicly at the White House with medical staff and captured on video. Independent fact-checks and live footage contradict the assertion, and the added claim that 'the entire Biden presidency is one giant charade' is a subjective, untestable opinion rather than a factual statement.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Multiple epidemiological studies and public health reports found that Omicron infections have generally caused less severe disease, lower rates of hospitalization and death, and shorter illness than the Delta variant, not greater toxicity or mortality. There is no credible evidence supporting a claim that Omicron is five times more toxic than Delta; if anything, population-level severity metrics were lower for Omicron, especially where immunity from vaccination or prior infection was present.

claim: "Nationally, the unemployment rate for veterans is far greater than the national unemployment rate," and Wisconsin is "one of those rare examples where unemployment is actually lower for veterans than it is for the population as a whole and certainly lower than it is nationally."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and inconsistent with historical BLS patterns: veteran unemployment has varied by year and subgroup but has not been consistently or “far greater” than the national unemployment rate across the nation. State-level differences exist and Wisconsin has at times had lower veteran unemployment than the statewide non-veteran rate, but calling Wisconsin a rare exception and asserting a clear national contrast without a timeframe is unsupported.

claim: "Most of the people that work in finance make $70,000, $80,000 a year."
rationale: The claim is not supported because pay in the broad "finance" sector varies widely by role, experience, and country; many finance workers (e.g., tellers, administrative/back-office staff, entry-level analysts) earn below $70k while senior/investment roles earn well above $80k. Even U.S. aggregate statistics show a broad distribution (a median can lie near $70–80k for certain finance-related occupation groups) but that does not mean most workers fall within that narrow band.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz’s father met or was physically “with” Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK’s assassination. Multiple reputable fact-checks and archival investigations have found the circulated claims and photos are misidentified or unsubstantiated and uncovered no documentation linking the two men. The allegation appears to be a debunked conspiracy claim rather than a verified fact.

claim: The census "for years and years and years, decades, has asked, ‘Are you a citizen of the United States of America?’"
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. While questions about citizenship or nativity have appeared on some census schedules, sample/long-form questionnaires, and the ongoing American Community Survey for many years, the short-form decennial census sent to every household has not consistently asked “Are you a citizen of the United States of America?” for decades. Whether a citizenship question appeared has varied by census form and year, so the blanket statement that the census has continuously asked that exact question for decades is incorrect.

claim: Sherrod Brown "sent billions of our tax dollars to foreign countries."
rationale: The claim is misleading and incorrect as stated: a U.S. senator does not unilaterally "send" taxpayer dollars abroad. Senators vote on appropriations and foreign-aid packages as part of Congress, and while Sherrod Brown may have supported or opposed bills that included foreign assistance, there is no basis to say he personally sent billions of tax dollars to foreign countries.

claim: Obamacare is a "massive, massive income redistribution" with "$250 billion a year in Medicaid expansion (and) in the subsidy structure that's basically being paid for by people on Medicare, through Medicare cuts, and a lot of tax increases."
rationale: The claim misstates both magnitudes and who bears costs. The Affordable Care Act did include Medicaid expansion, premium subsidies, Medicare payment reductions, and new taxes/fees, but the commonly cited $250 billion per year figure for Medicaid expansion is far larger than CBO and CMS estimates and not supported as an annual steady cost; many ACA costs were offset by Medicare payment reductions and other revenue, and most tax increases target higher‑income earners or insurers rather than broadly shifting $250 billion/year onto Medicare beneficiaries. Overall the statement is an exaggeration and mischaracterization of ACA financing.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that half of the Ottawa Police Service submitted resignations en masse. Such a large, newsroom-impacting event would have been widely reported and confirmed by official Ottawa Police Service statements or municipal officials, but no reliable sources corroborate this claim. It appears to be false or a misunderstanding of other staffing/leave issues.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or legal finding that Alex Sink personally engaged in predatory lending. While she has a background in banking and was the Florida Chief Financial Officer, accusations tying her to predatory lending have appeared as political attacks and are not substantiated by mainstream reporting or regulatory actions.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: There is no authoritative, widely accepted evidence that Wisconsin’s middle class is definitively the “most diminished” in the United States. Different studies use different metrics (share of middle-income households, income growth, mobility, job composition) and they rank states differently; Wisconsin does not consistently top such lists across credible analyses. The claim overstates the case without specifying the metric or time period.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: There is no clear record that Sen. Kelly Ayotte cast a vote for a Senate or House budget resolution that explicitly enacted $90 billion in Pell Grant cuts. Analyses that cite roughly $90 billion in Pell reductions refer to specific House GOP/Paul Ryan budget proposals or policy proposals scored over a decade, not to a single enacted budget that she voted to pass. Because the claim conflates different budget proposals and vote records, it is not supported as stated.

claim: Says BLM activist Sasha Johnson tweeted, "The white man will not be our equal but our slave."
rationale: This claim is false. Independent fact-checkers and searches of Sasha Johnson's verified accounts and public archives found no evidence she tweeted that phrase, and the circulating screenshot was determined to be manipulated or misattributed (often originating from parody/other accounts).

claim: Says Nelson Mandela "was a communist."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Mandela worked closely with the South African Communist Party, accepted its help, and was influenced by Marxist ideas, but he did not consistently describe himself as a Communist Party member or simply ‘a communist.’ Historians note strong ties and ideological overlap, yet Mandela more commonly presented himself as a democratic socialist and emphasized a broad anti-apartheid coalition rather than formal party allegiance.

claim: Says Sen. Kay Hagan "has missed half of the (Senate Armed Services) Committee's hearings in 2014."
rationale: Public attendance records and independent fact-checking do not support the assertion that Sen. Kay Hagan missed half of Senate Armed Services Committee hearings in 2014. She missed some sessions, but the claim overstates her absences and depends on a narrow or misleading counting of what counts as a 'hearing.'

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse used his COVID-19 stimulus check to purchase the AR-15 he used in the fatal Kenosha shooting."
rationale: Contemporary news reporting and court records indicate the AR-15-style rifle Rittenhouse used was obtained from an adult associate, not purchased by Rittenhouse himself. Rittenhouse was 17 at the time and could not legally buy a long gun through a licensed dealer, and there is no credible evidence or documentation that a COVID-19 stimulus payment was used to buy the weapon.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim gives a single absolute number with no timeframe or place, which is misleading. While a frequently cited U.S. estimate from older studies and federal reports has put the annual count of pregnant people experiencing intimate partner violence at roughly 300–325,000, estimates vary widely by year, data source, definitions, and country, so the naked statement as presented is not verifiable as a general fact.

claim: Cuts in local government and school funding in John Kasich’s budget caused "many communities to seek school levies, local tax increases, layoffs."
rationale: After Kasich’s 2011-2012 state budget significantly cut the Local Government Fund and reduced direct school aid, reporting at the time documented numerous Ohio school districts and municipalities responding by placing levies on ballots, raising local taxes, cutting services and enacting layoffs. While not every single locality was affected, the pattern of state aid reductions prompting local levies and personnel reductions was widely observed.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare."
rationale: There is no clear public record of Donald Trump explicitly saying he wants to remove thousands of children from Wisconsin’s BadgerCare. While Trump has supported policies—like lowering federal Medicaid funding, block grants, or allowing state waivers with work requirements—that critics say could indirectly reduce coverage, those proposals are not the same as an explicit intent to ‘‘kick thousands of kids off BadgerCare.’’

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: The claim portrays Texas Department of Agriculture as merely mailing stickers while retailers calibrate pumps unobserved. Weights-and-measures programs (including Texas') require official inspection/sealing or use of licensed service agents; retailers may perform routine maintenance but that does not substitute for official certification. While some jurisdictions have faced inspector staffing challenges, there is no substantiated evidence that TDA routinely sends stickers without inspection and lets H-E-B/Brookshire self-certify statewide.

claim: "On average, women make 77 cents for every dollar men make."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplified and outdated summary. The oft‑repeated “77 cents” figure comes from specific years and particular (unadjusted) measures of median earnings for U.S. women versus men; more recent unadjusted estimates are closer to about 80–83 cents and the gap changes substantially when controlling for hours, occupation, education and experience. Therefore the absolute claim that “on average, women make 77 cents for every dollar men make” is not accurate as a general, current fact.

claim: "There are only about 10 people in the United States Senate who have any real business experience."
rationale: The claim is false because far more than roughly ten U.S. senators have had substantive private‑sector business careers. Many current and recent senators served as company founders, CEOs, executives, investors or small‑business owners (for example, Mitt Romney, Rick Scott, Ron Johnson, Mark Warner and multiple others), so the count is well above ten. The statement is implausibly low given senators' varied pre‑political backgrounds.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There are well-documented instances where brand drug makers paid generic manufacturers to delay market entry — known as "pay-for-delay" or reverse-payment settlements — and regulators have called the practice anticompetitive. The U.S. FTC, court cases, and academic studies have documented these payments and their effect in keeping prices higher by postponing generic competition. However, the practice is not necessarily universal to every drug or company.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement overstates the comparison. Analyses of post‑recession labor markets show the 2007–2009 job recovery was unusually slow and is commonly described as the slowest since World War II, but the Great Depression era under Hoover/Roosevelt had far longer and deeper job losses. Saying it is the slowest “since Hoover” is inaccurate without very specific metrics and timeframes.

claim: "Jeb Bush recently noted, Reagan himself would have been too moderate, too reasonable for today's GOP."
rationale: I could not find a verified recent attribution of that exact claim to Jeb Bush in news coverage or transcripts through mid-2024. While commentators and some Republicans have argued that Reagan would be viewed as more moderate by today’s GOP, there is no clear, widely reported quote showing Jeb Bush recently saying Reagan himself would be “too moderate, too reasonable.” The claim appears to conflate a common opinion with a specific recent remark by Jeb Bush that isn’t substantiated.

claim: "The KKK was formed by the Democratic Party."
rationale: The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1865 in Pulaski, Tennessee by a small group of former Confederate veterans as a secret vigilante organization, not by the formal Democratic Party. While many early Klan members and much of Southern white politics at the time were aligned with the Democratic Party, that is not the same as the party formally creating the KKK.

claim: "I did not support the war in Iraq … The record shows that I’m right."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “I” refers to; whether someone did or did not support the Iraq War is a factual question answerable only by checking that individual’s voting record and public statements. Many public figures did vote for or against the 2002 Iraq War authorization, so without a named speaker the assertion cannot be confirmed and is treated as false under the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "Over the last several years, 40 percent (of) the jobs created in Texas were created for illegal aliens."
rationale: No credible data show that 40% of jobs created in Texas over recent years went to undocumented immigrants. Government labor statistics and research organizations report that unauthorized immigrants constitute only a modest share of the state workforce, and studies of job growth do not attribute nearly that large a share to undocumented workers. The claim appears to be an unsupported exaggeration or misinterpretation of employment data.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: Sarah Palin did quote the proverb "don't change horses in midstream" when discussing leadership and the Iraq war and sometimes invoked Lincoln in that context, but historians and primary-source checks show Abraham Lincoln did not actually say that phrase. The line is a later proverb/misattribution rather than a documented Lincoln quotation, so saying she was repeating Lincoln's words is incorrect.

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: This claim is misleading. State-by-state federal receipts vs. taxes data show Texas' net balance fluctuates by year and measure; Texas has been a modest net recipient in some years but is often close to parity rather than routinely getting "a lot more" than it pays. The size of any surplus is typically much smaller than the large imbalances seen in the states that are clear net recipients, and results depend on the time period and whether per‑capita or total figures are used.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "opposed Obamacare, didn't like the fact we didn't push a single-payer option."
rationale: Bernie Sanders has long criticized the Affordable Care Act as insufficient and has publicly said he opposed it for not going far enough. He has repeatedly argued the Democratic effort should have pushed a single‑payer/Medicare‑for‑All approach and introduced single‑payer legislation himself. These positions are well documented in his speeches and policy proposals.

claim: Says $6 billion projected to accumulate in the state’s rainy day fund is already used.
rationale: The statement conflates a projection with an actual balance. A projected $6 billion in a state's rainy day fund refers to an estimated future accumulation, not funds that have already been spent; unless there is specific evidence the legislature appropriated or diverted those dollars, the claim is incorrect. Without identifying the state and time period, there is no basis to assert the projected amount is already used.

claim: Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. His family publicly stated he died of natural causes, and mainstream fact-checkers and news organizations found no medical documentation linking his death to vaccination. Claims tying the vaccine to his death were debunked and rely on speculation rather than verified medical findings.

claim: "Wisconsin’s economy is in the best shape it’s been since 2000."
rationale: The statement is vague and not verifiable as written: "best shape" depends on specific metrics (unemployment, GDP, wages, labor force, etc.) and a date of comparison. While Wisconsin has seen low unemployment in recent years, other indicators such as GDP per capita, wage growth, and manufacturing employment have produced mixed results since 2000, so a blanket claim that the economy is the best since 2000 is unsupported without metric-specific evidence.

claim: "920 women lose their unborn babies after getting vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and lacks essential context (which vaccine, timeframe, or data source). It appears to conflate raw adverse-event reports with proven causation; surveillance systems and peer-reviewed studies have not shown COVID-19 vaccines increase miscarriage rates and observed pregnancy loss after vaccination is consistent with background rates. Therefore presenting a standalone figure of “920” as evidence of vaccine-caused fetal loss is misleading.

claim: "While 38 percent of (firearms) dealers that were inspected in 2011 were noncompliant with federal law, only 0.05 percent of inspected dealers had their licenses revoked."
rationale: I cannot confirm both percentages from authoritative ATF annual reports for 2011; while ATF inspections commonly find a substantial share of dealers with record-keeping or other violations, the claim’s specific figures (38% noncompliant and only 0.05% license revocations) appear to conflate different measures and enforcement categories. ATF reporting distinguishes ‘violations/deficiencies’ found during inspections from enforcement outcomes (administrative actions, denials, suspensions, revocations), so presenting those two numbers without context is misleading and not reliably supported by available summaries.

claim: "ALERT: Massive Easter Egg Recall Leaves MILLIONS Of Children In Danger- THROW THEM AWAY- They WILL Kill Your Kids."
rationale: The message is a vague, hyperbolic social-media style alert with no specific product, brand, date, or official recall reference. Major product recalls are announced publicly by regulators and manufacturers with detailed information; there is no evidence of any blanket 'massive Easter egg' recall that would 'kill' children. Such viral warnings are commonly exaggerated or fabricated.

claim: Small businesses "create 70 percent of the jobs in America."
rationale: That statement is inaccurate as written. Small businesses do not account for 70% of total U.S. jobs — they employ roughly about half of private‑sector workers — and the share of net new jobs created by small firms varies by timeframe and firm age. The 70% figure is sometimes cited for specific periods or for job creation by young startups, but it is not a correct characterization of total employment.

claim: A photo shows a recent White House event was actually filmed at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to support the claim as stated and no corroborating documentation provided. Official White House events are normally photographed and published by White House photographers and venues have distinctive architectural and heraldic markers; without image metadata, provenance, or an authoritative statement linking the photo to Tyler Perry Studios, the assertion is unverified and likely false.

claim: "US Capitol raided 2/2/21."
rationale: The well-documented breach of the U.S. Capitol occurred on January 6, 2021, when supporters of then-President Trump stormed the building. There are no credible reports or official records of a separate “raid” on February 2, 2021; the claim confuses or misstates the date.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally “set” Florida to a winner‑take‑all allocation specifically to deny Trump delegates. State party rules determine delegate allocation and Florida’s Republican Party adopted winner‑take‑all provisions before the 2016 contest; candidates may have supported or benefited from those rules but that is different from orchestrating them to target one rival. Reporting at the time did not substantiate a behind‑the‑scenes conspiracy by Bush and Rubio to block Trump’s delegates.

claim: Says Rep. Betty Sutton supports allowing "welfare fund withdrawals from strip clubs, casinos and liquor stores."
rationale: This claim misstates Sutton’s position. Contemporary fact-checks and reporting show she did not campaign for or explicitly endorse allowing welfare cash withdrawals at strip clubs, casinos or liquor stores; the allegation grew out of a specific vote or procedural stance that critics framed as endorsing such uses, but she did not advocate permitting those withdrawals. The claim therefore distorts the record.

claim: Says Texas ranks 44th nationally in education funding per pupil.
rationale: The statement gives a specific rank but provides no year or data source; per‑pupil funding rankings change by year and methodology. While Texas has often ranked in the low 40s in some recent datasets, I cannot verify the blanket claim that it ranks 44th without a specified year/source, so the precise assertion is not confirmed.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vietnamese authorities or a large portion of the population have been systematically killing and eating black cats as a COVID-19 cure. Multiple news organizations and fact-checkers reported the story as a rumor/misinfo and Vietnamese health and veterinary authorities denied any official recommendation to consume cats; isolated incidents of animal abuse linked to fear of the virus have been reported but do not support the broad claim.

claim: Rob Portman’s "plan to tax, slash and privatize" Social Security "would devastate Ohioans."
rationale: The characterization that Rob Portman has a specific “plan to tax, slash and privatize” Social Security is misleading. There is no record of Portman proposing outright privatization or a coordinated plan framed exactly that way; he has supported Republican fiscal reforms and some deficit-reduction measures critics say would reduce benefits for some beneficiaries, but labeling his positions as an explicit ‘tax, slash and privatize’ plan misstates the public record. The claim’s second half — that it “would devastate Ohioans” — is a subjective impact statement that lacks quantifiable proof and depends on which reforms are implemented and how.

claim: "Australia Closing Borders in a few hours for 6-months"
rationale: The claim states Australia will close its borders in a few hours for six months but provides no source or official announcement. Major border closures are nationally declared policies that are widely reported and were last used broadly during the COVID-19 pandemic; there was no verified government announcement as of mid‑2024 indicating an imminent six‑month shutdown. Without an authoritative source, the claim appears to be a rumor or misinterpretation of past events.

claim: Says there's a "100-year-old international norm not to use chemical weapons."
rationale: There has long been an international prohibition on the use of chemical weapons: the Hague Conventions already restricted asphyxiating gases at the turn of the 20th century and the 1925 Geneva Protocol explicitly banned their use in war. That prohibition was later codified and strengthened by the Chemical Weapons Convention (opened in 1993, entered into force 1997). Saying there is a “100‑year‑old” norm is a reasonable, if approximate, summary of this long‑standing international norm against chemical weapon use.

claim: "‘TrumpCare’ would allow insurance execs to personally make millions off your health care."
rationale: The claim is misleading. For‑profit insurers and their executives already earn large compensation under current law; no well‑defined version of “TrumpCare” uniquely or explicitly creates a new legal mechanism that suddenly lets executives personally take millions. While proposed Republican plans (e.g., AHCA/BCRA-style rollbacks of ACA rules and Medicaid funding) could plausibly increase insurer profits, that is different from a direct, novel authorization for executives to personally extract millions tied to an individual's care.

claim: Says Sen. Cory Booker wants to require a federal license for gun owners but criticizes voter ID laws as discriminatory.
rationale: Sen. Cory Booker has publicly supported stronger federal gun controls including proposals and statements endorsing a federal licensing requirement for gun purchasers/owners. He has also repeatedly criticized strict voter ID laws as discriminatory and intended to suppress minority turnout. Both positions are part of his documented public statements and policy positions on guns and voting rights.

claim: President Obama, Sen. Harry Reid and Rep. Nancy Pelosi passed a "$1.2 trillion stimulus bill."
rationale: The major 2009 stimulus backed by President Obama and congressional Democrats was the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, which was enacted at about $787 billion in budgetary cost, not $1.2 trillion. Also the President signs legislation rather than "passes" it; Harry Reid and Nancy Pelosi led Democratic chambers that supported the bill. Some counts that combine other tax provisions or later measures can yield larger multi‑year totals, but the specific claim that they "passed a $1.2 trillion stimulus bill" is inaccurate.

claim: "When Abraham Lincoln made the Gettysburg Address speech, the great speech, do you know he was ridiculed? He was ridiculed."
rationale: Contemporary accounts show that while the Gettysburg Address later became celebrated, some newspapers and commentators at the time did mock or criticize Lincoln’s brief, unconventional speech. So the claim that he was ridiculed is accurate in that a portion of contemporary reaction was derisive, though it was not universal.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unverified because it gives no specific election, office, or metric for “unusually close.” Whether an election was unusually close depends on measurable quantities (national popular‑vote margin, electoral college margin, margin in key states, turnout, recounts) and historical comparisons; without those specifics the assertion cannot be substantiated. Given the ambiguity and the fact that many elections are considered unusually close by at least one standard, I judge the blanket claim false.

claim: Oregon Rep. Tina Kotek, D-Portland, has "never held a job nor run a business"
rationale: This is false. Tina Kotek served as an elected Oregon state representative from 2007 to 2023 (including multiple years as Speaker), which is a paid public job, and she has held other professional roles in nonprofit/advocacy and government work prior to and during her legislative career. Saying she "never held a job nor run a business" contradicts her documented employment in public office and other positions.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: This is false. Social Security is a government-run, statutory social insurance program funded by payroll taxes and backed by law and the Treasury, not a secret fraudulent scheme that relies on recruiting new investors. Although it operates on a pay-as-you-go basis (current workers’ taxes fund current beneficiaries) and faces long-term solvency challenges, its benefits are explicit legal entitlements and the system lacks the deception and personal enrichment that define a Ponzi scheme.

claim: "'Wrong precinct' rules exacerbate our provisional ballot problems (and) HB 194 does nothing to solve the wrong-precinct problem."
rationale: This claim cannot be verified as stated because it lumps a general procedural issue (voters casting provisional ballots when at the wrong precinct) with a specific legislative text (HB 194) without identifying the jurisdiction. Whether wrong-precinct rules worsen provisional-ballot problems is context-dependent, and whether HB 194 addresses that depends entirely on the bill’s actual provisions and the state’s election structure, neither of which are specified. Because the necessary jurisdictional and textual details are missing, I cannot confirm the categorical assertion that HB 194 does nothing to solve the problem.

claim: Political activists are "being paid" to protest members of Congress.
rationale: The claim as stated is a broad, unsupported generalization. While isolated incidents exist where organizers or contracted individuals received payment or reimbursements, most protests are volunteer-driven or run by advocacy organizations with paid staff; there is no credible evidence that activists broadly are being paid to protest members of Congress. Accusations of universal "paid protestors" are commonly used as partisan smears without substantiation.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that human meat has been found in any McDonald’s meat processing facility; such sensational claims have been repeatedly debunked by independent fact‑checkers and rely on anonymous social media posts. McDonald’s uses regulated beef suppliers and meat-processing plants subject to inspection and traceability requirements, and discovery of human remains in a commercial processing plant would generate major verified reporting and legal action. The claim matches a common pattern of viral hoaxes rather than documented incidents.

claim: Dr. Phil and other celebrities are endorsing CBD gummies.
rationale: While many celebrities have publicly promoted or launched CBD products, there is no well-documented, verifiable evidence that Dr. Phil has endorsed CBD gummies. The claim likely conflates other celebrity CBD endorsements with an attribution to Dr. Phil or stems from misattributed/unauthorized uses of his likeness. Without clear, credible proof of Dr. Phil’s endorsement, the statement is unreliable.

claim: "The country is now in a manufacturing recession."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it does not identify which country or what time period is meant, and no evidence is provided. Whether a country is in a "manufacturing recession" requires recent, country-specific indicators (e.g., two consecutive quarters of declining manufacturing output or GDP, PMI below 50, falling manufacturing employment), so the blanket statement cannot be confirmed and is treated as false without supporting data.

claim: President Barack Obama’s policies "have resulted in gas prices being reduced from $3.07 per gallon when he was sworn in in 2009 to $2.30 today."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate on both the price baseline and the causal attribution. The U.S. national average pump price around Obama’s Jan 20, 2009 inauguration was substantially lower than $3.07 (roughly ~$1.80–$1.90), and gas prices fluctuate over time; any drop to ~$2.30 at a later date reflects global oil market forces and business cycles rather than solely "Obama’s policies."

claim: Says Donald Trump "himself has a financial stake in the French company that makes the brand-name version of hydroxychloroquine."
rationale: The brand-name hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) is produced by French drugmaker Sanofi, but there is no evidence that Donald Trump personally owned direct stock in Sanofi. His publicly filed financial disclosures list mutual funds and other assets whose underlying holdings could theoretically include foreign drug stocks, but those are indirect and not the claimed personal stake in the company. Multiple fact-checks and disclosures did not show a direct Sanofi shareholding by Trump himself.

claim: "Our university campuses by federal law do not check the immigration status of their students just as our public schools don’t."
rationale: There is no blanket federal law that forbids colleges and universities from checking students’ immigration status. K–12 public schools are limited by the Supreme Court’s decision in Plyler v. Doe (1982), which prevents denying access to children based on immigration status, but higher-education institutions routinely verify status for purposes like in‑state tuition, federal financial aid (FAFSA), and international student visa compliance (SEVIS). Some privacy laws (FERPA) and institutional policies may restrict sharing of status, and some states limit verification, but the claim as stated is inaccurate.

claim: "The richest 1 percent have more financial wealth than the bottom 95 percent combined."
rationale: The claim is presented without scope (global vs. national) or a definition of "financial wealth." Broadly cited global estimates (e.g., Credit Suisse) put the top 1% at roughly 40–45% of total global wealth, which is not generally larger than the combined share of the bottom 95%; while in some countries or for narrow measures of financial assets the top 1% may dominate, the unqualified universal claim is unsupported. Because the statement omits time, place, and asset definition, it cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: There is no general rule that landlords or authorities must refund rent simply because it was paid in March or April. Some local emergency rules, relief programs, or court orders in specific places and times provided rental assistance or limited refunds, but there is no blanket, universal right to get those months’ rent back.

claim: Says the Congressional Budget Office "is expecting a protracted economic malaise for at least the next decade under current policies."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. The Congressional Budget Office publishes projections showing slower economic growth and rising deficits under current-law assumptions, but it did not state or quote a judgment that it “is expecting a protracted economic malaise for at least the next decade.” The CBO uses technical forecasts and caveats rather than that normative phrasing.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The statement is an overly broad, universal claim that cannot be true in all contexts. Earnings for 'welders' versus 'philosophers' vary widely by country, experience, employer, and whether 'philosopher' refers to academic professionals, independent scholars, or people with philosophy degrees; some welders earn more than many philosophers, but many tenured philosophers or philosophy graduates in high-paying roles earn more than many welders. Because the claim lacks qualifiers it is misleading and therefore false as a blanket statement.

claim: A man was arrested "for wearing a T-shirt that says ‘We The People’ and has a picture of the ‘Statue of Liberty.’"
rationale: The claim as stated lacks any time/place details and I could not corroborate a credible news report of someone being arrested solely for wearing a ‘We The People’ T‑shirt with the Statue of Liberty. In the U.S. political clothing is generally protected speech and arrests for shirts typically involve additional conduct or context (trespass, disorderly conduct, court rules). Given absence of verifiable sources and the common pattern of viral misinformation about arrests for political apparel, the claim is likely false or at least unverified.

claim: "Regulations have quadrupled. The rate of regulations quadrupled under this president."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsubstantiated: it does not identify which president, what time period, or what metric of “regulations” (new rules, pages in the CFR, economically significant rules, etc.). Publicly reported regulatory metrics do not show a consistent four‑fold increase for any recent president once definitions and timeframes are specified. Without a precise measure and timeframe, the sweeping claim that the rate of regulations quadrupled is not supported.

claim: "Public sentiment in favor of collective bargaining and in favor of the unions has actually gone up as these governors, I think, have overreached and gone too far and tried to destroy the labor movement."
